notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Ptosis
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid beyond its normal position (normal upper lid covers the superior 1.5–2.0 mm of the cornea).
*   **Etiological Classification:**
    1.  *Neurogenic:* 3rd cranial nerve palsy, Horner syndrome (sympathetic paresis), Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome (synkinetic).
    2.  *Myogenic:* Myasthenia gravis (fluctuating, diurnal fatigue), myotonic dystrophy, congenital myogenic dystrophy.
    3.  *Aponeurotic (Involutional):* Disinsertion, dehiscence, or stretching of the levator aponeurosis (commonest in elderly; high lid crease).
    4.  *Mechanical:* Excessive weight of lid lesions (neurofibroma, chalazion, amyloidosis, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid).
    5.  *Traumatic:* Direct laceration or crush injury to the LPS muscle or its aponeurosis.
*   **Clinical Assessment:**
    *   *Amount of Ptosis:* Palpebral fissure height compared to normal eye (Mild: 2 mm; Moderate: 3 mm; Severe: ≥4 mm).
    *   *Levator Action (Burke’s Method):* Excursion of upper lid from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze while frontalis muscle is neutralized (Normal: ≥15 mm; Good: 8–14 mm; Fair: 5–7 mm; Poor: ≤4 mm).
    *   *Margin Reflex Distance-1 (MRD-1):* Distance from corneal light reflex to upper lid margin (Normal: 4–4.5 mm).
    *   *Bell’s Phenomenon:* Upward and outward rotation of eyeball on attempted forced eye closure (essential safety reflex before surgery).
*   **Surgical Treatment:**
    *   *Fasanella-Servat Procedure:* Tarso-conjunctivo-mullerectomy for mild ptosis (≤2 mm) with excellent levator action.
    *   *Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS) Resection:* Indicated for moderate to severe ptosis with fair-to-good levator action (≥5 mm).
    *   *Frontalis Brow Suspension (Sling Operation):* Indicated for severe ptosis with poor levator action (<4 mm) using autologous fascia lata or synthetic silicon rods.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Chalcosis Bulbi
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Specific systemic and ocular tissue degeneration resulting from the long-term retention of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) composed of copper alloys containing less than 85% copper (e.g., brass, bronze). *(Pure copper >85% induces violent acute suppurative panophthalmitis).*
*   **Pathophysiology:** Slow electrolytic dissociation releases cuprous ions, which possess a specific affinity for epithelial basement membranes throughout the ocular tunics without creating massive tissue necrosis.
*   **Characteristic Clinical Manifestations:**
    1.  **Cornea:** **Kayser-Fleischer (KF) Ring:** Golden-brown or greenish-yellow circumferential deposition of copper particles in the peripheral Descemet’s membrane.
    2.  **Crystalline Lens:** **Sunflower Cataract:** Characteristic powdery, brilliant golden-green opacity under the posterior lens capsule arranged in radial projections resembling petals of a sunflower.
    3.  **Iris:** Greenish discoloration (heterochromia) and sluggish pupillary response.
    4.  **Vitreous:** Liquefaction, syneresis, and strands impregnated with glistening copper flecks.
    5.  **Retina:** Deposition of brilliant metallic refractile golden plaques along retinal vessels and macula.
*   **Treatment:** Surgical extraction of the retained copper foreign body via pars plana vitrectomy; systemic chelation with D-penicillamine in refractory cases.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Orbital Cellulitis
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Severe acute suppurative bacterial infection of the intraorbital cellular tissue situated posterior to the orbital septum.
*   **Etiology & Sources:**
    *   *Direct Extension (Most common):* Secondary to paranasal sinusitis (ethmoiditis in children via lamina papyracea, frontal/maxillary sinusitis).
    *   *Exogenous:* Penetrating orbital trauma, post-evisceration/enucleation, retained foreign body.
    *   *Local Spread:* Facial erysipelas, dental root abscess, acute dacryocystitis.
    *   *Bacterial flora:* *S. pneumoniae*, *S. aureus*, *S. pyogenes*, *Haemophilus influenzae* (unvaccinated children).
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   Rapid onset of high-grade fever, prostration, severe deep retrobulbar pain aggravated by eye movements.
    *   Tense, brawny, dusky-red lid edema, intense conjunctival chemosis projecting through palpebral fissure.
    *   Marked axial proptosis (non-reducible, non-pulsatile).
    *   Painful limitation of all ocular movements (global external ophthalmoplegia).
    *   Rapid diminution of vision and Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) indicating optic nerve compression/ischemia.
*   **Management:**
    *   *Emergency Hospitalization:* Immediate systemic IV antibiotics: Ceftriaxone (1–2 g IV daily) + Vancomycin (1 g IV BD) + Metronidazole (500 mg IV TDS).
    *   *Supportive:* Analgesics, antipyretics, topical nasal decongestants, lubricant ointments.
    *   *Imaging:* Urgent Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of orbit and brain to detect subperiosteal abscess or intracranial extension.
    *   *Surgical Intervention:* Urgent drainage indicated if subperiosteal/orbital abscess is localized, vision deteriorates, or no clinical response occurs within 24–48 hours.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB)
notes.content:
*   **Inception:** Launched in **1976** as a 100% centrally sponsored scheme with the goal to reduce the prevalence of blindness from 1.38% (1974) to <0.3%.
*   **Newer Status:** Renamed in 2017 as **NPCB & VI** (*National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment*) under the National Health Mission (NHM).
*   **Revised Definition of Blindness (2017):** Aligned with WHO criteria: **Presenting visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye** (previously <6/60) [5].
*   **Objectives:**
    *   Reduce the backlog of avoidable blindness through identification and high-quality surgical cure of cataracts.
    *   Provide comprehensive primary, secondary, and tertiary eye care services.
    *   Decentralize operations through District Health Societies / District Blindness Control Societies (DBCS).
*   **Key Strategies and Components:**
    1.  *Cataract Blindness Control:* Shift from camp-based intracapsular surgeries to hospital-based IOL implantations (Manual SICS and Phacoemulsification). Free surgeries for underprivileged patients.
    2.  *Refractive Error Screening:* School Eye Screening (SES) programmes; free spectacle distribution to school-going children and near-vision presbyopic glasses to the elderly.
    3.  *Eye Banking & Corneal Transplantation:* Promotion of Voluntary Eye Donation ("National Eye Donation Fortnight": Aug 25 – Sept 8); Hospital Corneal Retrieval Programme (HCRP).
    4.  *Control of Childhood Blindness:* Prophylaxis against vitamin A deficiency, screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), and surgical management of congenital cataracts.
    5.  *Management of Emerging Non-Communicable Eye Diseases:* Diabetic Retinopathy screening/laser networks, Glaucoma clinics, and Tele-ophthalmology outreach units.

---

notes.title: Two Side Effects of Local Corticosteroid Therapy
notes.questionText: Two side effects of local corticosteroid therapy
notes.content:
1.  **Steroid-Induced Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma** (due to increased glycosaminoglycan accumulation and decreased outflow facility in the trabecular meshwork).
2.  **Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC)** and enhancement/reactivation of ocular infections (e.g., dendritic corneal ulcers from Herpes Simplex or Keratomycosis).

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Congenital Dacryocystitis
notes.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q15]]` (Paper 3 / General notes):
    *   *Etiology:* Non-canalization of the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct with persistent membranous obstruction at the **Valve of Hasner**.
    *   *Clinical Features:* Persistent epiphora starting within 1–2 weeks of life, sticky mucopurulent discharge, positive regurgitation test, non-tender swelling at medial canthus (mucocele).
    *   *Stepwise Management Protocol:*
        1.  *0–6 Months:* Conservative hydrostatic massage of the lacrimal sac (Crigler technique: 10 downward strokes, QID) + topical antibiotic drops. Cures >90% of cases.
        2.  *6–12 Months:* Lacrimal probing of NLD using a smooth Bowman's probe under local/general anesthesia if massage fails.
        3.  *1–2 Years:* Repeat probing $\pm$ Balloon Dacryoplasty or silastic intubation stenting.
        4.  *>3–4 Years:* Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) if all prior measures fail.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Vision 2020: The Right to Sight
notes.content:
*   **Inception:** Joint global initiative launched in **1999** by the **World Health Organization (WHO)** and the **International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB)** alongside international NGOs.
*   **Mission:** Eliminate avoidable (preventable and curable) blindness globally by the year **2020**.
*   **Target Diseases (Core Priorities):**
    1.  *Cataract* (High surgical output, IOL implantation, increasing Cataract Surgical Rate [CSR]).
    2.  *Childhood Blindness* (Vitamin A deficiency control, measles vaccination, congenital cataract, ROP).
    3.  *Trachoma* (Elimination via SAFE strategy).
    4.  *Refractive Errors & Low Vision* (School screening, affordable spectacles, low-vision clinics).
    5.  *Onchocerciasis* (River blindness control with Ivermectin/Mectizan distribution).
*   **Three Core Pillars of Implementation:**
    *   *Disease Control:* Targeted, cost-effective interventions for the 5 priority conditions.
    *   *Human Resource Development:* Training ophthalmologists, mid-level ophthalmic personnel (MLOP), optometrists, and community health workers.
    *   *Infrastructure & Technology:* Developing primary vision centers, secondary surgical eye centers, and tertiary centers of excellence equipped with appropriate, affordable technology.

notes.title: Siderosis Bulbi
notes.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q10]]` (Paper 1):
    *   *Definition:* Chronic degenerative changes resulting from retained iron-containing intraocular foreign bodies.
    *   *Mechanism:* Iron undergoes electrolytic dissociation, producing ferric ions that react with cellular proteins, selectively damaging epithelial structures.
    *   *Clinical Findings:* Rusty brown deposits in anterior lens capsule in a radial ring, heterochromia iridis (dark/rusty brown), pigmentary retinal degeneration mimicking retinitis pigmentosa, electroretinogram (ERG) showing progressive reduction in b-wave amplitude, secondary open-angle glaucoma.

```
   collagen lamellae & keratocytes, ~500 µm)
------------------------------------------------------
4. Dua's Layer (Pre-Descemet's acellular layer, 15 µm)
------------------------------------------------------
5. Descemet's Membrane (True basement membrane of
   endothelium, PAS-positive, 5–10 µm)
------------------------------------------------------
6. Endothelium (Single monolayer of hexagonal cells,
   metabolic pump, cell density 2500–3000/mm²)
======================================================
                 [ ANTERIOR CHAMBER ]
```

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Angular Conjunctivitis
notes.content:
*   **Etiology:** Caused predominantly by the **Moraxella axenfeld diplobacillus**; occasionally by *Staphylococcus aureus*. Infection resides in the nasal cavity and transfers to the eyes via fingers.
*   **Pathogenesis:** Moraxella produces a proteolytic enzyme (protease) that macerates the epithelium at the canthal regions where tears pool.
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   Symptoms: Persistent irritation, itching, burning, and white foamy discharge.
    *   Signs: Redness of the bulbar conjunctiva strictly localized near the canthi (inner and outer); excoriation and maceration of the surrounding skin of the lid margins at the angles; greasy, foamy discharge.
*   **Treatment:**
    *   Specific: Oxytetracycline 1% eye ointment or Chloramphenicol eye drops.
    *   Zinc therapy: Topical Zinc lotion/drops and Zinc oxide ointment (zinc inhibits the proteolytic enzyme produced by Moraxella).

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Signs of Anterior Uveitis (Iridocyclitis)
notes.content:
1.  *Ciliary (Circumcorneal) Flush:* Dull pinkish-violet deep perilimbal injection.
2.  *Keratic Precipitates (KPs):* Cellular deposits on corneal endothelium (Fine in non-granulomatous, Mutton-fat in granulomatous).
3.  *Aqueous Flare and Cells:* Flare due to protein leakage; cells floating in aqueous (graded 0 to +4).
4.  *Iris Changes:* Loss of normal pattern, muddy color, iris nodules (Koeppe's at pupillary border, Busacca's on stroma).
5.  *Pupillary Signs:* Miosed, irregular pupil; **posterior synechiae** (festooned pupil upon mydriasis).

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Complicated Cataract
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Cataract occurring secondary to chronic intraocular disease interfering with lens nutrition.
*   **Causes:** Chronic anterior uveitis/pars planitis (commonest), high degenerative myopia, retinitis pigmentosa, long-standing retinal detachment, absolute glaucoma.
*   **Clinical Features:** Typically begins as **posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC)**; presents early with "polychromatic luster" (iridescent particles of red, green, blue) and "bread-crumb" opacification; spreads diffusely through the cortex into a chalky white mature cataract with early calcification.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Difference between Paralytic and Non-Paralytic (Concomitant) Squint
notes.questionText: Difference between paralytic and non paralytic squint
notes.content:
| Feature | Paralytic (Incomitant) Squint | Non-Paralytic (Concomitant) Squint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Onset** | Acute, sudden | Insidious, gradual (early childhood) |
| **Angle of Deviation** | Incomitant (varies with gaze direction) | Concomitant (constant in all gaze directions) |
| **Primary vs Secondary Deviation**| Secondary deviation $>$ Primary deviation | Secondary deviation $=$ Primary deviation |
| **Ocular Movements** | Limited in field of paretic muscle | Full and unlimited |
| **Diplopia** | Binocular diplopia present | Absent (due to suppression / amblyopia) |
| **Head Posture** | Abnormal head posture (torticollis/turn) | Normal |
| **False Orientation** | Positive (past-pointing) | Negative |

notes.title: Difference between Optic Neuritis (Papillitis) and Papilledema

| Feature | Optic Neuritis (Papillitis) | Papilledema |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pathology** | Active inflammatory/demyelinating swelling | Passive edema secondary to raised ICP |
| **Laterality** | Usually Unilateral | Almost always Bilateral |
| **Visual Acuity** | Sudden, profound loss of vision | Normal (transient obscurations only) |
| **Pupillary Reaction**| Sluggish / Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD +) | Normal until late stages |
| **Pain** | Marked pain on eye movement | Absent (headache/vomiting present) |
| **Disc Elevation** | Usually $<2–3\text{ D}$ | Marked ($>2–6\text{ D}$, mushroom-shaped) |
| **Visual Field Defect**| Central or centrocecal scotoma | Enlargement of blind spot |

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Retinoblastoma Case (Leucocoria in a 2-Year-Old Child)
notes.questionText: A 2-year-old child is brought to the ophthalmology clinic by her parents after noticing a whitish reflex in the left eye while taking photographs. The parents report no history of trauma or infection but mention occasional misalignment of the left eye. On examination, the child has leucocoria in the left eye and strabismus. a) What is the most probable diagnosis b) Mention two differential diagnoses for leucocoria in a child c) Describe pathogenesis and investigations you would perform to confirm the diagnosis d) Describe the management plan for this child (1+2+3+4)
notes.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Left Eye Retinoblastoma (Intraocular Stage).**

#### b) Two Differential Diagnoses for Leucocoria in a Child
1.  *Congenital Cataract* (bilateral/unilateral, opacification within crystalline lens).
2.  *Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV) / PHPV* (microphthalmos, vascularized retrolental stalk).
3.  *(Alternatives: Retinopathy of Prematurity, Coats' Disease, Toxocara Endophthalmitis).*

#### c) Pathogenesis and Diagnostic Investigations
*   **Pathogenesis (Knudson’s Two-Hit Hypothesis):**
    *   Retinoblastoma is a malignant neuroepithelial tumor arising from primitive retinal photoreceptor precursor cells.
    *   Caused by homozygous loss/inactivation of both alleles of the **RB1 tumor suppressor gene** located on chromosome **13q14**.
    *   *Heritable (40%):* First mutation is germline (inherited or post-zygotic mutation in gametes); second hit occurs somatically in retinal cells $\rightarrow$ causes multifocal, bilateral tumors, and predisposition to secondary cancers (osteosarcoma, pineoblastoma [Trilateral Retinoblastoma]).
    *   *Non-heritable (60%):* Both hits occur somatically in a single retinal cell $\rightarrow$ unilateral, unifocal tumor; non-transmissible.
    *   *Histopathology:* Characterized by small round blue cells forming pathognomonic **Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes** (specific for photoreceptor differentiation), Homer-Wright rosettes, and calcified necrosis.
*   **Investigations:**
    1.  *Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA):* Bilateral direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation; plotting tumor number, dimensions, vitreous/subretinal seeding; IOP measurement.
    2.  *B-Scan Ultrasonography:* Demonstrates intraocular mass with characteristically high internal acoustic reflectivity and acoustic shadowing due to **calcification**.
    3.  *Non-Contrast CT Scan of Orbit and Brain:* Highly sensitive for tumor calcification and detects intracranial pineoblastoma or optic canal enlargement. *(MRI is preferred to avoid ionizing radiation).*
    4.  *MRI of Orbit and Brain:* Ideal to evaluate optic nerve invasion past the lamina cribrosa, extraocular spread, and intracranial pineoblastoma.
    5.  *Absolute Contraindication:* **Diagnostic Needle Biopsy (FNAC)** is strictly contraindicated due to the risk of extraocular tumor dissemination.

#### d) Management Plan
*   **Multimodal Staging (International Classification of Retinoblastoma - ICRB):**
    *   *Group A & B (Small, focal):* Chemoreduction followed by local consolidation.
    *   *Group C & D (Subretinal/vitreous seeds):* Systemic chemotherapy + local therapy.
    *   *Group E (Extensive, non-functional, secondary glaucoma):* Enucleation.
*   **Chemoreduction (Systemic Chemotherapy):**
    *   Standard **VEC Protocol**: Vincristine + Etoposide + Carboplatin administered every 3–4 weeks for 6 cycles.
*   **Local Consolidation Therapy:**
    *   *Transpupillary Thermotherapy (TTT):* Diode laser (810 nm) applied directly to small tumors (<3 mm).
    *   *Cryotherapy:* Triple freeze-thaw for anterior peripheral lesions.
    *   *Brachytherapy (Plaque Radiotherapy):* Iodine-125 or Ruthenium-106 radioactive plaques for localized refractory tumors.
*   **Targeted Chemotherapy:**
    *   *Intra-Arterial Chemotherapy (IAC):* Superselective catheterization of the ophthalmic artery infusing Melphalan/Topotecan.
    *   *Intravitreal Chemotherapy:* Melphalan for refractory vitreous seeding.
*   **Enucleation:**
    *   Indicated for Group E eyes (severe secondary glaucoma, anterior chamber involvement, opaque media), optic nerve invasion, or failure of conservative therapy.
    *   *Technique:* Long section of the optic nerve ($\ge 10–15\text{ mm}$) must be excised with the globe without puncturing the eyeball.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Trachoma
notes.questionText: Describe the etiopathogenesis, clinical features, complications and management of trachoma (2+3+2+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Etiopathogenesis
*   **Etiological Agent:** Obligate intracellular bacterium **Chlamydia trachomatis**; serovars **A, B, Ba, and C** are associated with hyperendemic blinding trachoma. (Serovars D–K cause inclusion conjunctivitis).
*   *Transmission:* Spreads via direct contact with ocular/nasal discharges of infected individuals, fomites (towels, clothing), and vectors (eye-seeking flies, *Musca sorbens*). Prevalent in dry, dusty climates with poor sanitation and overcrowding.
*   *Pathogenesis:* Chronic repeated reinfection triggers cell-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV reaction) to chlamydial heat-shock proteins, leading to lymphoid follicle formation, papillary hypertrophy, conjunctival scarring, and corneal pannus.

#### b) Clinical Features & WHO Grading (FISTO System)
*   **Symptoms:** Foreign body sensation, photophobia, tearing, chronic mucopurulent discharge, sticking of eyelids.
*   **WHO (FISTO) Simplified Grading:**
    1.  **TF (Trachomatous Inflammation - Follicular):** Presence of $\ge 5$ follicles (each $\ge 0.5\text{ mm}$ in diameter) on the upper tarsal conjunctiva.
    2.  **TI (Trachomatous Inflammation - Intense):** Severe inflammatory thickening of the upper tarsal conjunctiva obscuring $>50\%$ of normal deep tarsal blood vessels.
    3.  **TS (Trachomatous Scarring):** Presence of visible white fibrous bands or sheets of scarring on the tarsal conjunctiva (including Arlt's line in the sulcus subtarsalis).
    4.  **TT (Trachomatous Trichiasis):** At least one eyelash rubbing against the eyeball, or evidence of recent removal of in-turned lashes.
    5.  **CO (Corneal Opacity):** Easily visible corneal scarring over the pupil causing significant visual reduction ($<6/18$).
*   *Additional Classic Signs:*
    *   **Herbert’s Pits:** Circular pitted depressions at the limbus left behind by healed limbal follicles (pathognomonic).
    *   **Trachomatous Pannus:** Lymphocytic infiltration accompanied by superficial neovascularization invading the upper cornea.

#### c) Complications
*   Trichiasis and Cicatricial Entropion.
*   Corneal ulceration and secondary bacterial infections.
*   Severe dry eye disease due to destruction of goblet cells and accessory lacrimal ductules.
*   Symblepharon, tylosis (thickened lid margins), and ankyloblepharon.
*   Permanent bilateral blinding corneal opacities.

#### d) Management (The SAFE Strategy)
*   Endorsed by WHO for the Global Elimination of Trachoma (GET 2020):
    1.  **S — Surgery:** Bilamellar Tarsal Rotation (BTR) or Trabut procedure to correct trachomatous trichiasis (TT) and prevent corneal blindness.
    2.  **A — Antibiotics:**
        *   *Mass Drug Administration (MDA):* Single oral dose of **Azithromycin** (20 mg/kg up to 1 g) to all individuals in communities where TF prevalence in children is $\ge 10\%$.
        *   *Topical:* Tetracycline 1% eye ointment applied BD for 6 weeks.
    3.  **F — Facial Cleanliness:** Promoting regular face washing in children to remove ocular and nasal discharges that attract transmission flies.
    4.  **E — Environmental Improvement:** Improving access to clean water, constructing proper pit latrines, improving domestic waste disposal to reduce fly breeding populations.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Recurrent, bilateral, seasonal allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva, primarily affecting young boys (4–20 years) during hot summer months.
*   **Pathophysiology:** Combined **Type I (IgE-mediated)** and **Type IV (cell-mediated / Th2-lymphocyte)** hypersensitivity reaction to airborne allergens (pollen).
*   **Clinical Forms & Signs:**
    1.  *Palpebral Form:* Involves upper tarsal conjunctiva; hyperemic cobblestone / pavement-like giant flat-topped papillae coated with thick, ropy, stringy white discharge.
    2.  *Bulbar / Limbal Form:* Thickened, gelatinous confluent opacification around the limbus with discrete chalky-white elevated dots (**Horner-Trantas dots** composed of eosinophils and epithelial debris).
    3.  *Mixed Form:* Features of both palpebral and bulbar varieties.
    4.  *Vernal Keratopathy:* Punctate epithelial erosions, **Shield Ulcer** (transverse oval shallow epithelial defect in upper cornea), and vernal corneal plaques.
*   **Treatment:**
    *   *Mild/Seasonal:* Topical Mast Cell Stabilizers (Sodium Cromoglycate 2% QID) or Dual-action agents (Olopatadine 0.1% BD, Ketotifen).
    *   *Acute Exacerbations:* Short pulsed courses of weak topical corticosteroids (Fluorometholone 0.1%, Loteprednol 0.5%).
    *   *Severe / Steroid-Sparing:* Topical **Cyclosporine A (0.05%–1%)** or **Tacrolimus (0.03% ointment)**.
    *   *Shield Ulcer:* Debridement of plaque, topical antibiotics, cycloplegics, and amniotic membrane grafting if refractory.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO)
notes.content:
*   **Etiopathogenesis:** Thrombotic occlusion of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa. Predisposing factors: Hypertension, diabetes, arteriosclerosis, primary open-angle glaucoma, hyperviscosity syndromes.
*   **Types:**
    1.  *Non-Ischemic (75%):* Mild visual impairment, moderate venous dilatation and tortuosity, flame-shaped hemorrhages, mild disc edema. Good visual prognosis.
    2.  *Ischemic (25%):* Severe, sudden painless visual loss ($<6/60$), prominent RAPD, marked capillary non-perfusion ($>10$ disc areas on FFA), extensive intraretinal hemorrhages (**"blood and thunder" / "splashed tomato" appearance**), multiple cotton-wool spots, severe disc edema.
*   **Complications:** **Neovascular Glaucoma (100-day glaucoma)** occurring in ~20% of ischemic cases due to VEGF-induced rubeosis iridis; chronic cystoid macular edema (CME).
*   **Treatment:** Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) or intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) for macular edema; Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) if retinal or iris neovascularization develops.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Nerve Supply and Actions of Intraocular Muscles
notes.questionText: Describe the nerve supply and actions of intraocular muscles
notes.content:
1.  **Sphincter Pupillae Muscle:**
    *   *Nerve Supply:* Parasympathetic nerve fibers originating from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III) $\rightarrow$ ciliary ganglion $\rightarrow$ short ciliary nerves.
    *   *Action:* Pupillary constriction (Miosis).
2.  **Dilator Pupillae Muscle:**
    *   *Nerve Supply:* Sympathetic nerve fibers originating from the Ciliospinal Center of Budge ($C_8–T_2$) $\rightarrow$ superior cervical ganglion $\rightarrow$ carotid plexus $\rightarrow$ long ciliary nerves.
    *   *Action:* Pupillary dilatation (Mydriasis).
3.  **Ciliary Muscle:**
    *   *Nerve Supply:* Parasympathetic fibers via short ciliary nerves (CN III).
    *   *Action:* Contraction relaxes zonular tension on the lens capsule, increasing the curvature of the lens (Accommodation); opens trabecular meshwork to enhance aqueous outflow.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Case of Acute Anterior Uveitis (Iridocyclitis) with Joint Disease
notes.questionText: A 27 year old man presented to the Out Patient Department with severe pain in right eye radiating to right side of the face associated with redness, decreased vision, photophobia, mild degree of watering. Answer the following a) What other history will you elicit in this man in relation to joints b) What is the diagnosis c) What are the differential diagnosis d) What are the investigations you would request e) What is your treatment (1+1+3+2+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Joint History to Elicit
*   History of **lower back pain and morning stiffness** worsening with rest and improving with activity (suggestive of **Ankylosing Spondylitis / Spondyloarthropathy**; strongly associated with HLA-B27).
*   History of urethral discharge, burning micturition, and peripheral asymmetric oligoarthritis (Reiter syndrome / Reactive arthritis).
*   History of swelling, redness, and pain in small joints of the hands and wrists (Rheumatoid arthritis).
*   History of skin rashes, scaling over extensor surfaces, and joint pain (Psoriatic arthritis).

#### b) Diagnosis
**Right Eye Acute Anterior Uveitis (Acute Non-Granulomatous Iridocyclitis), likely HLA-B27 associated.**

#### c) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma:* Extremely high IOP, shallow anterior chamber, dilated vertically oval fixed pupil, steamy cornea without KPs.
2.  *Acute Mucopurulent Conjunctivitis:* Superficial conjunctival congestion, discharge, normal pupil, clear cornea, no ciliary tenderness.
3.  *Corneal Ulcer (Keratitis):* Fluorescein-staining epithelial defect, corneal infiltration.

#### d) Investigations
*   *Ocular:* Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (aqueous cells and flare, keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae), Applanation tonometry, B-scan USG (if posterior view obscured).
*   *Systemic:* HLA-B27 antigen typing, X-ray of Sacroiliac joints (sacroiliitis), ESR and CRP, Serum uric acid, CBC, Mantoux test, VDRL/Treponemal tests.

#### e) Treatment Plan
1.  **Mydriatic-Cycloplegic Agents:** **Atropine 1% eye ointment/drops TDS** or Cyclopentolate 1% TDS. Relieves painful ciliary muscle and pupillary sphincter spasm; prevents and breaks posterior synechiae; improves uveal blood flow.
2.  **Topical Corticosteroids:** **Prednisolone acetate 1%** or Dexamethasone 0.1% drops instilled hourly during the acute phase, tapered slowly over 4–6 weeks as intraocular inflammation regresses.
3.  **Periocular Injection:** Posterior sub-Tenon injection of triamcinolone acetonide (40 mg) in severe or refractory cases.
4.  **Systemic Anti-inflammatory Therapy:** Oral NSAIDs (Indomethacin, Naproxen) or oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg) in severe recalcitrant uveitis.
5.  **Dark Goggles & Hot Compresses:** Symptomatic relief for photophobia and deep ciliary pain.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Hypermetropia
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Refractive error where parallel light rays focus behind the retina with accommodation at rest.
*   **Etiological Types:**
    *   *Axial:* Short eyeball (1 mm shortening = +3 D).
    *   *Curvatural:* Flattened cornea or lens (1 mm increase in radius = +6 D).
    *   *Index:* Decreased refractive index of lens cortex in old age.
    *   *Positional:* Backward displacement of lens.
    *   *Aphakia:* Total absence of lens (+10 to +11 D error).
*   **Components:** Total = Latent (corrected by inherent ciliary tone) + Manifest (Facultative [corrected by accommodation] + Absolute [uncorrected]).
*   **Clinical Features:** Asthenopia (frontal headache, eye strain on reading), defective near vision earlier than distant vision, convergent accommodative squint in children, amblyopia.
*   **Treatment:** Optical correction with **highest plus (convex) spherical lens** giving maximum visual acuity; contact lenses; refractive surgery (Hyperopic PRK/LASIK, Conductive Keratoplasty).

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Scleritis
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Severe, destructive, chronic granulomatous inflammation of the sclera proper. Peak age 40–60 years; associated with systemic autoimmune disease in >50% (Rheumatoid Arthritis, Wegener's granulomatosis, Polyarteritis nodosa).
*   **Classification:**
    1.  *Anterior Scleritis (98%):*
        *   Non-necrotizing: Diffuse (commonest) or Nodular (immobile, deep purplish-red nodule).
        *   Necrotizing: With inflammation (vaso-occlusive, severe ischemia, scleral thinning) or Without inflammation (**Scleromalacia perforans** — painless melting of sclera in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis).
    2.  *Posterior Scleritis (2%):* Involves sclera posterior to equator; causes proptosis, exudative retinal detachment, choroidal folds.
*   **Clinical Features:** Deep, boring, excruciating ocular pain radiating to temple and jaw, waking the patient at night; deep violaceous/purplish scleral injection that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine 10%.
*   **Treatment:** Systemic NSAIDs (Indomethacin 75 mg BD) for non-necrotizing; oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg daily) or immunosuppressives (Methotrexate, Cyclophosphamide) for necrotizing scleritis. Topical steroids alone are ineffective.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Prednisolone Eye Drops
notes.content:
*   **Mechanism & Pharmacodynamics:** Synthetic glucocorticoid (Prednisolone acetate 1% / Prednisolone sodium phosphate 1%). Possesses potent anti-inflammatory, anti-allergic, and anti-fibrotic activity by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and decreasing capillary permeability, leukocyte chemotaxis, and fibroblast proliferation.
*   **Preparations:** Acetate suspension (superior corneal and intraocular penetration) vs. Sodium phosphate solution.
*   **Indications:** Acute and chronic anterior uveitis, postoperative inflammation following cataract/glaucoma surgery, allergic conjunctivitis (VKC flare-up), episcleritis, stromal keratitis, rejection prevention after keratoplasty.
*   **Ocular Adverse Effects:**
    1.  Ocular hypertension and secondary open-angle glaucoma (steroid responders).
    2.  Posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) with long-term use.
    3.  Exacerbation of fungal keratitis and herpes simplex dendritic ulcers (geographic melting).
    4.  Delayed corneal wound healing.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Optic Atrophy
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Degeneration and loss of axons of the optic nerve anywhere between the retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate body, accompanied by proliferation of glial tissue.
*   **Types & Ophthalmoscopic Appearance:**
    1.  *Primary (Simple):* Chalky-white disc, sharply demarcated margins, visible lamina cribrosa, normal retinal vessels. Causes: Multiple sclerosis, retrobulbar neuritis, compressive pituitary tumors.
    2.  *Secondary (Post-neuritic):* Dirty-white/grey disc, blurred indistinct margins, filled-in physiological cup, perivascular sheathing. Causes: Long-standing papilledema, papillitis.
    3.  *Consecutive:* Yellowish-waxy pallor, attenuated thread-like retinal arterioles. Causes: Retinitis pigmentosa, extensive chorioretinitis.
    4.  *Glaucomatous:* Deep, wide excavation/cupping reaching the disc margin, nasalization of vessels.
    5.  *Vascular (Ischemic):* Pallor of disc with attenuated vessels (AION).

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Ptosis - Definition
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Ptosis (blepharoptosis) is the abnormal downward drooping of the upper eyelid beyond its physiological level, covering more than the superior 2.0 mm (one-sixth) of the cornea in primary position of gaze.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Acute Microbial Keratitis in a Contact Lens Wearer
notes.questionText: A 25-year-old male complains of acute onset redness, pain, and photophobia in his right eye for the last two days. He has a history of contact lens use and admits to occasional non-compliance with lens hygiene. On examination, there is circumcorneal congestion, and fluorescein staining shows a central corneal ulcer with surrounding edema. a) What is the most likely diagnosis. b) List two differential diagnoses. c) How will you manage this condition. d) Mention the preventive measures for this condition in contact lens users. (1+2+4+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Most Likely Diagnosis
**Right Eye Acute Bacterial Corneal Ulcer (Microbial Keratitis), most likely secondary to *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* infection** (due to contact lens non-compliance). *Acanthamoeba* keratitis is a close co-suspect.

#### b) Two Differential Diagnoses
1.  *Acanthamoeba Keratitis* (strongly linked to contact lens wear cleaned with non-sterile water; characterized by severe pain out of proportion, perineural radial infiltrates).
2.  *Fungal Keratitis* (feathery margins, satellite lesions, hypopyon).

#### c) Management Plan
*   **Emergency Contact Lens Discontinuation:** Cease lens wear immediately; submit the contact lens, lens case, and storage solution for microbiological culture.
*   **Diagnostic Corneal Scraping:** Obtain immediate scrapings for Gram/Giemsa stain, KOH mount, and cultures (Blood, Chocolate, Sabouraud, Non-nutrient agar with *E. coli* overlay for *Acanthamoeba*).
*   **Intensive Topical Antibacterial Therapy:**
    *   *Fortified drops:* Fortified Tobramycin (1.3%) or Gentamicin alternating with Fortified Cefazolin (5%) or Vancomycin (5%) every 30–60 minutes round the clock.
    *   *Alternative:* Fourth-generation Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin 0.3%) 1-hourly.
*   **Cycloplegics:** Atropine 1% or Homatropine 2% BD to relieve ciliary spasm.
*   **Systemic Analgesics:** Ibuprofen/Paracetamol.
*   *Therapeutic Keratoplasty:* Indicated if non-responsive to antibiotics or if perforation supervenes.

#### d) Preventive Measures for Contact Lens Users
1.  Strict hand hygiene with soap and water before handling lenses.
2.  Never use tap water, homemade saline, or saliva to clean or rinse lenses or cases.
3.  Use only commercially available sterile disinfecting solutions; discard used solution daily (no "topping off").
4.  Clean, rinse, and air-dry the lens storage case daily; replace the storage case every 1–3 months.
5.  Strictly avoid overnight lens wear (sleeping with lenses in place increases ulcerative keratitis risk 5- to 10-fold).
6.  Remove lenses before swimming, showering, or using hot tubs.
7.  Immediate removal and ophthalmic consultation at the earliest sign of redness, irritation, or pain.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Case of Acute Anterior Uveitis Associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis
notes.questionText: A 40 year old female patient came to casualty with pain in her left eye associated with defective vision and intolerance to light for the last 3 days. she gives history of joint pain and morning stiffness of her hand for the last 10 years. On examination there is circum corneal congestion and sluggish pupillary reactions in her left eye a) What is the most probable diagnosis b) Name four conditions causing circum corneal congestion c) Describe the clinical signs you will get in this patient on detailed ocular examination d) Outline the investigations e) Write the treatment and rationale for the drugs you will use for this patient (1+2+2+2+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Left Eye Acute Non-Granulomatous Anterior Uveitis (Iridocyclitis)** associated with systemic autoimmune disease (**Rheumatoid Arthritis**).

#### b) Four Conditions Causing Circumcorneal Congestion
1.  Acute Anterior Uveitis (Iridocyclitis).
2.  Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma.
3.  Corneal Ulcer (Keratitis).
4.  Acute Scleritis / Episcleritis.

#### c) Clinical Signs on Detailed Ocular Examination
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q09]]` (Paper 6) for detailed description of:
    *   Circumcorneal ciliary flush.
    *   Keratic precipitates (small, discrete, non-pigmented lymphocytic KPs).
    *   Aqueous flare (Tyndall phenomenon) and aqueous cells floating in anterior chamber.
    *   Muddy iris with loss of architectural pattern.
    *   Miosed, sluggish, irregular pupil.
    *   Posterior synechiae (fibrinous adherence of iris to anterior lens capsule).
    *   Normal or transiently decreased intraocular pressure (ciliary shock).

#### d) Outline of Investigations
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q11]]` (Paper 2) for:
    *   Hematological markers: Rheumatoid Factor (RF), Anti-CCP antibodies, ESR, CRP, ANA.
    *   Hand/wrist X-rays showing periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, and bony erosions.
    *   Slit-lamp biomicroscopy, Applanation tonometry, and OCT macula.

#### e) Treatment and Rationale for Drugs
1.  **Topical Cycloplegics (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% TDS):**
    *   *Rationale:* Paralyzes the ciliary muscle and pupillary sphincter, providing comfort by relieving painful spasm; prevents the formation of permanent posterior synechiae; breaks newly formed synechiae; restores local blood flow by relieving vascular compression.
2.  **Topical Corticosteroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% drops hourly):**
    *   *Rationale:* Potent anti-inflammatory agent; stabilizes the disrupted blood-aqueous barrier, suppresses leukocyte infiltration, reduces exudation, and prevents fibrinous pupillary membrane formation.
3.  **Periocular Corticosteroid Injections (Sub-Tenon Triamcinolone 40 mg):**
    *   *Rationale:* Achieves sustained, high posterior segment and anterior uveal concentrations in severe disease refractory to topical drops.
4.  **Systemic NSAIDs / Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs):**
    *   *Rationale:* In collaboration with a rheumatologist (e.g., Methotrexate, Hydroxychloroquine) to control the underlying rheumatoid arthritis driving the uveal inflammation.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Types of Astigmatism
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** A condition of refractive error where a point-focus of light cannot be formed upon the retina because the refracting power of the eye varies across different meridians.
*   **Classifications:**
    1.  **Regular Astigmatism:** Refractive power changes uniformly from one principal meridian to the other (meridians are $90^\circ$ apart).
        *   *With-the-Rule (WTR):* Vertical meridian is more curved/refractive than the horizontal (corrected by minus cylinder at $180^\circ$ or plus cylinder at $90^\circ$).
        *   *Against-the-Rule (ATR):* Horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical (corrected by minus cylinder at $90^\circ$ or plus cylinder at $180^\circ$).
        *   *Oblique Astigmatism:* Principal meridians are perpendicular but lie obliquely ($45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$).
        *   *Bi-oblique:* Principal meridians are not perpendicular to each other.
    2.  **Optic Subtypes (Sturm’s Conoid Positioning Relative to Retina):**
        *   *Simple Myopic:* One meridian focused on the retina, other in front.
        *   *Simple Hypermetropic:* One meridian on the retina, other behind.
        *   *Compound Myopic:* Both principal meridians focused in front of the retina.
        *   *Compound Hypermetropic:* Both principal meridians focused behind the retina.
        *   *Mixed:* One meridian focused in front of the retina, the other behind it.
    3.  **Irregular Astigmatism:** Refractive power changes irregularly without any distinct principal meridians (caused by corneal scars, keratoconus); treated with rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lenses or keratoplasty.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Buphthalmos (Primary Congenital Glaucoma)
notes.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q07]]` (Paper 3 / MCQs) & `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q02]]` (Paper 6 / Notes):
    *   *Pathogenesis:* Maldevelopment of trabecular meshwork and anterior chamber angle (**trabeculodysgenesis**) arising from neural crest cells without gross ocular anomalies. Barkan's membrane blocks outflow.
    *   *Clinical Triad:* **Epiphora (watering), Photophobia, and Blepharospasm**.
    *   *Signs:*
        *   **Corneal Enlargement (Megalocornea):** Horizontal corneal diameter $>12\text{ mm}$ in infants ($>13\text{ mm}$ after 1 year).
        *   **Haab’s Striae:** Curvilinear horizontal or concentric tears in Descemet's membrane.
        *   Corneal edema and cloudiness (hazy frosted-glass look).
        *   Deep anterior chamber, thin blue sclera, lens flattening.
        *   Glaucomatous cupping of optic disc (reversible if treated early).
    *   *Treatment:* Primary surgical management: **Goniotomy** (under direct gonioscopic visualization if cornea is clear) or **Trabeculotomy** (ab-externo approach if cornea is cloudy). Combined Trabeculotomy-Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C in refractory cases.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Entropion
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Inward inversion of the eyelid margin towards the globe, causing pseudotrichiasis.
*   **Etiological Classification:**
    1.  *Involutional (Senile):* Lower lid only; caused by horizontal lid laxity, disinsertion of lower lid retractors, and preseptal orbicularis over-riding pretarsal fibers.
    2.  *Cicatricial:* Scarring and contraction of palpebral conjunctiva and tarsal plate (trachoma, burns, pemphigoid).
    3.  *Congenital:* Rare structural dysgenesis of lower lid retractors.
    4.  *Acute Spastic:* Sustained orbicularis spasm following ocular irritation/surgery.
*   **Surgical Correction:**
    *   *Senile Entropion:* Wies procedure (transverse lid split + everting sutures), Quickert procedure, or lower lid retractor plication (Jones procedure).
    *   *Cicatricial Entropion:* Tarsal wedge resection, anterior lamellar repositioning, or posterior lamellar grafting (mucous membrane / hard palate).

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Interstitial Keratitis
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Chronic, non-ulcerative, non-suppurative inflammation primarily involving the corneal stroma without initial primary involvement of the epithelium or endothelium.
*   **Etiology:**
    *   *Congenital Syphilis (90%):* Bilateral, late manifestation presenting between 5–15 years of age as an antigen-antibody hypersensitivity reaction to treponemal antigens.
    *   *Tuberculosis:* Usually unilateral and sectoral.
    *   *Cogan Syndrome:* Non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis associated with vestibuloauditory dysfunction (sensorineural deafness, vertigo).
    *   *Herpetic (HSV, VZV):* Direct viral invasion or immune response.
*   **Clinical Stages of Syphilitic Interstitial Keratitis:**
    1.  *Progressive Stage:* Pain, photophobia, intense ciliary flush, endothelial edema, ground-glass corneal haze.
    2.  *Florid Stage:* Deep stromal neovascularization arising from anterior ciliary vessels invading the stroma as dense, brush-like radial pink patches (**"Salmon-patch appearance"**).
    3.  *Regressive Stage:* Vascular clearing leaving non-perfused **"ghost vessels"**, patchy stromal opacities, and thinned cornea.
*   **Treatment:** Intensive topical corticosteroids (Dexamethasone/Prednisolone) to minimize scarring; topical Atropine 1%; systemic treatment of underlying syphilis (Penicillin therapy).

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Chemical Injury to the Eye
notes.content:
*   **Etiology:** Alkali (severe liquefactive necrosis, deeper penetration) or Acid (coagulative necrosis with protein barrier).
*   **Roper-Hall Staging:**
    *   *Grade I:* Clear cornea, no limbal ischemia (Good prognosis).
    *   *Grade II:* Hazy cornea (iris details visible), $<1/3$ limbal ischemia (Good).
    *   *Grade III:* Corneal epithelium sloughed, stroma hazy (iris details obscured), $1/3$ to $1/2$ limbal ischemia (Guarded).
    *   *Grade IV:* Opaque white cornea, $>1/2$ limbal ischemia (blanched marble cornea; Poor prognosis).
*   **Immediate Management:**
    1.  **Copious Emergency Irrigation:** Immediate flushing with sterile saline or water for at least 15–30 minutes until neutral pH (7.0–7.4) is restored.
    2.  *Debridement:* Mechanical removal of chemical particulate matter (e.g., lime particles) from conjunctival fornices.
    3.  *Medical Therapy:* Topical antibiotics, topical steroids (first 10 days to inhibit inflammation), Ascorbate 10% drops + oral Vitamin C (promotes collagen synthesis), Doxycycline 100 mg BD (collagenase inhibitor), Cycloplegics, Preservative-free tear substitutes.
    4.  *Surgical:* Amniotic membrane transplantation, limbal stem cell transplantation.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Horner Syndrome
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Clinical syndrome caused by disruption/interruption of the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway supplying the eye and orbit.
*   **Anatomical Pathway:**
    *   *First-Order (Central):* Posterior hypothalamus $\rightarrow$ brainstem $\rightarrow$ Ciliospinal center of Budge ($C_8–T_2$).
    *   *Second-Order (Preganglionic):* Exits spinal cord $\rightarrow$ sympathetic chain over lung apex $\rightarrow$ synapses in Superior Cervical Ganglion.
    *   *Third-Order (Postganglionic):* Carotid plexus $\rightarrow$ enters orbit via nasociliary nerve $\rightarrow$ long ciliary nerves to dilator pupillae and Müller's muscle.
*   **Clinical Features (Classic Tetrad):**
    1.  *Mild Ptosis (1–2 mm):* Due to denervation of Müller’s superior tarsal muscle.
    2.  *Miosis:* Due to unopposed parasympathetic sphincter action (pupillary anisocoria greater in the dark; dilation lag).
    3.  *Anhidrosis:* Loss of ipsilateral facial sweating (seen in central and preganglionic lesions).
    4.  *Apparent Enophthalmos:* Due to narrowing of the palpebral fissure.
    5.  *Other Signs:* Heterochromia iridis (in congenital Horner's), elevation of the lower eyelid ("upside-down ptosis").
*   **Pharmacological Diagnostic Tests:**
    *   *Cocaine Test (4%–10%):* Normal pupil dilates; Horner pupil fails to dilate.
    *   *Apraclonidine Test (0.5%):* Normal pupil shows no change; Horner pupil undergoes reversal of anisocoria (dilates due to denervation supersensitivity).
    *   *Hydroxyamphetamine Test (1%):* Differentiates preganglionic (dilates) from postganglionic lesion (fails to dilate).

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Types of IOL (Intraocular Lens)
notes.content:
1.  *By Anatomical Fixation Site:*
    *   Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL) — in-the-bag (gold standard) or ciliary sulcus.
    *   Anterior Chamber IOL (ACIOL) — angle-supported (e.g., Kelman multiflex).
    *   Iris-fixated IOL (e.g., Artisan/iris claw lens).
    *   Scleral-Fixated IOL (SFIOL) / Glued IOL.
2.  *By Material:* Rigid PMMA (polymethylmethacrylate), Foldable Hydrophobic Acrylic, Hydrophilic Acrylic, Silicone, Collamer.
3.  *By Optical Focus:* Monofocal, Toric (corrects astigmatism), Multifocal (bifocal/trifocal), Extended Depth of Focus (EDOF), Accommodative.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Newer Antiglaucoma Drugs
notes.content:
1.  **Prostaglandin Analogues:**
    *   *Latanoprost (0.005%)*, *Travoprost (0.004%)*, *Bimatoprost (0.03%)*, *Tafluprost (0.015% preservative-free)*.
    *   *Action:* Enhance uveoscleral outflow; once-daily bedtime dosing.
2.  **Rho-Kinase (ROCK) Inhibitors:**
    *   *Netarsudil (0.02%)*, *Ripasudil (0.4%)*.
    *   *Action:* Directly lowers trabecular outflow resistance by remodeling the trabecular meshwork cytoskeleton; lowers episcleral venous pressure.
3.  **Selective Alpha-2 Adrenergic Agonist:**
    *   *Brimonidine (0.2%)*: Decreases aqueous production and increases uveoscleral outflow; neuroprotective potential.
4.  **Topical Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors:**
    *   *Dorzolamide (2%)*, *Brinzolamide (1%)*: Inhibits ciliary carbonic anhydrase without systemic acidosis.
5.  **Fixed-Dose Combination Drops:**
    *   Timolol-Latanoprost, Timolol-Brimonidine, Timolol-Dorzolamide. Improves patient compliance.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Indications of Keratoplasty
notes.content:
1.  **Optical:** To improve visual acuity by replacing an opaque cornea (e.g., corneal leucoma, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, Fuchs' dystrophy, advanced keratoconus).
2.  **Therapeutic:** To replace infected tissue unresponsive to antimicrobial therapy (e.g., refractory severe bacterial or fungal corneal ulcer).
3.  **Tectonic / Structural:** To restore and preserve globe anatomy in extensive corneal thinning, descemetocele, or perforation.
4.  **Cosmetic:** To improve appearance in a disfigured, vascularized, blind eye (where optical rehabilitation is not possible).

notes.content:
*Reference Image Link:* [Human Eyeball Cross-Section (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/1413_Structure_of_the_Eye.jpg)

#### a) Three Concentric Tunics (Layers)
1.  **Outer Fibrous Tunic:**
    *   *Cornea:* Transparent anterior one-sixth; major refracting surface (+43 D).
    *   *Sclera:* Opaque, tough, protective posterior five-sixths.
    *   *Limbus:* Corneoscleral transition zone containing trabecular meshwork and limbal stem cells.
2.  **Middle Vascular Tunic (Uveal Tract):**
    *   *Iris:* Anterior diaphragm regulating pupillary aperture.
    *   *Ciliary Body:* Pars plicata (produces aqueous) and Pars plana (smooth posterior zone).
    *   *Choroid:* Highly vascular posterior coat nourishing outer retinal layers.
3.  **Inner Nervous Tunic (Retina):**
    *   Consists of outer Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) and inner 9 layers of neurosensory retina terminating anteriorly at the ora serrata.

#### b) Compartments and Refractive Media
*   *Anterior Segment:*
    *   **Anterior Chamber:** Between cornea and iris ($0.25\text{ mL}$ aqueous).
    *   **Posterior Chamber:** Triangular space between posterior iris and lens ($0.06\text{ mL}$ aqueous).
*   *Posterior Segment:*
    *   **Vitreous Cavity:** Large cavity behind lens filled with vitreous gel ($4.0\text{ mL}$).
*   *Refractive Media:* Cornea $\rightarrow$ Aqueous humor $\rightarrow$ Crystalline lens $\rightarrow$ Vitreous humor.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Leucocoria (White Pupillary Reflex)
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Abnormal white, pale, or yellow reflection seen through the pupil instead of the normal orange-red fundal glow.
*   **Important Causes in Children:**
    1.  *Congenital Cataract* (most common treatable cause).
    2.  *Retinoblastoma* (most critical life-threatening cause).
    3.  *Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV) / PHPV*.
    4.  *Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)* (Stage 5 cicatricial retrolental mass).
    5.  *Coats' Disease* (exudative retinal detachment).
    6.  *Toxocara Endophthalmitis*.
    7.  *Coloboma of Choroid*.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Lasers in Ophthalmology
notes.content:
1.  **Photocoagulation (Thermal Lasers — Argon, Diode 810 nm, Frequency-Doubled Nd:YAG 532 nm):**
    *   Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) in proliferative diabetic retinopathy and ischemic CRVO.
    *   Focal/Grid laser for macular edema.
    *   Barrier laser around retinal tears to prevent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
    *   Laser trabeculoplasty (ALT / SLT) for open-angle glaucoma.
2.  **Photodisruption (Neodymium:YAG Laser 1064 nm):**
    *   Nd:YAG Posterior Capsulotomy for Posterior Capsular Opacification (After-Cataract).
    *   Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) for angle-closure glaucoma.
    *   Vitreolysis of vitreous strands.
3.  **Photoablation (Excimer Laser 193 nm):**
    *   Refractive surgery: LASIK, PRK for myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism.
    *   Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) for superficial corneal dystrophies and scars.
4.  **Femtosecond Laser (1053 nm Infrared):**
    *   Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS): Precision capsulotomy, nuclear fragmentation, clear corneal incisions.
    *   Flap creation in Femto-LASIK; lenticule extraction in SMILE.
5.  **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT - 689 nm Diode):**
    *   Activated Verteporfin dye for subfoveal choroidal neovascular membranes (CNVM) and central serous chorioretinopathy.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Senile Cataract Case
notes.questionText: A 50-year-old female presents with a gradual, painless loss of vision in both eyes over the past two years. She reports difficulty reading and recognizes faces only when close. On examination, her visual acuity is 6/36 in both eyes, and a slit-lamp examination reveals lens opacities. a) What is the most probable diagnosis. b) Mention two differential diagnoses. c) How will you confirm the diagnosis d) Describe the treatment options and the role of preoperative counseling. (1+2+3+4)
notes.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Bilateral Senile (Age-Related) Immature Cortical / Nuclear Cataract.**

#### b) Two Differential Diagnoses
1.  *Open-Angle Glaucoma* (also causes painless, gradual, progressive visual deterioration).
2.  *Age-Related Macular Degeneration (Dry ARMD)*.

#### c) Confirmation of Diagnosis
1.  *Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy:* Examination under full pupillary mydriasis confirms opacification within the lens fibers or nucleus, demonstrates iris shadow (in immature stages), and allows grading of nuclear sclerosis (LOCS III system).
2.  *Distant Direct Ophthalmoscopy:* Reveals black silhouettes/opacities against the red fundus glow.
3.  *Visual Acuity & Refraction:* Documents best-corrected visual acuity and index myopic shift ("second sight").
4.  *Preoperative Evaluation:* B-scan ultrasonography (if dense, to rule out retinal detachment), optical/ultrasound biometry (A-scan + Keratometry for IOL power calculation), macula assessment.

#### d) Treatment Options and Preoperative Counseling
*   **Treatment Options:**
    *   *Surgical Extraction with IOL Implantation:* Only definitive cure:
        1.  **Phacoemulsification with Foldable Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL):** Standard modern surgical approach; small 2.2–2.8 mm clear corneal incision, sutureless, rapid visual recovery.
        2.  **Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS):** Sclerocorneal tunnel, cost-effective, ideal for hard cataracts.
*   **Preoperative Counseling:**
    *   Educate the patient regarding the nature of the condition and explain that surgery is an elective procedure to restore functional vision.
    *   Inform about the available intraocular lenses (Monofocal vs. Toric vs. Multifocal/EDOF).
    *   Detail the surgical procedure, anesthesia method (topical/peribulbar), post-op recovery expectations, and need for postoperative reading glasses.
    *   Disclose potential risks and complications (capsular tear, infection/endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, retinal detachment) and secure informed written consent.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Papilledema
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Non-inflammatory passive edema and swelling of the optic nerve head (optic disc) secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP). Almost always bilateral.
*   **Etiopathogenesis (Hayreh’s Axoplasmic Stasis Theory):** Increased ICP transmitted along the subarachnoid sheath surrounding the optic nerve $\rightarrow$ compression of the retrobulbar optic nerve $\rightarrow$ interruption of slow and fast axoplasmic flow at the lamina cribrosa $\rightarrow$ axonal swelling (axoplasmic stasis) in the prelaminar optic disc $\rightarrow$ capillary congestion, venous engorgement, and extracellular fluid extravasation.
*   **Causes of Raised ICP:** Intracranial space-occupying lesions (tumors, abscess, hematoma), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), meningitis, encephalitis, hydrocephalus, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
*   **Clinical Stages & Features:**
    1.  *Early:* Blurring of nasal and vertical disc margins, loss of spontaneous venous pulsation, subtle nerve fiber layer edema. Vision is characteristically normal.
    2.  *Fully Developed:* Marked forward elevation of disc (mushroom configuration), obliterated physiological cup, circumferential Paton's retinal lines, engorged tortuous veins, splinter peripapillary hemorrhages, cotton wool spots. Patient experiences transient visual obscurations (amaurosis fugax lasting seconds).
    3.  *Chronic (Vintage):* Hemorrhages and exudates resolve; disc resembles a "champagne cork"; optociliary shunt vessels and hard round corpora amylacea bodies appear.
    4.  *Atrophic (Post-papilledemic Optic Atrophy):* Dirty-white pallor, blurred margins, secondary perivascular sheathing, severe concentric visual field loss, and irreversible blindness.
*   **Diagnostic Evaluation & Treatment:** Urgent MRI brain with MRV to identify the intracranial mass or sinus thrombosis; Lumbar puncture (after neuroimaging confirms no mass lesion/herniation risk) to record opening pressure. Treatment is aimed at eliminating the underlying intracranial cause; optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting (ventriculo-peritoneal / lumbo-peritoneal) if medical management of IIH (Acetazolamide, weight loss) fails.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Paralytic Squint
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** An incomitant strabismus resulting from paresis or paralysis of one or more extraocular muscles, characterized by an angle of deviation that varies with the direction of gaze.
*   **Etiology:** Head injury, vascular lesions (diabetes, hypertension, stroke), intracranial aneurysms, intracranial tumors, demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis), myasthenia gravis.
*   **Cardinal Clinical Features:**
    1.  *Limitation of Movement:* Restricted ocular rotation in the diagnostic field of action of the paralyzed muscle.
    2.  *Incomitant Deviation:* Primary deviation (squinting eye deviating when sound eye fixes) is **less than** Secondary deviation (sound eye deviating under cover when paralyzed eye is forced to fix), based on **Hering’s Law of Equal Innervation**.
    3.  *Diplopia:* Binocular diplopia, maximal in the direction of the paralyzed muscle’s action.
    4.  *Compensatory Abnormal Head Posture (AHP):* Face turn, head tilt (ocular torticollis), or chin elevation/depression adopted to eliminate diplopia.
    5.  *False Orientation (Past-Pointing):* Inaccurate pointing toward the field of action of the paretic muscle due to excessive motor innervation.
    6.  *Autonomic Symptoms:* Vertigo, nausea, and disorientation.
*   **Diagnostic Tests:** Diplopia charting with red-green goggles, Hess / Lees screen, Park-Bielschowsky three-step test (for vertical/oblique palsies), Forced Duction Test (FDT - negative in pure neurogenic paralysis).
*   **Treatment:** Medical treatment of underlying cause (control diabetes, hypertension); occlusion of one eye to relieve disabling diplopia; prisms in spectacles; botulinum toxin injection to antagonist; corrective strabismus surgery deferred for at least 6 months to allow spontaneous recovery.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Complications and Sequelae of Anterior Uveitis
notes.questionText: Complications and Sequalae of Anterior Uveitis.
notes.content:
1.  **Band-Shaped Keratopathy (BSK):** Deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in Bowman's membrane, especially in chronic anterior uveitis associated with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
2.  **Posterior Synechiae:** Adhesions between the posterior iris surface and anterior lens capsule:
    *   *Segmental:* Causes irregular/festooned pupil upon mydriasis.
    *   *Annular (Ring Synechiae / Seclusio Pupillae):* $360^\circ$ pupillary margin adherence blocking aqueous flow $\rightarrow$ **Iris Bombe** formation.
    *   *Occlusio Pupillae:* Organization of inflammatory exudate across the entire pupil aperture.
3.  **Secondary Glaucoma:**
    *   *Early (Hypertensive Uveitis):* Trabecular meshwork clogging by inflammatory cells and fibrinous exudate, or trabeculitis.
    *   *Late:* Pupil block from seclusio pupillae (iris bombe), or peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) leading to secondary angle closure.
4.  **Complicated Cataract:** Rapidly progressing posterior subcapsular lens opacification showing typical polychromatic luster ("rainbow" appearance) and breadcrumb deposits.
5.  **Cyclitic Membrane:** Fibrous organization of retro-lenticular exudates behind the crystalline lens; contraction leads to ciliary body detachment, hypotony, and **Phthisis Bulbi**.
6.  **Cystoid Macular Edema (CME):** Breakdown of perifoveal capillary permeability causing accumulation of fluid in Henle's outer plexiform layer (major cause of permanent visual reduction).
7.  **Papillitis / Optic Disc Edema:** Inflammatory swelling of the optic nerve head.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Stages of Maturation of Cortical Cataract
notes.questionText: Explain stages of maturation of cortical type of Cataract.
notes.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q09]]` (Paper 2) & `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q16]]`:
    1.  *Stage of Lamellar Separation:* Fluid vacuoles and water-clefts separate cortical fibers; reversible.
    2.  *Stage of Incipient Cataract:* Wedge-shaped opacities with clear areas in between radiating from the periphery like spokes of a wheel (cuneiform) or saucer-shaped posterior subcapsular opacity (cupuliform).
    3.  *Stage of Immature Senile Cataract (ISC):* Opacities become confluent, partial lens cortex remains clear; iris shadow is demonstrable; lens may become swollen by hydration (Intumescent cataract) shallowing the anterior chamber.
    4.  *Stage of Mature Senile Cataract (MSC):* Total opacification of the cortex up to the capsule; pearly-white; no iris shadow visible; anterior chamber depth normal.
    5.  *Stage of Hypermature Cataract:*
        *   *Morgagnian type:* Liquid milky cortex with small brownish dense nucleus sunken to the bottom of the capsular bag.
        *   *Sclerotic type:* Resorption of cortical fluid leaving a shrunken, flattened, calcified lens with a wrinkled anterior capsule and deep anterior chamber.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Contraindications to Eye Donation
notes.content:
1.  **Death of Unknown / Unascertained Cause.**
2.  **Viral and Systemic Infections:** HIV/AIDS, Hepatitis B and C, Rabies, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), Active viral encephalitis, Congenital rubella.
3.  **Hematological Malignancies & Disseminated Tumors:** Leukemia, Lymphoma, Active systemic septicemia, Meningococcemia.
4.  **Intrinsic Eye Malignancies & Active Ocular Infections:** Retinoblastoma, Malignant melanoma of choroid, Active ocular tuberculosis, Syphilis, Endophthalmitis, Active viral keratitis (HSV/VZV).

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Enucleation and Its Indications
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Surgical removal of the entire eyeball after severing the extraocular muscles and optic nerve, leaving the orbital contents (fascia, fat, muscles) intact within the socket.
*   **Absolute Indications:**
    1.  *Malignant Intraocular Tumors without extrascleral extension:* Retinoblastoma in children, Malignant Melanoma of the choroid.
*   **Relative Indications:**
    2.  *Severe, Mutilating Ocular Trauma:* Severely ruptured, unsalvageable globe with total prolapse of intraocular contents.
    3.  *Prevention of Sympathetic Ophthalmitis:* Severely injured blind eye involving the ciliary body region removed within 10–14 days of injury.
    4.  *Painful Blind Eye:* Absolute glaucoma, chronic end-stage uveitis.
    5.  *Eye Banking:* Cadaveric donor eye retrieval for corneal transplantation.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Functions of an Eye Bank
notes.content:
1.  **Public Awareness & Advocacy:** Education to promote voluntary eye donation pledges.
2.  **Donor Tissue Harvesting:** 24-hour collection of donor eyes (enucleation or corneoscleral rim excision) from deceased individuals within 6 hours of death.
3.  **Tissue Processing & Evaluation:** Slit-lamp biomicroscopy and specular microscopy to grade endothelial cell density ($\ge 2000\text{ cells/mm}^2$) and corneal clarity.
4.  **Serological Screening:** Mandatory testing of donor blood for HIV-1/2, HBsAg, HCV, and Syphilis.
5.  **Preservation:** Storing corneas in cold storage media (McCarey-Kaufman medium up to 4 days, Optisol-GS up to 14 days).
6.  **Fair Distribution:** Allocation of quality-assured donor corneas to certified corneal surgeons for optical, therapeutic, and tectonic keratoplasties.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Tonometry
notes.content:
*   **Definition:** Objective measurement of Intraocular Pressure (IOP).
*   **Types & Principles:**
    1.  *Indentation (Impression) Tonometry:* **Schiotz Tonometer:** Plunger indents the cornea; greater indentation indicates softer eye / lower IOP. Affected by scleral rigidity.
    2.  *Applanation Tonometry (Imbert-Fick Law: $P = F/A$):*
        *   **Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT):** Gold standard. Measures force required to flatten a fixed corneal area (diameter 3.06 mm). Biprism splits the fluorescein rings; endpoint is reached when inner margins of two fluorescein semicircles align. Independent of scleral rigidity.
        *   *Perkins Tonometer:* Handheld portable applanation tonometer.
        *   *Non-Contact Tonometry (Air-Puff):* Uses a puff of pressurized air; useful for screening.
        *   *Tono-Pen / Icare Rebound Tonometer:* Portable, micro-transducers.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Case
notes.questionText: A 50 year old lady came with complaints of frequent decrease in near vision and change of glasses to improve the same. She also complained of clouding of peripheral vision in both eyes at times. She has no other comorbid problems. Answer the following questions: a) What other history will you elicit from her b) What is the probable diagnosis c) What differential diagnosis can you offer d) What investigations you would request e) How will you plan your treatment (1+1+3+3+2)
notes.content:
#### a) Additional History to Elicit
*   Family history of glaucoma or irreversible blindness in parents/siblings.
*   History of systemic comorbidities: Diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, peripheral vasospasm (migraine, Raynaud's phenomenon).
*   History of long-term use of systemic or topical corticosteroids.
*   History of high myopia.
*   History of transient blackouts, difficulty with night vision (dark adaptation), or bumping into side objects (tunnel vision).

#### b) Probable Diagnosis
**Bilateral Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG).**
*(Frequent change of presbyopic glasses due to accommodative failure + progressive peripheral visual field clouding).*

#### c) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG):* Glaucomatous disc and field damage with IOP consistently $\le 21\text{ mm Hg}$.
2.  *Ocular Hypertension:* Consistently elevated IOP $>21\text{ mm Hg}$ with normal discs and normal visual fields.
3.  *Chronic Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma:* Closed angle on gonioscopy with PAS.
4.  *Pseudoexfoliative / Pigmentary Glaucoma:* Secondary open-angle glaucomas with characteristic biomicroscopic flakes or pigment dispersion.

#### d) Investigations to Request
*   *Tonometry:* Baseline diurnal IOP phasing using Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT).
*   *Central Corneal Thickness (CCT):* Pachymetry (thin cornea $<555\text{ µm}$ underestimates true IOP).
*   *Gonioscopy:* Confirms wide open angles (Shaffer Grade 3–4) and excludes secondary blockages.
*   *Optic Nerve Head Imaging:* Stereoscopic fundus photography, Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of peripapillary Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL).
*   *Automated Perimetry:* Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer (HFA central 24-2 or 30-2 SITA-Standard protocol) to map paracentral, arcuate, or nasal step defects.

#### e) Treatment Plan
*   **Establish Target IOP:** Lower baseline IOP by at least 25%–30% (target $<15\text{ mm Hg}$).
*   **Medical Monotherapy (First Line):** Topical **Latanoprost 0.005%** at bedtime or **Timolol maleate 0.5% BD**.
*   **Combination Therapy:** Add Brimonidine 0.2% or Dorzolamide 2% if target IOP is not achieved.
*   **Laser Therapy:** Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) to improve trabecular outflow.
*   **Surgical Intervention:** **Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C (0.02%)** if target IOP is not achieved despite maximal medical/laser therapy or if visual field loss progresses.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Eye Signs of Thyroid Orbitopathy
notes.content:
1.  **Dalrymple’s Sign:** Pathognomonic retraction of the upper eyelid in primary gaze, revealing white sclera above the superior limbus.
2.  **Von Graefe’s Sign:** Dynamic lid lag of the upper eyelid on slow downward gaze.
3.  **Stellwag’s Sign:** Infrequent, incomplete, and sluggish blinking.
4.  **Mobius’ Sign:** Impaired convergence on attempted near focus.
5.  **Joffroy’s Sign:** Absence of normal forehead wrinkling on looking upward.
6.  **Enroth’s Sign:** Puffy, non-inflammatory fullness and edema of the eyelids.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Pilocarpine
notes.content:
*   **Class:** Direct-acting parasympathomimetic (cholinergic) agonist.
*   **Ocular Actions:**
    1.  *Miosis:* Stimulates muscarinic ($M_3$) receptors of pupillary sphincter.
    2.  *Lowers IOP:* Ciliary muscle contraction pulls the scleral spur posteriorly, opening trabecular meshwork pores.
    3.  *Accommodative Spasm:* Causes transient myopia in young patients.
*   **Preparations & Dosing:** Pilocarpine nitrate/hydrochloride 1%, 2%, 4% eye drops instilled TDS/QID; 4% gel at bedtime.
*   **Clinical Uses:** Acute angle-closure glaucoma (after IOP drops $<30\text{ mm Hg}$), primary open-angle glaucoma, reversal of mydriasis.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Ciliary spasm with browache/headache, blurred vision in dim light, visual field constriction, retinal detachment in high myopes.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Two Tests to Evaluate Epiphora

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Phacomorphic Glaucoma
notes.questionText: A 70-year-old female patient presents with pain, redness and diminution of vision in the right eye since 10 days. She gives history of having undergone cataract surgery in the left eye 2 years back. On examination, there is circumcorneal congestion, hazy cornea due to corneal edema, shallow anterior chamber and the lens is cataractous and intumescent. Intraocular pressure is high in the right eye. a) What is the probable diagnosis b) What is the immediate medical management c) What is the definitive treatment d) What are the complications if not treated e) What are the differential diagnosis f) What are the surgical complications g) What are the preoperative advice to this patient (1+2+2+3+3+2+2)
notes.content:
#### a) Probable Diagnosis
**Right Eye Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Secondary Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma induced by an Intumescent Senile Cataract).**
*Clinical pointers:* 70-year-old female, acute pain, redness, blurred vision, circumcorneal congestion, steamy corneal edema, shallow anterior chamber, swollen intumescent cataractous lens, elevated IOP, with history of pseudophakia in the fellow eye.

#### b) Immediate Medical Management
*   **Intravenous Hyperosmotic:** IV Mannitol 20% (1.5–2.0 g/kg body weight infused over 30 minutes) to rapidly dehydrate the vitreous humor and lower IOP.
*   **Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor:** Acetazolamide 500 mg IV stat, followed by 250 mg orally TDS.
*   **Topical Beta-Blocker:** Timolol maleate 0.5% eye drops BD.
*   **Topical Alpha-2 Agonist:** Brimonidine 0.2% eye drops BD.
*   **Topical Steroid:** Prednisolone acetate 1% drops QID to reduce secondary uveal inflammation.
*   *Note:* Strong miotics (Pilocarpine) should be avoided initially as they may exacerbate pupillary block by increasing lens-iris contact and allowing the lens to shift forward.

#### c) Definitive Treatment
*   **Cataract Extraction with Posterior Chamber Intraocular Lens (PCIOL) Implantation:**
    *   Performed once IOP is normalized and corneal edema clears.
    *   *Techniques:* Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS) or Phacoemulsification.
    *   *Key steps:* Puncture of anterior capsule with a 26G needle to aspirate milky cortical fluid, decompressing the swollen lens; followed by continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC), nuclear delivery, and in-the-bag PCIOL placement.

#### d) Complications if Left Untreated
1.  Permanent peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) formation and intractable secondary chronic angle-closure glaucoma.
2.  Glaucomatous optic atrophy resulting in permanent blindness.
3.  Endothelial cell loss causing bullous keratopathy.
4.  Ciliary staphyloma and phthisis bulbi.

#### e) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Acute Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG):* Fellow eye shows a shallow anterior chamber and narrow occludable angle (in phacomorphic glaucoma, the fellow eye is often pseudophakic or has a normal open angle).
2.  *Phacolytic Glaucoma:* Lens is hypermature (Morgagnian); anterior chamber is deep (not shallow); white protein flakes present in AC.
3.  *Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG):* Rubeosis iridis visible at pupillary border and angle; history of CRVO or PDR.

#### f) Surgical Complications
1.  *Runaway Capsulorhexis:* Due to high intralenticular pressure and tense capsule.
2.  *Posterior Capsular Rupture (PCR):* Due to zonular laxity in mature cataracts.
3.  *Zonular Dialysis:* Fragile zonules stressed by the swollen lens mass.
4.  *Endothelial Damage:* Due to proximity of the anteriorly displaced lens to the cornea during manipulation.
5.  *Expulsive Choroidal Hemorrhage:* Triggered by sudden intraocular decompression in an eye with pre-existing high IOP.

#### g) Preoperative Advice
*   Strict compliance with IOP-lowering medications prior to surgery.
*   Avoid coughing, sneezing, bending forward, or straining.
*   Counseling on guarded visual prognosis, explaining that final vision depends on the health of the optic nerve and macula behind the dense cataract.

---

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Causes of Secondary Glaucoma in the Eye
notes.questionText: Causes of secondary glaucoma in the eye
notes.content:
1.  **Lens-Induced (Phacogenic):** Phacomorphic, phacolytic, lens particle, phacoantigenic.
2.  **Inflammatory (Uveitic):** Trabecular clogging by inflammatory cells/fibrin, trabeculitis, pupil block via seclusio pupillae (iris bombé), peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
3.  **Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG):** Retinal ischemia (PDR, CRVO) stimulating pre-trabecular fibrovascular membrane formation.
4.  **Traumatic:** Angle recession, traumatic hyphema (red cell/ghost cell glaucoma), lens subluxation.
5.  **Pigmentary & Pseudoexfoliative:** Mechanical shedding of pigment or fibrillar pseudoexfoliation material obstructing the intertrabecular spaces.
6.  **Steroid-Induced:** Glycosaminoglycan accumulation in the trabecular meshwork due to prolonged corticosteroid therapy.
7.  **Intraocular Tumors:** Trabecular infiltration or forward displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm by retinoblastoma or melanoma.

notes.subject: Ophthalmology
notes.title: Corneal Edema
notes.content:
*   **Definition & Pathophysiology:** Abnormal accumulation of fluid within the corneal epithelium and/or stroma, increasing corneal thickness ($>540\text{ µm}$) and causing loss of transparency. Occurs when fluid inflow exceeds the endothelial dehydrating capacity (endothelial cell count $<500–700\text{ cells/mm}^2$) or when intraocular pressure exceeds stromal swelling pressure.
*   **Causes:**
    1.  *Endothelial Pump Failure:* Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy (PBK), surgical trauma during phacoemulsification.
    2.  *Acute Severe IOP Elevation:* Acute angle-closure glaucoma, neovascular glaucoma.
    3.  *Inflammatory Endotheliitis:* Acute iridocyclitis, herpes simplex disciform keratitis, corneal graft rejection.
    4.  *Mechanical / Traumatic:* Tears in Descemet's membrane (birth trauma, keratoconus acute hydrops).
*   **Clinical Features:** Hazy, ground-glass appearance; Descemet's folds; microcystic epithelial edema; coalesce into subepithelial bullae (bullous keratopathy) which rupture, causing severe pain, foreign body sensation, and photophobia.
*   **Management:**
    *   *Topical Hypertonic Agents:* Sodium chloride 5% eye drops or ointment to draw fluid osmotically from the epithelium.
    *   *Lowering IOP:* Topical beta-blockers, CAIs.
    *   *Therapeutic Bandage Contact Lens (BCL):* Provides pain relief by shielding exposed nerve endings from ruptured bullae.
    *   *Endothelial Keratoplasty (Definitive):* Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) or Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK).
