notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Presbycusis
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Bilateral, symmetrical, progressive sensorineural hearing loss associated with physiological aging, typically manifesting past 60–65 years of age.
* **Schuknecht’s Clinicopathological Classification:**
  1. **Sensory Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Epithelial atrophy with loss of sensory hair cells and supporting cells in the basal turn of the organ of Corti.
     * *Audiogram:* Abrupt, steeply down-sloping high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; speech discrimination remains well-preserved.
  2. **Neural Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Loss of neurons in the spiral ganglion and central auditory pathways (>50% neuron loss occurs with age).
     * *Audiogram:* Flat or gently sloping curve; marked, disproportionate loss of speech discrimination (**phonemic regression** — "hears sound but cannot understand words").
  3. **Strial / Metabolic Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Patchy atrophy and vascular degeneration throughout the stria vascularis, impairing endolymph production and endocochlear DC potential (+80 mV "battery").
     * *Audiogram:* Characteristically flat audiogram across all frequencies with excellent speech discrimination.
  4. **Cochlear Conductive (Mechanical) Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Stiffening and calcification of the basilar membrane and spiral ligament hyalinization.
     * *Audiogram:* Smooth, linear, gently down-sloping audiometric curve.
* **Clinical Characteristics:** Difficulty hearing in background noise (cocktail party effect), recruitment positive, bilateral high-pitched tinnitus.
* **Rehabilitation:** Binaural behind-the-ear (BTE) or in-the-canal (ITC) digital hearing aids with wide dynamic range compression (WDRC), assistive listening devices, speech reading, and cochlear implants in profound cases.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Causes of Referred Otalgia
notes.content:
Referred otalgia occurs because sensory nerves supplying the ear (cranial nerves V, IX, X, and cervical nerves C2, C3) share central neural pathways with distant head and neck sites:

```
                  PATHWAYS OF REFERRED OTALGIA
                               |
   +------------+--------------+--------------+------------+
   |            |                             |            |
  CN V         CN IX                         CN X        C2, C3
(Auriculo-   (Jacobson's                   (Arnold's    (Greater Auricular,
 temporal)      Nerve)                        Nerve)      Lesser Occipital)
   |            |                             |            |
Dental caries  Acute tonsillitis            Laryngeal    Cervical spondylosis
Impacted molar Quinsy, Tonsil cancer        malignancy   Cervical spine injury
TMJ arthritis  Base of tongue cancer        Pyriform CA  Cervical lymphadenitis
Mouth ulcers   Elongated styloid (Eagle)    Vallecula CA
```

1. **Via Mandibular Division of Trigeminal Nerve (CN $V_3$) through Auriculotemporal Nerve:**
   * Carious lower molars, impacted third molars, apical dental abscesses.
   * Temporomandibular joint dysfunction (Costen syndrome).
   * Carcinoma or ulcerative lesions of the oral tongue, floor of mouth, or buccal mucosa.
2. **Via Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX) through Tympanic Branch (Jacobson’s Nerve):**
   * Acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), post-tonsillectomy slough.
   * Malignancy of the palatine tonsil, anterior pillar, or base of the tongue.
   * Elongated styloid process (**Eagle syndrome**).
3. **Via Vagus Nerve (CN X) through Auricular Branch (Arnold’s Nerve):**
   * Carcinoma of the pyriform sinus, postcricoid area, vallecula, or supraglottic larynx.
   * Ulcerative conditions and foreign bodies of the hypopharynx and upper cervical oesophagus.
4. **Via Cervical Nerves (C2, C3) through Greater Auricular and Lesser Occipital Nerves:**
   * Cervical spondylosis, whiplash injury, caries of cervical vertebrae, and tender upper cervical lymphadenitis.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Topodiagnostic Tests for Intratemporal Lesions of Facial Nerve
notes.questionText: Topodiagnostic tests for lesions in intratemporal part of facial nerve
notes.content:
These tests localize the site of facial nerve compromise along its bony intratemporal path:

1. **Schirmer’s Test (Tests Greater Superficial Petrosal Nerve / Lacrimation):**
   * *Site:* Geniculate ganglion or proximal (labyrinthine segment).
   * *Method:* Strips of filter paper folded into lower conjunctival fornices for 5 minutes. >50% reduction in unilateral wetting indicates a lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion.
2. **Acoustic Stapedial Reflex (Tests Nerve to Stapedius):**
   * *Site:* Tympanic or vertical mastoid segment proximal to the pyramidal eminence.
   * *Method:* Impedance tympanometry with loud acoustic stimulation (70–100 dB SL). Absence of stapedial reflex with normal hearing confirms a lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius.
3. **Electrogustometry / Chemical Taste Test (Tests Chorda Tympani):**
   * *Site:* Mastoid segment proximal to the takeoff of chorda tympani.
   * *Method:* Application of sugar, salt, citric acid, and quinine solutions to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Impaired or absent taste perception localizes the lesion above the exit of chorda tympani.
4. **Submandibular Salivary Flow Test (Blatt’s Test — Tests Chorda Tympani Secretomotor Fibres):**
   * *Method:* Cannulation of both Wharton’s ducts with polyethylene tubes; saliva drop output is stimulated with 6% citric acid on the tongue. A reduction in salivary flow >25% on the affected side indicates chorda tympani denervation.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Aetiology of Perforation of Nasal Septum
notes.questionText: Aetiology of perforation of nasal septum
notes.content:
1. **Traumatic / Iatrogenic (Most Common):**
   * Complication of submucous resection (SMR) or septoplasty due to opposing tears of bilateral mucoperichondrial flaps.
   * Habitual digital nose picking (**ulcus septi perforans** of Hajek).
   * Chemical cautery (silver nitrate/trichloroacetic acid) or galvanocautery for epistaxis applied symmetrically to opposing septal sides.
   * Neglected septal haematoma or septal abscess leading to ischemic chondronecrosis.
   * Longstanding retained unilateral nasal foreign body or rhinolith.
2. **Infective & Chronic Granulomatous Diseases:**
   * *Cartilaginous Septum:* Lupus vulgaris, tuberculosis, leprosy.
   * *Bony Septum:* Tertiary syphilis (gumma of the vomer/perpendicular plate).
   * *Midline Destructive Lesions:* Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener’s), sinonasal NK/T-cell lymphoma.
3. **Chemicals & Drugs:**
   * Chronic illicit intranasal cocaine snorting (causes intense local vasospasm and ischemic necrosis).
   * Chronic exposure to industrial dust/vapours: Chromium plating, arsenic, mercury, sodium carbonate.
   * Prolonged, improper topical nasal corticosteroid spray directed straight onto the anterior nasal septum.
4. **Neoplastic:** Squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, malignant melanoma of the nasal septum.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Pathology of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
notes.questionText: Pathology of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
notes.content:
* **Definition:** A peripheral vestibular end-organ disorder presenting as brief, episodic, violent vertigo and rotatory nystagmus provoked by specific changes in head position relative to gravity.
* **Underlying Pathophysiological Mechanisms:**
  1. **Source of Pathology:** Degeneration, fragmentation, and shedding of dense calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$) crystals (**otoconia / statoconia**) from the otolithic gelatinous membrane of the **utricular macula** (due to head trauma, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuronitis, ischemia, or aging).
  2. **Canalithiasis Theory (Hall et al. — Most Accepted):**
     * Dislodged otoconial debris migrates and floats freely within the endolymph of the most dependent semicircular canal (usually the **posterior semicircular canal** in 85–90% of cases, due to its gravitationally inferior position).
     * When the head is moved into the provoking plane (e.g., Dix–Hallpike position), gravity causes the heavier otoconial mass to move along the canal.
     * This fluid movement acts like a piston, producing an abnormal hydrodynamic suction/pressure that displaces the **cupula**, sending a false discharge of intense excitation to the vestibular nuclei, causing rotatory vertigo and nystagmus.
     * *Latency (2–20 seconds):* Represents the time taken for the detached otolith mass to overcome inertia and move within the viscous endolymph.
     * *Fatigability:* Repeated provocation disperses the particles along the canal, reducing their ability to deflect the cupula.
  3. **Cupulolithiasis Theory (Schuknecht):**
     * The detached otoconia settle and become physically adhered directly to the gelatinous cupula of the posterior canal ampulla.
     * This transforms the normally neutrally buoyant cupula into a heavy, gravity-sensitive organ that deflects whenever the head changes spatial orientation.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (Safe / Tubotympanic Type)
notes.questionText: A forty-year-old female patient came with complaints of bilateral ear discharge, mucoid type, increases with bouts of upper respiratory tract infection and associated with reduced hearing on both sides. Tympanic membranes show bilateral central perforation. There is active discharge and no mastoid tenderness. Rinne’s test is negative bilaterally, Weber’s test is lateralized to left side and absolute bone conduction test is normal on both sides. a) What is your provisional complete diagnosis b) Describe the aetiopathology of this condition. c) Write relevant investigations with expected findings. d) How will you treat this condition. e) Discuss the complications of this condition, if untreated. (1+2+2+3+2)
notes.content:
#### a) Provisional Complete Diagnosis
* **Bilateral Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Tubotympanic (Mucosal / Safe) Type, Active Stage, with Moderate Left Conductive Hearing Loss**.
* *Justification:* Non-fetid, mucoid bilateral discharge worsening with upper respiratory tract infections, bilateral central perforations with preserved annulus, absence of mastoid tenderness, bilateral negative Rinne (conductive hearing loss), Weber lateralized to the poorer (left) ear, and normal ABC on both sides.

#### b) Aetiopathology
* **Site Involved:** Confined to the anteroinferior middle ear cleft (Eustachian tube, mesotympanum, hypotympanum).
* **Pathogenesis:**
  * Initiated by an episode of acute necrotizing otitis media in childhood or recurrent ascending Eustachian tubal infections from adenoids, tonsils, or sinusitis.
  * The tympanic membrane perforation becomes permanent when squamous epithelium of the drum surface migrates around the margin to fuse with the middle ear mucosa, preventing spontaneous closure.
  * Water entry or upper respiratory tract infection triggers active mucosal inflammation, causing oedema, hypertrophy of mucin-secreting goblet cells, and profuse mucoid discharge.
* **Bacteriology:** *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus mirabilis*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and oral anaerobes.

#### c) Relevant Investigations with Expected Findings
1. **Examination Under Microscope (EUM):** Direct visualization of margins of central perforation; confirms intact annulus tympanicus; rules out cholesteatoma flakes; assesses ossicular status and excludes deep mucosal granulations.
2. **Ear Swab for Aerobic and Anaerobic Culture and Sensitivity:** Identifies causative pathogens and guides targeted topical/systemic antibiotic therapy.
3. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):** Demonstrates bilateral conductive hearing loss (typically 25–40 dB) with normal bone conduction thresholds and an air-bone gap (greater on the left side).
4. **X-ray / HRCT Temporal Bone:** Shows cellular or sclerotic mastoid without bony destruction or erosion of the scutum, tegmen, or sinus plate.

#### d) Treatment Plan
```
            MANAGEMENT OF SAFE CSOM (TUBOTYMPANIC)
                               |
       +-----------------------+-----------------------+
       |                                               |
Active Stage (Control Infection)            Inactive / Dry Stage (Reconstruct)
  - Meticulous aural toilet                   - Keep ear dry strictly
  - Non-ototoxic topical antibiotics          - Myringoplasty / Tympanoplasty
    (Ciprofloxacin / Ofloxacin drops)           (Temporalis fascia underlay graft)
  - Eradicate focal sepsis (T&A, Sinuses)     - Ossiculoplasty if incus eroded
  - Water precautions
```
1. **Phase 1: Control of Active Infection (Medical):**
   * *Aural Toilet:* Meticulous dry mopping or microscopic suction clearance of discharge and debris.
   * *Topical Antibiotic Ear Drops:* Non-ototoxic topical fluoroquinolones (**Ciprofloxacin or Ofloxacin 0.3% drops**, 3–4 drops TID) $\pm$ topical dexamethasone for 7–10 days.
   * *Water Precautions:* Strict prevention of water entry during bathing and washing.
   * *Treat Sepsis:* Address concurrent tonsillitis, adenoids, or chronic sinusitis.
2. **Phase 2: Surgical Reconstruction (Once Ear is Dry for 6–12 Weeks):**
   * **Myringoplasty / Type I Tympanoplasty:** Underlay or overlay grafting using autologous **temporalis fascia** or tragal perichondrium to close the central perforation, eradicate middle ear vulnerability, and restore hearing.

#### e) Complications if Left Untreated
* While tubotympanic CSOM is classified as "safe," longstanding neglect can lead to:
  1. Permanent, progressive ossicular chain necrosis (most commonly necrosis of the long process of the incus due to its tenuous blood supply).
  2. Progressive mixed hearing loss from round window membrane absorption of bacterial toxins into the scala tympani, causing secondary sensorineural cochlear damage.
  3. Secondary tympanosclerosis of the ossicles and drum, leading to severe conductive loss.
  4. Atrophy, collapse, and retraction pockets, predisposing to secondary acquired cholesteatoma.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Acute Epiglottitis: Aetiology, Clinical Features, and Management
notes.questionText: Aetiology, clinical features and management of acute epiglottitis
notes.content:
* **Aetiology:** Rapidly progressive, potentially lethal cellulitis of the supraglottic larynx (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids).
  * *Organism:* Primarily ***Haemophilus influenzae* type B (Hib)**; occasionally *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Strep. pyogenes*, *Staph. aureus*. Most common in children aged 2–7 years.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Abrupt onset with rapid progression over hours.
  * High fever, severe sore throat, odynophagia, inability to swallow, resulting in **drooling of saliva**.
  * **Tripod Position:** Child sits upright, leaning forward with the neck extended, chin thrust forward, and mouth open to maintain the airway.
  * Voice is muffled and throaty (**"hot potato voice"**); cough is absent (differs from croup).
  * Rapidly progressive inspiratory stridor with suprasternal/intercostal retraction.
* **Management:**
  1. **Do Not Agitate the Child:** **Never examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor** or force the child to lie down (risks fatal reflex laryngospasm and immediate cardiac arrest).
  2. **Airway Security (First Priority):** Transfer immediately to the operation theatre with an ENT surgeon and anesthesiologist present. Perform gentle inhalational induction and nasotracheal intubation. Keep an emergency tracheostomy set open and ready.
  3. **Parenteral Antibiotics:** IV Ceftriaxone (50–100 mg/kg/day) or Cefotaxime for 7–10 days.
  4. **IV Corticosteroids:** Dexamethasone to accelerate supraglottic oedema resolution. Extubation is typically possible after 48–72 hours following endoscopic confirmation of decreased swelling.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Differential Diagnoses of Membrane over the Palatine Tonsil
notes.questionText: Discuss the differential diagnoses of membrane over the palatine tonsil with its distinguishing features
notes.content:
| Condition | Appearance of Membrane | Removal / Bleeding | Constitutional Signs | Diagnostic Confirmation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Acute Membranous Tonsillitis** | Yellowish-white, thin, limited to tonsil surface. | Easily wiped away; **does not bleed**. | High fever, marked throat pain, tender jugulodigastric nodes. | Throat swab: *Streptococcus pyogenes*. |
| **Faucial Diphtheria** | Dirty greyish-green, leathery, extends beyond tonsil onto pillars, uvula, and soft palate. | **Firmly adherent**; forcible peeling causes **copious capillary bleeding**. | Toxic look, low-grade fever, marked tachycardia, **"bull-neck"** cervical lymphadenopathy. | Albert's stain / Loeffler’s slope: *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. |
| **Vincent’s Angina** | Greyish pseudomembrane over an irregular, punched-out unilateral tonsillar ulcer. | Sloughs off easily, revealing a friable ulcer bed. | Minimal fever, foul fetor, unilateral sore throat. | Smear: Spirochaetes (*Borrelia vincentii*) + fusiform bacilli. |
| **Infectious Mononucleosis** | Thick, confluent white-grey exudative membrane over kissing tonsils. | Strips off with difficulty. | Generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, hepatosplenomegaly; rash on ampicillin. | Atypical lymphocytes on blood smear, positive Paul–Bunnell / Monospot test. |
| **Agranulocytosis** | Dirty grey-black necrotic slough covering tonsils and oral cavity. | Sloughs with extensive deep tissue necrosis. | Profound prostration, septicemia; absent inflammatory rim. | CBC: Marked absolute neutropenia ($<500/\mu\text{L}$). |
| **Candidiasis (Oral Thrush)** | Curd-like, creamy white spotty patches. | Scrapes off easily leaving an **erythematous base**. | Mild oral discomfort; common in diabetics, HIV, post-antibiotic/steroid use. | KOH mount: Budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae. |

notes.title: Differences Between Ethmoidal and Antrochoanal Polypi
notes.questionText: Differences between the ethmoidal and antrochoanal polypi Draw and label: (2x2=4)
notes.content:
| Feature | Antrochoanal Polyp (Killian’s Polyp) | Ethmoidal Polypi |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age** | Common in children and young adults. | Common in older adults ($>30$ years). |
| **Etiology** | Chronic infection / sinusitis. | Allergy, chronic inflammation, AERD/asthma. |
| **Number & Laterality** | **Solitary and unilateral**. | **Multiple, bilateral, grape-like clusters**. |

| **Morphology** | Trilobed: Antral, nasal, and choanal parts. | Multiple, pale, translucent, pedunculated, grape-like masses. |
| **Recurrence** | Uncommon if antral base is removed completely. | High recurrence rate. |
| **Treatment** | FESS with wide Middle Meatal Antrostomy and complete avulsion of the antral stalk. | FESS (anterior and posterior ethmoidectomy) + medical steroid therapy. |

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Puberphonia (Mutational Falsetto Voice)
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Failure of the male voice to break and descend from the high pitch of childhood to the characteristic low pitch of an adult male at puberty, resulting in a persistent, inappropriate high-pitched falsetto voice.
* **Aetiology:** Psychogenic/emotional immaturity, overprotective parenting, excessive self-consciousness, fixation on mother's voice; physical and endocrinal development of the larynx is completely normal.
* **Laryngeal Examination:** Completely normal laryngeal anatomy; on phonation, the vocal folds are held tightly stretched and over-adducted, with only their thin margins vibrating.
* **Diagnosis:** **Gutzmann’s Pressure Test:** Backward and downward digital pressure applied over the thyroid cartilage prominence relaxes the overstretched vocal cords, immediately dropping the pitch to a normal low-pitched male voice.
* **Treatment:** Voice therapy by a speech-language pathologist (training to phonate during throat clearing/coughing and sustaining low tones; excellent prognosis); refractory cases can undergo **Type III Isshiki Thyroplasty** (relaxation thyroplasty) to shorten and relax the cords.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Technique of Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (DNE)
notes.content:
* **Equipment & Preparation:** 0° and 30° rigid Hopkins rod nasal endoscopes (4 mm or 2.7 mm); topical decongestion and anesthesia using 4% lignocaine with 1:100,000 adrenaline.

```
Three-Pass Technique of Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy:
Pass 1: Along nasal floor -> Inferior meatus, Hasner's valve -> Choana -> Nasopharynx & Eustachian tube
Pass 2: Medial to middle turbinate -> Sphenoethmoidal recess -> Superior meatus -> Sphenoid ostium
Pass 3: Inside middle meatus -> Uncinate, Bulla, Infundibulum, Hiatus semilunaris, Frontal recess
```
* **First Pass:** Along the nasal floor into the nasopharynx. Evaluates the inferior turbinate, inferior meatus (nasolacrimal duct opening/valve of Hasner), posterior choana, Eustachian tube opening, torus tubarius, and fossa of Rosenmüller.
* **Second Pass:** Passes medial to the middle turbinate into the sphenoethmoidal recess. Evaluates the superior turbinate/meatus, sphenoid sinus ostium, and posterior ethmoid drainage.
* **Third Pass:** Directed into the middle meatus after gently lateralizing the middle turbinate. Evaluates uncinate process, bulla ethmoidalis, hiatus semilunaris, ethmoid infundibulum, and the frontal recess.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Fistula Test: Elicitation and Interpretation
notes.questionText: How to elicit and interpret fistula test
notes.content:
* **Technique:** Alternating positive and negative pressure is applied to the external acoustic canal using a **Siegle’s pneumatic speculum** or intermittent tragal compression with a finger.
* **Interpretation:**
  * **Positive Fistula Test:** Induction of transient rotatory vertigo and horizontal/rotatory nystagmus (slow component away from the affected ear, fast component towards it on positive pressure). Indicates an erosion of the bony labyrinthine capsule (most commonly the **horizontal semicircular canal**) by cholesteatoma, with an intact, functional membranous labyrinth.
  * **False Negative Test:** Negative test despite a fistula, seen when cholesteatoma matrix or granulation tissue plugs the fistula, or when the **labyrinth is completely dead**.
  * **False Positive (Hennebert’s Sign):** Positive test with an intact drum and no fistula, seen in **congenital syphilis** (hypermobile stapes footplate) and Meniere's disease (fibrous adhesions between saccule and footplate).

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Four Distinct Functions of Larynx
notes.questionText: Write four distinct functions of larynx
notes.content:
1. **Protection of Lower Airway (Phylogenetically Most Important):** Acts as a multi-tiered sphincter during deglutition via closure of: (a) laryngeal inlet (aryepiglottic folds), (b) false vocal cords, and (c) true vocal cords, preventing pulmonary aspiration.
2. **Phonation:** Voice generation via the controlled vibration of adducted vocal folds in response to an expired subglottic air column (aerodynamic-myoelastic theory).
3. **Respiration:** Active regulation of airway resistance through vocal cord abduction during inspiration and partial adduction during expiration.
4. **Thoracic Fixation (Effort Closure):** Tight glottic closure traps air within the thoracic cage, stabilizing the chest wall during heavy lifting, coughing, vomiting, micturition, defaecation, and parturition.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Four Surgical Landmarks of Facial Nerve in Middle Ear and Mastoid Surgery
notes.questionText: Four surgical landmarks of facial nerve while doing middle ear and mastoid surgery
notes.content:
1. **Processus Cochleariformis:** Marks the first genu and the origin of the tympanic (horizontal) segment of the nerve running immediately posterior and superior to it.
2. **Horizontal Semicircular Canal and Oval Window:** The tympanic segment runs directly between the horizontal semicircular canal above and the oval window (stapes) below.
3. **Short Process of Incus in Fossa Incudis:** The second genu lies immediately medial and inferior to the tip of the short process of the incus at the aditus ad antrum.
4. **Digastric Ridge:** The mastoid (vertical) segment exits the stylomastoid foramen immediately anterior to the anterior end of the digastric ridge.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Otosclerosis
notes.questionText: A 35-year-old female patient presents with hearing loss in both ears since past 5 years. She also gives past history of exacerbation of hearing loss during pregnancy. On otoscopic examination both the tympanic membranes appear normal. a) What is your diagnosis b) What are the other clinical features of this condition c) Discuss the audiological investigations of this patient d) Discuss the treatment options for this patient. (1+2+3+4)
notes.content:
#### a) Diagnosis
* **Clinical Otosclerosis (Stapedial Otosclerosis)**.

#### b) Other Clinical Features
* **Progressive Hearing Loss:** Painless, insidious, bilateral conductive hearing loss starting in the 2nd–3rd decades; aggravated by pregnancy, lactation, or menopause.
* **Paracusis Willisii (Pathognomonic):** The patient paradoxically hears better in noisy environments than in quiet surroundings (because normal speakers subconsciously raise their voice in noise, which the otosclerotic patient perceives clearly through unmasked bone conduction).
* **Tinnitus:** Constant, low-pitched roaring or buzzing tinnitus.
* **Speech Character:** Soft, well-modulated, quiet speech (because their own voice sounds abnormally loud to them via bone conduction).
* **Schwartze Sign (Flamingo Pink Sign):** Pinkish or reddish glow seen through an intact drum over the promontory, indicating active hypervascularity of an active focus.

#### c) Audiological Investigations
1. **Tuning Fork Tests:** Rinne test negative bilaterally (BC > AC); Weber test central or lateralized to the worse ear; Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) test normal.
2. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):**
   * Shows a conductive hearing loss with a significant Air-Bone Gap (A-B gap), predominantly affecting lower frequencies.
   * **Carhart’s Notch:** Characteristic dip in the **bone conduction curve** maximal at **2000 Hz (15 dB at 2 kHz)**, caused by disruption of normal ossicular inertial resonance; disappears following successful stapedectomy.
3. **Impedance Audiometry:**
   * **Type As Tympanogram:** Normal peak pressure ($0\text{ daPa}$), but significantly reduced static compliance ($<0.3$ mL) due to stapedial ankylosis.
   * **Absent Stapedial Reflex:** Reflex is absent because the fixed stapes footplate cannot be moved by the stapedius muscle.
4. **Speech Audiometry:** Speech Discrimination Score is characteristically excellent ($>90–100\%$) unless cochlear otosclerosis supervenes.

#### d) Treatment Options
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF OTOSCLEROSIS
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
Medical / Conservative                               Surgical Therapy
  1. Hearing Aids (BTE/ITE)                            - Small-Fenestra Stapedotomy
  2. Sodium Fluoride Therapy                             (Standard of Care)
     (20-40 mg/day; arrests active focus)              - Total / Partial Stapedectomy
  3. Bisphosphonates                                     (Piston: Teflon / Platinum)
```
1. **Surgical Treatment (Stapedotomy / Stapedectomy — Treatment of Choice):**
   * *Selection Criteria:* Conductive loss $\ge 30$ dB, A-B gap $\ge 20–25$ dB, speech discrimination $\ge 60\%$. Always operate on the poorer hearing ear first.
   * *Procedure (Small-Fenestra Stapedotomy):* Under local anesthesia $\rightarrow$ transcanal approach via Rosen’s incision $\rightarrow$ elevate tympanomeatal flap $\rightarrow$ verify stapedial fixation $\rightarrow$ divide stapedius tendon $\rightarrow$ disarticulate incudostapedial joint $\rightarrow$ fracture and remove stapes superstructure $\rightarrow$ create a 0.6 mm micro-fenestra in the center of the footplate using a micro-drill, pick, or laser $\rightarrow$ insert a 0.4–0.6 mm Teflon piston hooked over the incus long process.
2. **Hearing Aids:** Air-conduction digital hearing aids provide an effective non-surgical alternative for patients refusing surgery, unfit for anesthesia, or with an only-hearing ear.
3. **Medical Therapy (Sodium Fluoride):** Indicated only in **active otosclerosis** (positive Schwartze sign) or rapidly progressing cochlear otosclerosis to accelerate bone remineralization and arrest sensorineural decline.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)
notes.questionText: A 14-year-old male patient is brought to the ENT Out Patient Department with history of repeated nasal bleed for 2 months. There is no history of trauma. On anterior rhinoscopy a reddish mass is seen in the left nasal cavity. a) What is your probable diagnosis b) What is the etiopathogenesis c) What are the other clinical symptoms and signs of this condition d) Radiological signs of this condition e) Discuss its surgical management. (1+2+2+2+3)
notes.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 14yo male, repeated unprovoked epistaxis, left nasal mass, no trauma history.

#### a) Probable Diagnosis
* **Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)**.

#### b) Etiopathogenesis
* **Demographics:** Occurs almost exclusively in **adolescent males** (second decade of life, 10–20 years).
* **Hormonal Dependence:** Highly sensitive to androgenic stimulation; growth is driven by testosterone receptor activation within vascular tissue.
* **Site of Origin:** Arises from a vascular nidus ofembryonic tissue located in the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity, specifically at the superior margin of the **sphenopalatine foramen**.
* **Histopathology:** Non-encapsulated, benign lesion composed of two components:
  1. *Vascular network:* Thin-walled, irregular endothelial channels lacking a complete muscularis layer (tunica media) and elastic lamina. Because the vessels cannot contract or vasconstrict, manipulation or biopsy causes massive, uncontrollable hemorrhage.
  2. *Fibrous stroma:* Dense to loose collagenous connective tissue background.

#### c) Other Clinical Symptoms and Signs
* **Symptoms:**
  * Unilateral, progressive nasal obstruction leading to bilateral blockage as the mass grows into the nasopharynx.
  * Hyponasal speech (*rhinolalia clausa*).
  * Unilateral conductive hearing loss, autophony, and recurrent otitis media with effusion due to mechanical obstruction of the Eustachian tube cushion.
  * Anosmia/hyposmia.
  * Facial deformity, headache, diplopia, and cheek numbness (CN $V_2$ compression).
* **Signs:**
  * *Anterior Rhinoscopy / Endoscopy:* Lobulated, firm, pinkish-to-dark-red or purplish mass filling the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx.
  * *External Deformity:*
    * Protrusion of the cheek due to extension into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae.
    * Proptosis, lateral displacement of the eyeball, and broadening of the nasal root (**"frog-face deformity"**).
  * **Clinical Caveat:** **Biopsy is strictly contraindicated in the outpatient department** due to the catastrophic risk of torrential, life-threatening hemorrhage.

#### d) Radiological Signs
1. **Holman–Miller Sign (Antral Sign):**
   * Seen on axial CT/MRI and lateral radiographs: Pathognomonic **anterior bowing and forward push of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum** caused by tumour expansion within the pterygomaxillary/pterygopalatine fossa.
2. **Widening of Sphenopalatine Foramen & Pterygomaxillary Fissure:** Expansion and bony remodeling without osteoclastic infiltration.
3. **Contrast-Enhanced CT / MRI:** Demonstrates intense, vivid, heterogeneous contrast enhancement and delineates extension into the orbit, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and sphenoid sinus.

#### e) Surgical Management
```
                     MANAGEMENT WORKFLOW FOR JNA
                                  |
              Preoperative Digital Subtraction Angiography
                                  |
                                  v
           Superselective Embolization (24–48 hours prior)
                                  |
                                  v
                  Definitive Surgical Resection
                                  |
      +---------------------------+---------------------------+
      |                                                       |
Endoscopic / Transnasal Approach                     Open External Approaches
  - Radkowski Stage I & II                             - Transpalatal
  - Powered microdebriders, coblation                  - Lateral Rhinotomy / Weber-Ferguson
  - Strict preservation of ICA                         - Sublabial Midfacial Degloving
                                                       - Infratemporal Fossa Approach (Fisch)
```
1. **Preoperative Angiography & Embolization (Mandatory):**
   * Superselective catheterization of the internal maxillary artery branches.
   * Transarterial embolization using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles or Gelfoam performed **24 to 48 hours prior to surgery** to reduce intraoperative blood loss by up to 70–80%.
2. **Surgical Approaches (Selected by Stage):**
   * **Transnasal Endoscopic Resection:** Currently the standard of care for Radkowski Stages I and II (tumours confined to the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, ethmoids, sphenoid, and medial pterygopalatine fossa).
   * **Transpalatal Approach:** Provides direct midline exposure of the nasopharynx for localized posterior choanal tumours.
   * **Lateral Rhinotomy / Weber–Fergusson Approach:** For large tumours involving the maxilla, orbit, and anterior ethmoids.
   * **Sublabial Midfacial Degloving:** Provides bilateral, wide exposure of the midface without visible external facial incisions.
   * **Infratemporal Fossa Approach (Fisch Type C/D):** For massive lesions invading the infratemporal fossa, parasellar region, or cavernous sinus.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess: Clinical Features and Management
notes.questionText: Clinical features and management of acute retropharyngeal abscess.
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Suppuration within the potential retropharyngeal space of Gillette, situated between the buccopharyngeal fascia anteriorly and the alar/prevertebral fascia posteriorly.

#### Clinical Features
* **Demographics:** Most commonly seen in infants and children under 3–4 years of age due to suppuration of the lymph nodes of Rouviere (which atrophy after age 4–5).
* **Symptoms:**
  * Sudden onset high fever with toxaemia and irritability.
  * Inability or refusal to suckle/swallow (**odynophagia/dysphagia**), with persistent drooling of saliva.
  * Inspiratory stridor, dyspnea, and a muffled, croupy, **"quacking duck"** cry.
  * Torticollis: Child holds the neck extended and tilted to one side; passive neck flexion produces severe pain.
* **Signs:**
  * *Oropharyngeal Inspection:* Unilateral, smooth, rounded bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall (confined to one side of the midline due to the median raphe).
  * Tender, enlarged upper deep cervical lymph nodes.

#### Management
1. **Airway Security (Primary Concern):** Maintain the child in a propped-up or Trendelenburg position. Emergency endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy if stridor is severe.
2. **Parenteral Antibiotic Therapy:** Broad-spectrum IV coverage against *Staph. aureus*, *Streptococcus*, and anaerobes:
   * IV Amoxicillin-Clavulanic acid + IV Metronidazole **OR** IV Ceftriaxone + Clindamycin.
3. **Incision and Drainage (Transoral I&D — Treatment of Choice):**
   * Performed in the operation theatre under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, or in the conscious child secured in a **steep Trendelenburg (head-low) position** to prevent aspiration.
   * A vertical incision is made over the most prominent fluctuant area of the posterior pharyngeal wall using a guarded knife.
   * An assistant applies continuous, powerful suction to evacuate pus immediately upon entering the cavity.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Bell’s Palsy: Etiology and Management
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Acute, isolated, idiopathic, lower motor neuron paralysis or paresis of the facial nerve, presenting over a period of $<72$ hours.

#### Etiology
1. **Viral Reactivation (Primary Cause):** Latent **Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1)** or Varicella-Zoster Virus reactivation within the geniculate ganglion.
2. **Microvascular Ischaemia & Entrapment Neuropathy:** Primary neural ischemia $\rightarrow$ capillary breakdown $\rightarrow$ endoneurial oedema within the rigid, unyielding **labyrinthine segment** of the fallopian canal $\rightarrow$ secondary venous compression and conduction block (**neurapraxia**).
3. **Autoimmune Reactions:** Cell-mediated demyelination following acute viral prodromes.
4. **Hereditary Susceptibility:** Narrowed bony fallopian canal in a subset of patients.

#### Management
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF BELL'S PALSY
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
Medical Pharmacotherapy                     Supportive & Eye Care
  1. Systemic Corticosteroids                 1. Lubricating Drops (Daytime)
     - Oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day x 10d)  2. Ointment & Eye Taping (Night)
  2. Antiviral Therapy (Severe cases:         3. Dark Sunglasses
     House-Brackmann Grade IV-VI)             4. Facial Physiotherapy
     - Oral Valacyclovir / Acyclovir
```
1. **Medical Pharmacotherapy (Standard of Care):**
   * **Systemic Oral Corticosteroids:** Most critical drug. Must be initiated within 72 hours of onset:
     * **Oral Prednisolone: 1 mg/kg/day (typically 60 mg daily)** for 5–7 days, followed by a 5-day taper (total 10–12 days). Reduces endoneurial oedema within the fallopian canal.
   * **Antiviral Therapy:** 
     * Indicated in severe cases (House-Brackmann Grade IV–VI): Oral **Valacyclovir (1000 mg TID)** or **Acyclovir (400 mg 5 times daily)** for 7 days in combination with steroids.
2. **Eye Protection (Crucial to Prevent Exposure Keratitis):**
   * Due to lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) and loss of corneal blink reflex:
     * Preservative-free artificial tear drops (0.5% carboxymethylcellulose) instilled hourly during waking hours.
     * High-viscosity eye lubricating ointment and nocturnal eye taping/pad.
     * Sunglasses to protect against dust and wind trauma.
3. **Surgical Decompression:**
   * Indicated only if Electroneuronography (ENoG) reveals **$>90\%$ nerve degeneration within 14 days** of complete paralysis and EMG shows no voluntary motor unit potentials.
   * Involves transmastoid/middle cranial fossa decompression of the labyrinthine and tympanic segments.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Peripheral Vertigo: Causes and Management of BPPV
notes.questionText: Enumerate the causes of peripheral vertigo. Discuss the management of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo.
notes.content:
* **Causes of Peripheral Vertigo:**
  1. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV — most common).
  2. Meniere’s Disease (Endolymphatic hydrops).
  3. Vestibular Neuronitis.
  4. Labyrinthitis (Circumscribed, Serous, Suppurative).
  5. Perilymph Fistula.
  6. Labyrinthine concussion / Temporal bone trauma.
  7. Ototoxicity (Aminoglycosides).
* **Management of BPPV:**
  * **Diagnostic Confirmation:** **Dix–Hallpike Manoeuvre:** Diagnostic test of choice; demonstrates latency (2–20s), geotropic torsional/rotatory nystagmus lasting $<60$ seconds, fatigability, and vertigo when the affected ear is dependent.
  * **Particle Repositioning Maneuvers (Definitive Treatment):**
    * **Epley’s Canalith Repositioning Manoeuvre (for Posterior Canal BPPV):**
      * Sequentially rotates the head through 5 spatial orientations to guide free-floating otolith particles (canaliths) out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle by gravity.
      * *Success Rate:* $>85–90\%$ complete resolution with a single manoeuvre.
    * **Semont’s Liberatory Manoeuvre:** Rapid side-to-side body-swinging repositioning.
    * **Barbeque Roll Manoeuvre (Lempert):** Indicated for lateral (horizontal) canal BPPV.
  * **Vestibular Rehabilitation:** Brandt–Daroff home exercises for persistent mild symptoms.

---

  7. **Rima Glottidis & Subglottis:** Triangular airway space between the vocal cords; upper rings of the trachea may be visible deep within.
  8. **Pyriform Sinuses:** Smooth recesses situated laterally between the aryepiglottic fold and thyroid cartilage lamina on each side.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
notes.content:
* **Embryological Basis:** Results from failure of complete obliteration of the embryonic thyroglossal duct, which descends from the **foramen caecum** at the base of the tongue through the midline neck, crossing the hyoid bone, to form the mature thyroid gland.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Most common congenital neck anomaly; commonly presents in children and young adults ($<20$ years).
  * Painless, smooth, cystic, fluctuant, non-tender midline neck mass, most commonly located **subhyoid** (60%).
  * **Pathognomonic Clinical Sign:** Moves upward with **both deglutition and active tongue protrusion** (due to fibrous tethering of the tract to the foramen caecum via the hyoid bone).
  * May undergo secondary infection following upper respiratory infection, causing rapid enlargement, redness, or rupture forming a **thyroglossal fistula**.
* **Management:**
  * Preoperative ultrasound or CT neck is mandatory to confirm the presence of a normally located orthotopic thyroid gland.
  * **Sistrunk’s Operation (Treatment of Choice):**
    * Complete en bloc surgical excision of the cyst, the entire fibrous tract, the **central one-third (body) of the hyoid bone**, and a core of muscle tissue around the tract extending to the foramen caecum.
    * Simple enucleation carries a recurrence rate $>50\%$; Sistrunk's procedure reduces recurrence to $<3\%$.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media with Postaural Mastoid Abscess
notes.questionText: A 24 -year-old male presents to the OPD with fever, otalgia and swelling over the right mastoid. He also gives history of foul smelling scanty right ear discharge for the last three years. On examination there is a retraction pocket in the right tympanic me mbrane with whitish flakes and a boggy swelling in the right postaural region. a) What is your provisional diagnosis b) What is the immediate intervention to be planned c) What are the other clinical features of this condition d) What are the investigations to be done in this patient e) Discuss the treatment options for this patient (1+1+2+3+3)
notes.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 24yo male, fever, right otalgia, mastoid swelling, scanty foul-smelling otorrhoea for 3 years, attic retraction pocket with white flakes, boggy postaural swelling.

#### a) Provisional Diagnosis
* **Right Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Atticoantral (Squamosal / Unsafe) Type, with Cholesteatoma, complicated by Acute Coalescent Mastoiditis and Postaural Subperiosteal Abscess**.

#### b) Immediate Intervention to be Planned
1. **Immediate Hospitalization & Resuscitation:** Secure IV access, initiate broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, and administer analgesics.
2. **Subperiosteal Abscess Aspiration:** Urgent needle aspiration of the fluctuant postaural abscess using an 18G needle under aseptic conditions to decompress tissues, reduce pain, and obtain pus for aerobic/anaerobic culture and sensitivity.
3. **Emergency Mastoid Surgery:** Urgent surgical exploration (**Modified Radical Mastoidectomy**) within 24–48 hours once initial stabilization is achieved.

#### c) Other Clinical Features of this Condition
* **Ear Discharge:** Scanty, thick, creamy-yellow, and characteristically **foul-smelling (fetid)** due to bone destruction and anaerobic infection.
* **Otoscopy / Micro-otoscopy:** Attic or posterosuperior marginal perforation; retraction pocket packed with white, desquamated, keratotic cholesteatoma flakes; red, fleshy granulation tissue or an aural polyp presenting in the external auditory canal.
* **Conductive / Mixed Hearing Loss:** Significant hearing impairment due to necrosis of the ossicular chain (especially the long process of incus and stapes superstructure).
* **Warning Signs of Impending Complications:** Vertigo with a positive fistula sign, severe persistent hemicranial headache, projectile vomiting, facial nerve weakness, chills, rigors, and neck stiffness.

#### d) Investigations to be Done
1. **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of Temporal Bone (Mandatory):**
   * *Findings:* Soft-tissue mass in the attic, aditus, and antrum; erosion of the scutum (early sign of attic cholesteatoma); demineralization of mastoid trabeculae with coalescence; breach of the outer mastoid cortex (confirming subperiosteal abscess); integrity of tegmen tympani, sigmoid sinus plate, and lateral semicircular canal.
2. **Pus Culture and Sensitivity:** Identifies *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus*, *Staph. aureus*, and *Bacteroides fragilis*.
3. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):** Quantifies conductive or mixed hearing loss and assesses cochlear reserve before surgery.
4. **Contrast MRI Brain:** Indicated if headache, vomiting, or neurological signs suggest intracranial extension.

#### e) Treatment Options
```
                MANAGEMENT OF ATTICOANTRAL CSOM
                               |
         +---------------------+---------------------+
         |                                           |
Phase 1: Emergency Stabilization            Phase 2: Definitive Surgery
  - IV Antibiotics (Ceftriaxone +             - Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
    Metronidazole / Piperacillin-Tazobactam)    (Exteriorizes attic & antrum)
  - Postaural Abscess Needle Aspiration       - Concomitant Meatoplasty
  - Pain control & supportive care            - Tympanoplasty / Ossiculoplasty
```
* **Definitive Surgical Intervention (Canal Wall Down — Modified Radical Mastoidectomy):**
  * Approached via a postaural incision.
  * Subperiosteal abscess is drained and granulation tissue cleared.
  * The mastoid cortex is drilled to open the antrum and exteriorize the attic, aditus, and mastoid cells into a single, smooth cavity.
  * The posterior bony meatal wall is lowered to the level of the facial ridge.
  * All cholesteatoma matrix, diseased bone, and granulations are removed.
  * A wide **meatoplasty** is fashioned to ensure adequate aeration and lifelong access for cavity cleaning.
  * Hearing reconstruction (tympanoplasty/ossiculoplasty) is performed primarily or staged.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Adenoidectomy Operation
notes.content:
* **Indications:** Obstructive sleep apnoea / loud snoring in children; recurrent acute otitis media / persistent otitis media with effusion; chronic rhinosinusitis refractory to medical therapy; dental malocclusion and adenoid facies.
* **Contraindications:** Cleft palate or submucous cleft palate (causes severe velopharyngeal insufficiency and hypernasal speech); active acute upper respiratory infection; uncorrected bleeding disorders.
* **Anesthesia & Position:** General anesthesia with oral endotracheal intubation. **Rose’s position** (supine with a shoulder roll extending the neck, head stabilized on a doughnut ring).
* **Steps of Curettage Method:**
  1. A **Boyle–Davis mouth gag** is inserted and suspended with Draffin bipods.
  2. Palpation of the nasopharynx to assess size and rule out choanal atresia or pulsating vessels.
  3. A guarded **St. Clair Thomson adenoid curette** is introduced into the nasopharynx until it engages the superior border of the adenoid mass at the roof.
  4. With a gentle, shaving, curved downward sweep conforming to the posterior pharyngeal wall, the adenoid mass is resected in a single piece. Neck is slightly flexed to avoid injury to the atlas anterior tubercle.
  5. Immediate hemostasis achieved by firm packing of the nasopharynx with dry gauze swabs for 5 minutes.
  6. Persistent bleeding points are cauterized under direct vision using suction diathermy or endoscopic coblation.
* **Modern Alternative:** **Endoscopic Coblation / Microdebrider-assisted Adenoidectomy** under transoral 70° telescope vision.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Objective Tinnitus
notes.content:
* **Definition:** A rare form of tinnitus where the sound perceived by the patient is an actual physical sound generated within the body that can also be heard by the examining clinician (via auscultation with a stethoscope over the skull, neck, or external ear).
* **Causes:**
  1. **Vascular Causes (Pulsatile Tinnitus):**
     * Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) and dural AV fistulae.
     * Glomus jugulare and glomus tympanicum tumours.
     * Atherosclerotic internal carotid artery stenosis, aneurysm, or aberrant carotid artery.
     * Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumour cerebri; produces venous hum).
  2. **Muscular Causes (Clicking / Fluttering Tinnitus):**
     * **Palatal Myoclonus:** Rhythmic, involuntary contractions of the tensor veli palatini or levator veli palatini muscles.
     * Middle ear myoclonus: Clonic spasms of the stapedius or tensor tympani muscle.
  3. **Respiratory / Mechanical Causes:**
     * **Patulous Eustachian Tube:** Tube remains abnormally open; patient hears roaring sounds synchronous with nasal respiration, accompanied by autophony.
     * Temporomandibular joint clicking during mastication.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Odynophagia
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Severe, sharp, burning, or aching pain triggered specifically by the act of swallowing.
* **Distinction:** Differs from dysphagia (which represents mechanical difficulty or food arrest during transit); odynophagia and dysphagia frequently coexist.
* **Common Causes:**
  1. *Infective / Inflammatory:* Acute follicular tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), acute epiglottitis, retropharyngeal/parapharyngeal abscess, candidal/herpetic oesophagitis, Vincent’s angina.
  2. *Ulcerative:* Severe aphthous ulcers, Behçet syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris.
  3. *Traumatic:* Ingested sharp foreign bodies (fish bone in tonsil/vallecula), corrosive acid/alkali ingestion, post-tonsillectomy slough.
  4. *Neoplastic:* Advanced infiltrating ulcerated carcinomas of the hypopharynx, base of tongue, and tonsil.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Inverted Papilloma (Ringertz Tumour)
notes.questionText: Inverted papilloma – clinical features and treatment Give precise answers: (4x1=4)
notes.content:
* **Definition:** A unique, locally aggressive benign epithelial neoplasm of the sinonasal tract characterized histologically by the **inversion of surface respiratory epithelium into the underlying connective tissue stroma**, rather than outward exophytic growth.
* **Aetiology & Features:** Associated with Human Papilloma Virus (HPV types 11 and 16). Typically seen in men aged 40–70 years. Arises from the **lateral nasal wall** (middle meatus/ethmoids).
* **Clinical Features:** Unilateral progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, purulent rhinorrhoea, and hyposmia. On rhinoscopy/endoscopy, presents as a firm, lobulated, fleshy, pale-pink or dark red mulberry-like mass that bleeds on probing.
* **Clinical Significance:** 
  1. High propensity for local bone destruction and invasion into the orbit/skull base.
  2. High rate of local recurrence ($30–40\%$) if incompletely resected.
  3. Associated with **synchronous or metachronous Squamous Cell Carcinoma in 10% to 15% of cases**.
* **Treatment:** **Complete wide surgical excision with negative margins**. Modern standard is **Transnasal Endoscopic Medial Maxillectomy (TEMM)**; historically performed via lateral rhinotomy or midfacial degloving.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Tripod Fracture
notes.content:
* **Definition:** Fracture of the zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) resulting from a direct blunt blow to the malar prominence, separating the zygoma from its three primary anatomical attachments:
  1. Frontozygomatic suture (lateral orbital wall).
  2. Zygomaticomaxillary buttress and infraorbital rim (anterior maxillary wall/orbital floor).
  3. Zygomaticotemporal suture (zygomatic arch).
* **Triad of Clinical Signs:** Flattening of the malar prominence + step deformity of the infraorbital margin + anesthesia of the cheek/upper lip (injury to the infraorbital nerve).

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Foreign Body Aspiration in a 4-Year-Old Child
notes.questionText: A 4 year old boy came to emergency department with foreign body aspiration. a) Write the prominent symptoms and signs when foreign body lodges at larynx and trachea. b) What is stridor. Classify it. How it differs from stertor. c) Write the procedures of immediate airway management. d) Complications of foreign body aspiration if not treated. e) Discuss definitive treatment options of this patient. (1+2+2+2+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Symptoms and Signs Based on Site of Lodgement
* **Laryngeal Foreign Body:**
  * *Symptoms:* Immediate violent paroxysmal coughing, choking, gagging, acute aphonia or hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, retrosternal retraction, and severe dyspnoea. Complete occlusion causes sudden asphyxia and death.
  * *Signs:* Cyanosis, suprasternal/intercostal indrawing, muffled cry, palpable impact over the thyroid cartilage.
* **Tracheal Foreign Body:**
  * *Symptoms:* Choking spells, brassy cough, dyspnoea, asthmatoid wheeze heard at the open mouth.
  * *Signs:* 
    1. **Audible Slap:** Sound heard as the loose foreign body is thrown upward against the subglottis during expiration.
    2. **Palpatory Thud:** Impact felt by the examiner's thumb over the subcricoid trachea at the end of expiration.

#### b) Stridor: Definition, Classification, and Differences from Stertor
* **Definition:** A high-pitched, musical/turbulent respiratory sound produced by airflow disruption through a partially obstructed airway (from the supraglottis to the secondary bronchi).
* **Classification of Stridor:**
  1. **Inspiratory Stridor:** Originates in the supraglottis or glottis (e.g., laryngomalacia, acute epiglottitis).
  2. **Expiratory Stridor:** Originates in the lower trachea or bronchi (e.g., bronchial foreign body, tracheal stenosis).
  3. **Biphasic Stridor:** Originates at the subglottis or cervical trachea (e.g., subglottic stenosis, croup, fixed tracheal mass).
* **Differences Between Stridor and Stertor:**
  | Feature | Stridor | Stertor |
  | :--- | :--- | :--- |
  | **Site of Origin** | Larynx, trachea, or bronchi. | Nasopharynx, oropharynx, or soft palate. |
  | **Character of Sound** | High-pitched, harsh, musical/whistling. | Low-pitched, heavy, snoring, gurgling sound. |
  | **Pathology** | Subglottic stenosis, croup, foreign body. | Adenoid hypertrophy, quinsy, retropharyngeal abscess. |

#### c) Procedures for Immediate Airway Management
1. **Heimlich Manoeuvre (Abdominal Thrusts):**
   * *Mechanism:* Rapid upward diaphragm elevation compresses intrathoracic lungs, creating an artificial cough to dislodge foreign bodies.
   * *Technique:* Stand behind the child, place a clenched fist between the xiphoid and umbilicus, and deliver rapid inward and upward thrusts.
2. **Back Blows and Chest Thrusts (for Infants $<1$ year):** Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts with the infant held prone/supine on the rescuer's forearm.
3. **Endotracheal Intubation or Rigid Bronchoscopy:** Direct visualization and insertion of a ventilating bronchoscope to bypass obstruction.
4. **Needle / Surgical Cricothyroidotomy:** Rapid emergency access through the cricothyroid membrane when transoral access fails.

#### d) Complications of Retained Foreign Body
* Acute complete asphyxia and death.
* Severe necrotizing tracheobronchitis ("vegetal bronchitis" from organic seeds releasing fatty acids).
* Ball-valve bronchial obstruction causing lobar obstructive emphysema.
* Complete bronchial obstruction leading to obstructive atelectasis (lung collapse).
* Secondary lung suppuration: Bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonitis, lung abscess, bronchopleural fistula, and empyema.

#### e) Definitive Treatment Options
* **Rigid Ventilating Bronchoscopy (Treatment of Choice):**
  * Performed under general anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation.
  * Appropriate-sized rigid ventilating bronchoscope is introduced.
  * The foreign body is visualized and grasped using dedicated optical foreign body forceps.
  * The foreign body, forceps, and bronchoscope are extracted together as a single unit, keeping the bevel horizontal at the glottis.
  * Re-introduction of the bronchoscope is mandatory to clear fragments and rule out a second foreign body.
* **Flexible Bronchoscopy:** Useful for distally impacted subsegmental foreign bodies; carries risk of airway loss in children.
* **Thoracotomy and Bronchotomy:** Rarely indicated ($<1\%$) for foreign bodies that cannot be removed endoscopically.

---

notes.title: Unsafe CSOM with Cholesteatoma
notes.questionText: A 35-year-old female patient presents with complaints of discharge in the left ear since childhood. The discharge is scanty, purulent and foul smelling. Otoscopic examination revealed a posterosuperior marginal perforation with whitish flakes in the ear. a) What is your diagnosis. b) Etiopathogenesis of this condition. c) Enumerate the complications associated with this disease. d) Describe the surgical management of this disease. (1+3+3+3)
notes.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 35yo female, chronic scanty foul-smelling left ear discharge, posterosuperior marginal perforation with whitish flakes.

#### a) Diagnosis
* **Left Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Atticoantral (Squamosal / Unsafe) Type, Active Stage with Cholesteatoma**.

#### b) Etiopathogenesis of Cholesteatoma
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]] (2025_MARCH) AND Standard Theories:
1. **Wittmaack’s Invagination Theory:** Negative middle ear pressure pulls pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa inward, creating a deep retraction pocket that accumulates trapped keratin.
2. **Habermann’s Epithelial Invasion Theory:** Canal squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation where the annulus is destroyed.
3. **Ruedi’s Basal Cell Hyperplasia Theory:** Basal layers of Shrapnell’s membrane proliferate downward into subepithelial layers in response to infection.
4. **Sade’s Metaplasia Theory:** Middle ear columnar/cuboidal mucosa undergoes squamous metaplasia secondary to chronic infection.

#### c) Complications Associated with this Disease
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q03]] (2026_MARCH)

#### d) Surgical Management

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)
notes.questionText: Previously healthy 40 year old male presented with unexplained unilateral rapid loss of hearing all at once. a) Give your diagnosis by defining it. b) Describe the aetiological factors. c) Write relevant investigations with expected findings. d) What are the good and bad prognostic factors. e) Elaborate the principles of treatment. (1+2+2+2+3)
notes.content:
#### a) Definition
* An abrupt, unexplained sensorineural hearing impairment of **at least 30 dB over a minimum of 3 contiguous audiometric frequencies**, developing rapidly within **72 hours (3 days) or less**.

#### b) Aetiological Factors
1. **Idiopathic:** Accounts for $>85–90\%$ of cases.
2. **Viral Infections:** Viral labyrinthitis or cochlear neuritis due to Mumps, Measles, Rubella, Herpes Simplex, Cytomegalovirus, or Influenza.
3. **Vascular Occlusion / Ischaemia:** Sudden thrombosis, embolism, hemorrhage, or severe vasospasm of the labyrinthine artery (a terminal end-artery), seen in diabetes, hypertension, and hypercoagulable states.
4. **Intracochlear Membrane Rupture:** Sudden rupture of Reissner’s membrane, the round window membrane, or oval window annular ligament (perilymph fistula) caused by physical strain, diving, or blast trauma.
5. **Autoimmune Inner Ear Disease (AIED):** Systemic lupus erythematosus, Cogan syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis.
6. **Neoplastic:** Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma presents with sudden SNHL in 10% of cases).
7. **Ototoxic Medications:** Rapid administration of aminoglycosides or loop diuretics.

#### c) Relevant Investigations and Expected Findings
* **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):** Confirms SNHL of $\ge 30$ dB across at least 3 contiguous frequencies; helps evaluate audiogram shape (flat, up-sloping, down-sloping, or profound/dead ear).
* **Impedance Audiometry:** Type A (normal) tympanogram excludes middle ear effusion.
* **Speech Discrimination Score (SDS):** Typically reduced in sensory and markedly depressed in retrocochlear lesions.
* **Contrast-Enhanced MRI of Brain & IAC (Mandatory):** Rule out an intracanalicular acoustic neuroma or multiple sclerosis.
* **Laboratory Battery:** Complete blood count, ESR, blood glucose, lipid profile, thyroid function tests, autoimmune work-up (ANA, RF), and viral/syphilitic serology (FTA-ABS).

#### d) Prognostic Factors
| Favourable (Good) Prognosis | Unfavourable (Poor) Prognosis |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mild to moderate hearing loss ($<60$ dB). | Severe to profound hearing loss / flat or total loss ($>90$ dB). |
| Up-sloping (low-frequency) audiogram. | Down-sloping (high-frequency) or flat audiogram. |
| **Absence of vertigo / vestibular symptoms.** | **Presence of concurrent severe vertigo** (indicates extensive labyrinthine damage). |
| Young patients ($<40$ years). | Extremes of age ($<15$ years or $>65$ years). |
| Early initiation of treatment ($<7–10$ days). | Delayed presentation ($>2–3$ weeks). |
| Significant recovery starting within 14 days. | Elevated ESR and underlying untreated systemic disease. |

#### e) Principles of Treatment
```
                   MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL FOR SSNHL
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
Primary Medical Therapy                      Salvage / Adjunctive Therapy
  - High-dose Systemic Corticosteroids          - Intratympanic Dexamethasone
    (Oral Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day x 7-14 d)    - Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)
  - Strict Bed Rest & Low-Salt Diet             - Rheological Agents & Vasodilators
```
1. **Systemic Corticosteroid Therapy (Cornerstone of Treatment):**
   * Oral Prednisolone: **1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg/day)** as a single morning dose for 7–14 days, followed by a gradual taper over the next 7–10 days. Relieves cochlear inflammation and microvascular oedema.
2. **Intratympanic Corticosteroid Injections:**
   * Dexamethasone (4 mg/mL) or Methylprednisolone instilled into the middle ear via a posterior-inferior quadrant needle puncture.
   * *Indications:* Primary therapy for patients with contraindications to systemic steroids (uncontrolled diabetes, active peptic ulcer, severe hypertension) or as **salvage therapy** when systemic therapy fails.
3. **Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT):**
   * Inhalation of 100% $O_2$ at 2.0–2.5 atmospheres absolute (ATA) for 90 minutes daily (10–20 sessions). Increases dissolved oxygen levels in perilymph, restoring hair cell metabolism; approved by UHMS if started within 2 weeks of onset.
4. **Supportive / Rheological Measures:**
   * Bed rest, avoiding straining/Valsalva, low-salt diet, carbogen inhalation (95% $O_2$ + 5% $CO_2$) to promote cerebral/labyrinthine vasodilation.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Impedance Audiometry: Indications, Procedure, and Interpretation
notes.questionText: Impedance audiometry: Indications, procedure, and interpretation.
notes.content:
* **Indications:**
  1. Diagnosis and monitoring of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME).
  2. Differentiation between ossicular chain fixation (otosclerosis) and discontinuity.
  3. Objective hearing threshold screening in neonates and young children.
  4. Evaluating Eustachian tube function.
  5. Topodiagnosis of facial nerve paralysis (stapedial reflex arc).
  6. Detection of retrocochlear lesions (acoustic reflex decay).
* **Procedure:** An airtight probe is inserted into the external auditory meatus containing three channels:
  1. *Loudspeaker:* Delivers a probe tone (226 Hz at 85 dB SPL).
  2. *Microphone:* Measures the reflected sound energy.
  3. *Air pump/manometer:* Changes canal pressure from $+200$ to $-400\text{ daPa}$.

#### Interpretation of Tympanograms (Jerger Classification)

```
Compliance
      ^       Type A (Normal)          Type Ad (Discontinuity)
      |            /\                           | |
      |           /  \                          | |
      |          /    \                         | |
      |         /      \                        | |
      |   Type As (Stiffness)             Type B (Flat - Fluid)
      |          /\                     ---------------------
      |    +----+--+----+               Type C (Negative Pressure)
      |    |            |                       /\
      |    |            |                      /  \
      +----+-----+------+-----+--------->     /    \
        -400   -200     0   +200 daPa      -200     0
```

* **Type A (Normal):** Symmetrical peak at ambient pressure (between $-100\text{ and }+50\text{ daPa}$) with normal compliance (0.3–1.6 mL).
* **Type As (Stiffness):** Peak at normal pressure ($0\text{ daPa}$), but with abnormally reduced compliance ($<0.3$ mL). Seen in **otosclerosis** and malleus fixation.
* **Type Ad (Deep/Discontinuity):** Normal pressure peak with high/open-ended compliance ($>1.6$ mL). Seen in **ossicular chain disruption** or flaccid atrophic scars of the drum.
* **Type B (Flat/Dome):** Flat curve with no compliance peak. Seen in **middle ear effusion** (normal canal volume), hemotympanum, or drum perforation (large canal volume).
* **Type C:** Peak shifted to marked negative pressure ($<-100\text{ daPa}$). Seen in **Eustachian tube obstruction** and early/resolving OME.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Vasomotor Rhinitis (VMR)
notes.questionText: Pathogenesis, clinical features and treatment of vasomotor rhinitis.
notes.content:
* **Definition:** A non-infectious, non-allergic form of chronic rhinosinusitis characterized by autonomic neurovascular instability of the nasal mucosa with hyper-reactivity to non-specific physical and emotional stimuli.
* **Pathogenesis:**
  * Imbalance between the parasympathetic and sympathetic nerve supply to the nasal turbinate erectile tissue:
    * *Parasympathetic overactivity* (via greater superficial petrosal / Vidian nerve) $\rightarrow$ excessive acetylcholine release $\rightarrow$ arteriolar and cavernous sinusoid vasodilation + hypersecretion from seromucinous nasal glands.
    * *Sympathetic underactivity* (loss of vasoconstrictor tone).
  * Provoked by non-specific triggers: Sudden changes in temperature/humidity, cold wind, spicy foods, cigarette smoke, emotional stress.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Paroxysmal sneezing (especially on stepping out of bed in the morning).
  * Profuse watery rhinorrhoea that drips on leaning forward.
  * Alternating, positional nasal obstruction (worse on the dependent side during sleep).
  * *Rhinoscopy:* Nasal mucosa over the inferior turbinates appears swollen, congested, and purplish/hypertrophic, but shrinks promptly on application of topical vasoconstrictors. All allergy tests (skin prick, serum IgE) are negative.
* **Treatment:**
  1. *Avoidance:* Identify and avoid precipitating thermal, chemical, and atmospheric triggers.
  2. *Topical Anticholinergics:* **Ipratropium bromide** nasal spray (0.03–0.06%); drug of choice for pure rhinorrhoea ("runny nose").
  3. *Topical Nasal Steroids:* Fluticasone or Budesonide to reduce mucosal hyper-reactivity.
  4. *Oral Antihistamines & Decongestants:* Provide symptomatic relief for congestion and sneezing.
  5. *Surgical Options (for refractory cases):*
     * Surgical reduction of hypertrophic inferior turbinates (submucosal diathermy, radiofrequency ablation, partial turbinectomy).
     * **Vidian Neurectomy:** Sectioning of the Vidian nerve to eliminate parasympathetic secretomotor drive; reserved for intractable, disabling rhinorrhoea.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Tympanoplasty: Definition and Types (Wullstein Classification)
notes.questionText: Define tympanoplasty and write the different types.
notes.content:
* **Definition:** An operative procedure designed to eradicate middle ear cleft disease and reconstruct the sound-conducting mechanism (tympanic membrane and/or ossicular chain), with or without mastoidectomy.

#### Wullstein Classification of Tympanoplasty

```
Type I: Myringoplasty      Type II: Bridge to Incus   Type III: Myringostapediopexy
    [ Graft ]                 [ Graft ]                  [ Graft ]
       |                         |                          |
    [Malleus]                 [Remnant Malleus]             |
       |                         |                          |
    [Incus]                   [Incus]                       |
       |                         |                          |
    [Stapes]                  [Stapes]                   [Stapes Head]
       |                         |                          |
   (Footplate)               (Footplate)                (Footplate)

Type IV: Cavum Minor                                  Type V: Fenestration
    [ Graft to Promontory ]                               [ Graft ]
       |                                                     |
    [Stapes Footplate exposed]                            (HSC Fenestra)
    (Protects Round Window)
```

1. **Type I (Myringoplasty):** 
   * Defect is limited to the tympanic membrane; ossicular chain is intact and fully mobile. Graft is placed over the denuded drum remnant/malleus.
2. **Type II:** 
   * Perforation of the drum with partial erosion of the malleus handle. The graft is placed directly onto the incus or the healthy remnant of the malleus handle.
3. **Type III (Myringostapediopexy / Columella Tympanoplasty):** 
   * Malleus and incus are absent or eroded; stapes superstructure is intact and mobile. The graft is placed directly onto the head (capitulum) of the stapes.
4. **Type IV (Cavum Minor):** 
   * Malleus, incus, and stapes superstructure are lost; mobile stapes footplate remains. The graft is placed over the promontory, shielding the round window niche (creating an air pocket from the Eustachian tube to the round window) while leaving the stapes footplate directly exposed to sound waves.
5. **Type V (Fenestration Operation):** 
   * Stapes footplate is fixed (e.g., otosclerosis); a new window is surgically created in the horizontal semicircular canal and covered with a graft.

notes.title: Precancerous (Premalignant) Lesions of Oral Mucosa
notes.content:
* **Definition:** A morphologically altered tissue in which oral cancer is significantly more likely to occur than in its apparently normal counterpart (WHO definition).

#### 1. Leukoplakia
* *Definition:* A predominantly white lesion or plaque of the oral mucosa that cannot be wiped away and cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other specific disease entity.
* *Aetiology:* Heavy smoking, chewing gutkha/tobacco with slaked lime, alcohol abuse, chronic trauma from a sharp tooth.
* *Clinical Varieties:*
  * *Homogenous (Flat/Wrinkled):* Low malignant potential (~1–3%).
  * *Non-Homogenous (Nodular, Verrucous, Speckled / Erythroleukoplakia):* High malignant transformation rate (up to 15–20%).
* *Pathology:* Hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, with varying degrees of epithelial dysplasia (mild, moderate, severe, carcinoma-in-situ).

#### 2. Erythroplakia
* *Definition:* A clinically fiery-red velvety patch or plaque on the oral mucosa that cannot be attributed pathologically to any other identifiable inflammatory/dermatological condition.
* *Significance:* Carries the **highest malignant potential** of all oral lesions; $>85–90\%$ of erythroplakic lesions demonstrate severe epithelial dysplasia, carcinoma-in-situ, or frank invasive squamous cell carcinoma at initial biopsy.

#### 3. Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSF)
* Associated with areca nut and pan masala chewing. Characterized by submucosal band formation, severe trismus, epithelial atrophy, and a malignant transformation rate of **3% to 7.6%**. (REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:315001:Q23]]`).

#### 4. Lichen Planus (Erosive / Atrophic Type)
* T-cell mediated chronic autoimmune disease. The non-healing erosive and bullous forms have a small but definite risk ($0.5–2\%$) of malignant change.

#### 5. Actinic Cheilitis: Premalignant dysplastic change on the vermilion border of the lower lip due to chronic ultraviolet solar radiation.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR / BERA): Generators and Uses
notes.questionText: What is Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR). Describe the anatomic site of neural generators for various waves and uses of ABR.
notes.content:
* **Definition:** An objective electrophysiological measurement of far-field electrical potentials generated by the 8th cranial nerve and ascending brainstem auditory pathways within the first 10 milliseconds following acoustic transient stimuli (clicks or tone-bursts).

#### Anatomic Site of Neural Generators
* In a normal individual, a series of **7 positive vertex waves** are recorded within 10 msec:

```
Wave Number             Anatomic Site of Neural Generator
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Wave I     -----------> Distal segment of Cranial Nerve VIII (Cochlear Nerve)
Wave II    -----------> Proximal segment of Cranial Nerve VIII (near brainstem)
Wave III   -----------> Cochlear Nucleus (Lower Pons)
Wave IV    -----------> Superior Olivary Complex (Pons)
Wave V     -----------> Lateral Lemniscus / Inferior Colliculus (Midbrain)
Wave VI    -----------> Inferior Colliculus
Wave VII   -----------> Medial Geniculate Body / Thalamocortical Radiations
----------------------------------------------------------------------
*Mnemonic for primary waves:* "E - E - CO - L - I"
(Eighth nerve, Eighth nerve proximal, Cochlear nucleus, Lateral lemniscus, Inferior colliculus)
```
* Waves I, III, and V are the most robust, consistent, and clinically analyzed components.

#### Clinical Uses of ABR
1. **Universal Newborn & Infant Hearing Screening:** Objective threshold screening in neonates and high-risk nursery graduates; passes if Wave V is identified at 30–35 dB nHL.
2. **Objective Hearing Threshold Determination:** Quantifies hearing threshold within 10–15 dB in uncooperative individuals, mentally challenged patients, and infants.
3. **Diagnosis of Retrocochlear Pathology (Acoustic Neuroma):** High sensitivity ($>95\%$ for tumours $>1$ cm); characteristic findings include:
   * Prolongation of absolute latency of Wave V.
   * Prolongation of interpeak latency between Wave I and V ($>4.0$ msec) or Wave I and III.
   * Interaural Wave V latency difference ($IT_5$) $>0.2$ msec.
4. **Evaluation of Auditory Neuropathy Spectrum Disorder (ANSD):** ABR is characteristically absent or grossly abnormal despite preserved cochlear outer hair cell function (demonstrated by intact normal OAEs).
5. **Detection of Brainstem Lesions:** Useful in confirming brainstem demyelination in multiple sclerosis, brainstem gliomas, and confirming brainstem death in ICU patients.
6. **Intraoperative Monitoring:** Real-time monitoring of CN VIII and brainstem integrity during acoustic neuroma surgery or microvascular decompression.

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Complications of Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)
notes.content:
Complications of FESS are categorized into major and minor, based on proximity to the orbit, skull base, and carotid artery:

#### 1. Major (Life-Threatening / Vision-Threatening) Complications
* **Orbital Complications:**
  * *Intraorbital Haemorrhage / Retrobulbar Haematoma:* Caused by injury and retraction of the **anterior ethmoidal artery** into the orbit. Manifests with sudden proptosis, stony-hard globe, and progressive ischemia of the optic nerve; requires immediate emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to avoid permanent blindness.
  * *Direct Optic Nerve Injury:* Leading to irreversible blindness (especially when entering an Onodi cell).
  * *Extraocular Muscle Injury:* Most commonly involves the medial rectus muscle, causing permanent diplopia.
* **Intracranial Complications:**
  * *Cribriform Plate / Ethmoid Roof Perforation:* Leading to immediate or delayed **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Rhinorrhea**.
  * *Intracranial Infection:* Acute pyogenic meningitis, subdural abscess, or frontal lobe abscess.
  * *Intracranial Haemorrhage:* Subarachnoid or frontal lobe parenchymal haemorrhage.
* **Vascular Injury:**
  * Laceration of the **Internal Carotid Artery** (during sphenoid sinus instrumentation, especially with a dehiscent lateral wall); results in catastrophic hemorrhage and high mortality.

#### 2. Minor Complications
* Adhesions and synechiae formation between the middle turbinate and lateral nasal wall (most common late complication; leads to ostial stenosis).
* Postoperative epistaxis.
* Periorbital ecchymosis and emphysema (breach of lamina papyracea without retrobulbar bleed).
* Injury to the nasolacrimal duct (during aggressive enlargement of the maxillary ostium anteriorly), leading to persistent epiphora.
* Anosmia or hyposmia from olfactory neuroepithelium injury.
* Maxillary sinus or frontal recess ostial stenosis.
