notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Adolescent Male with Recurrent Severe Epistaxis and Nasopharyngeal Mass
notes.questionText: A 13 years old boy came to the OPD with torrential bleeding from the right nasal cavity. He gives a hi story of a similar episode of profuse, unprovoked bleeding from the right nasal cavity 6 months back, when the bleeding stopped by itself. Post nasal examination revealed a smooth, lobulated pink swelling blocking the choana. Answer the following:  What is the most probable diagnosis  Discuss the etiopathogenesis of the condition  Mention four relevant investigations and the expected findings in each  Discuss the treatment options for this patient ( 1+2+4+3)
notes.content:
#### A. Most Probable Diagnosis **Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)** of the right side [49]. --- #### B. Etiopathogenesis 1. **Nature of the Lesion**: * It is a histologically benign, non-encapsulated, locally invasive, and highly vascular tumor [49]. * Microscopically, it is composed of an irregular network of thin-walled, endothelium-lined vascular spaces lacking a muscular contractile coat (tunica media), embedded in a fibrous stroma [49]. Because of the absence of a muscular coat, vessels cannot constrict when lacerated, leading to profuse, torrential hemorrhage that fails to stop with topical vasoconstrictors [49]. 2. **Age and Gender Predilection**: * Occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males (second decade of life, typically 10–20 years) [49]. * **Hormonal Theory**: The tumor is androgen/testosterone-dependent [49]. A hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the posterolateral nasal wall is stimulated to proliferate at puberty under the influence of male sex hormones [49]. 3. **Site of Origin**: * Arises from the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity, specifically near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen, at the junction where the sphenoidal process of the palatine bone meets the pterygoid process [49]. 4. **Pattern of Spread**: * **Anteriorly**: Extends into the nasal cavity, pushing the septum and causing unilateral/bilateral nasal obstruction [49]. * **Posteriorly**: Expands into the nasopharynx and projects behind the soft palate or into the contralateral choana [49]. * **Laterally**: Traverses the sphenopalatine foramen into the pterygopalatine fossa, displacing the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus forwards (giving the pathognomonic **Holman-Miller sign** / antral sign on imaging) [49, 50]. Further lateral spread enters the infratemporal fossa and cheek, producing a characteristic facial cheek swelling [49]. * **Superiorly / Intracranially**: Erodes the sphenoid sinus, sella turcica, and middle cranial fossa (lying medial or lateral to the internal carotid artery), or enters the orbit via the inferior orbital fissure (proptosis, "frog-face deformity") [49]. ``` [Sphenopalatine Foramen Origin] | +-----------------------+-----------------------+ | | | (Anteriorly) (Posteriorly) (Laterally) Nasal Cavity Nasopharynx Pterygopalatine Fossa | | | Nasal Obstruction Blocks Choana Anterior bowing of & Epistaxis post. antral wall (Holman-Miller Sign) | Infratemporal Fossa and Cheek ``` --- #### C. Four Relevant Investigations and Expected Findings * **Diagnostic Rule**: **Preoperative biopsy is strictly contraindicated** in an outpatient setting due to the danger of torrential, uncontrollable hemorrhage [50]. | Investigation | Expected Findings | | :--- | :--- | | **1. Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Head, Neck, & PNS** (Bone & Soft Tissue Windows) [50] | • **Holman-Miller Sign (Antral Sign)**: Pathognomonic anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum [50, 503f].
• Widening of the sphenopalatine foramen and pterygopalatine fossa [50].
• Bony erosion of the sphenoid sinus base, pterygoid plates, and skull base [49, 50].
• Lobulated, strongly enhancing soft-tissue mass filling the nasopharynx and nasal cavity [49, 50]. | | **2. Contrast MRI (with Gadolinium)** [50] | • Delineates deep soft-tissue boundaries, dura mater integrity, and cavernous sinus or intracranial intradural/extradural extension [50].
• Demonstrates typical "salt and pepper" appearance on T1/T2 sequences due to multiple flow voids within large vascular channels [49, 50]. | | **3. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) — 4-Vessel Angiography** [50] | • Maps the vascular supply: Primary blood supply arises from the **internal maxillary artery** (branch of external carotid artery) [50].
• Identifies additional feeders: Ascending pharyngeal artery, accessory meningeal artery, or internal carotid branches (in cases with skull base/intracranial invasion) [50].
• Serves as an immediate conduit for **transfemoral therapeutic embolization** [50]. | | **4. Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (Rigid 0°/30°)** [50] | • Under strict visualization without manipulation: Smooth, lobulated, fibrous, reddish-pink to purplish mass covered with intact mucosa filling the right posterior choana and postnasal space [49].
• Visualizes contact bleed or pooling of fresh blood in the nasopharynx [49]. | --- #### D. Treatment Options 1. **Preoperative Embolization**: * Superselective catheterization and embolization of feeding branches (Internal Maxillary Artery) with Gelfoam, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles, or coils, performed **24 to 48 hours prior to surgical resection** [50, 281f]. This substantially reduces intraoperative blood loss [50]. 2. **Surgical Resection (Mainstay of Treatment)** [50]: * The approach is determined by tumor staging and anatomical extent: * **Transnasal Endoscopic Approach**: Ideal for tumors confined to the nose, nasopharynx, sphenoid sinus, and medial pterygopalatine fossa [50, 282t]. * **Transpalatal Approach (Wilson’s / Sardana’s)**: Provides direct exposure for midline tumors confined to the nasopharynx [50, 282f, 282t]. * **Lateral Rhinotomy / Weber-Ferguson with Medial Maxillectomy**: Employed for large tumors with substantial extension into the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae [50, 282t]. * **Midfacial Degloving (Sublabial) Approach**: Provides wide exposure without external facial incisions [50]. * **Infratemporal Fossa Approach (Fisch Type C)**: Required for extensive lateral spread to the infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa base, or parasellar region [50, 282t]. * **Craniofacial / Combined Approach**: Indicated for massive intracranial extradural/intradural extension [50, 282t]. 3. **Radiotherapy**: * Reserved for inoperable tumors, residual/recurrent intracranial extension involving the cavernous sinus, or optic chiasm (dose: 30–35 Gy in divided fractions or Stereotactic Radiosurgery/CyberKnife) [50, 417t]. 4. **Hormonal & Chemotherapy**: * Flutamide (anti-androgen) or diethylstilbestrol was historically used to diminish vascularity [282]. Chemotherapy (doxorubicin, vincristine) is reserved as palliative salvage in unresectable, multi-recurrent disease [283]. ---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Unpaired Laryngeal Cartilages
notes.content:
The skeletal framework of the larynx consists of **three unpaired** and **three paired** cartilages [319]. The unpaired cartilages are:

```
                     UNPAIRED CARTILAGES OF LARYNX
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
      THYROID                   CRICOID                  EPIGLOTTIS
   (Hyaline, C4-C5)         (Hyaline, C6 Ring)        (Elastic, Leaf-like)
   • Shield-like            • Signet-ring shape       • Covers laryngeal
   • 90° male / 120° female • Only complete ring        inlet in deglutition
   • Adam's apple           • Subglottic support      • Does not ossify
```

1. **Thyroid Cartilage**:
   * **Type**: Hyaline cartilage; undergoes progressive ossification after 25 years of age [319].
   * **Structure**: Composed of two quadrilateral laminae (alae) that fuse anteriorly in the midline to form the **laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple)** [319, 508].
   * **Angle of Fusion**: 90° in adult males (prominent), 120° in adult females (less prominent) [319].
   * **Processes**: Each posterior border projects upwards as the **superior cornu** (attached to the tip of the greater horn of hyoid bone by the lateral thyrohyoid ligament) and downwards as the **inferior cornu** (articulates with the cricoid cartilage at the cricothyroid synovial joint) [319, 320].
   * **Attachments**: Inner surface of the thyroid angle gives attachment to:
     * Stem of the epiglottis (thyroepiglottic ligament) [320].
     * Ventricular bands (vestibular ligaments) [320].
     * True vocal cords (vocal ligaments) [320].
     * Thyroarytenoid and vocalis muscles [320].

2. **Cricoid Cartilage**:
   * **Type**: Hyaline cartilage [319].
   * **Structure**: Shaped like a **signet-ring** [319]. It has a deep, broad quadrate lamina posteriorly and a narrow arch anteriorly [319].
   * **Significance**: It is the **only complete, unbroken cartilaginous ring** in the entire respiratory tract [319]. It lies at the level of C6 vertebra, marking the junction between the larynx and trachea [319].
   * **Articulations**:
     * Posterosuperior border of the lamina articulates with the base of the arytenoid cartilages (cricoarytenoid joint) [319].
     * Lateral facets articulate with the inferior cornua of the thyroid cartilage (cricothyroid joint) [320].

3. **Epiglottis**:
   * **Type**: Yellow elastic fibrocartilage; **never ossifies** with age [319, 508].
   * **Structure**: A leaf-shaped, flexible lamella situated behind the hyoid bone and root of the tongue, projecting obliquely upwards behind the tongue base and forming the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet [319, 321].
   * **Attachments**:
     * Slender inferior stalk (petiole) is attached to the thyroid angle by the thyroepiglottic ligament [319].
     * Anterior surface is connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament, creating the boundary of the pre-epiglottic space [319, 320f].
   * **Function**: Directs the food bolus laterally into the pyriform fossae and provides sphincteric protection during deglutition [323].

*Reference diagram*: [Cartilages of the Larynx - Anterior & Posterior Views](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/2307_Cartilages_of_the_Larynx.jpg)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Treatment of Bell’s Palsy
notes.content:
Bell's palsy is an acute, idiopathic, lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial nerve [103].

#### A. General & Supportive Measures
1. **Eye Care (Critical to prevent exposure keratitis and corneal ulceration)** [104, 108]:
   * Frequent instillation of artificial tears (0.5% carboxymethylcellulose / methylcellulose drops) during waking hours (every 1–2 hours) [108].
   * Application of lubricating antibiotic eye ointment at bedtime [108].
   * Nighttime eye patching or protective sunglasses during the day to guard against foreign body injury and wind desiccation [108].
   * Temporary tarsorrhaphy or gold weight eyelid implant in prolonged refractory paralysis [108].
2. **Reassurance and Psychological Support**: Alleviate patient anxiety regarding permanent disfigurement or stroke [104].
3. **Physiotherapy**: Gentle upward facial massage and facial muscle retraining exercises once voluntary movement initiates [104].

#### B. Medical Therapy
* Must be started as early as possible, ideally **within 72 hours of onset** [104].
1. **Oral Corticosteroids (Drug of Choice)** [104]:
   * Reduces inflammatory edema of the nerve within the narrow fallopian canal (labyrinthine segment) [99, 104].
   * **Regimen**: Oral Prednisolone **1 mg/kg/day** (usually 50–60 mg daily in divided doses) for 5 days [104].
   * If recovery begins or paresis is incomplete, taper over the next 5 days [104].
   * If paralysis remains complete and unyielding, continue full dosage for 10–14 days, followed by a 5-day taper (total duration: 15–20 days) [104].
2. **Antiviral Agents**:
   * Synergistic therapy in severe complete cases (targeting Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 reactivation) [104]:
   * Oral Acyclovir (400 mg 5 times daily for 7–10 days) or Valacyclovir (1000 mg 3 times daily for 7 days) combined with prednisolone [104].

#### C. Surgical Decompression of Facial Nerve
* **Indications**:
   * Reserved for refractory, severe cases demonstrating **≥90% axonal degeneration on Electroneuronography (ENoG)** within 14 days of complete paralysis [103, 105].
   * Complete loss of voluntary motor units on electromyography (EMG) [103].
* **Procedure**:
   * Transmastoid extralabyrinthine approach to decompress the vertical (mastoid) and horizontal (tympanic) segments [105].
   * Middle cranial fossa approach if decompression of the narrow **labyrinthine segment** and meatal foramen is warranted [99, 105].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Indications for Tracheostomy
notes.content:
Tracheostomy is an operative procedure that creates an artificial opening in the anterior tracheal wall, exteriorizing it onto the cervical skin [359].

```
                     INDICATIONS FOR TRACHEOSTOMY
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
RESPIRATORY OBSTRUCTION    RETAINED SECRETIONS     RESPIRATORY INSUFFICIENCY
• Laryngeal infections     • Comatose states       • Chronic lung disease
• Trauma (laryngotracheal) • Bulbar paralysis      • Prolonged mechanical
• Bilateral cord palsy     • Ineffective cough       ventilation (>7–10 days)
• Foreign body impact      • Chest injuries        • Dead space reduction
• Malignancies (larynx)                              (decreases by 30-50%)
```

#### 1. Respiratory Obstruction (Upper Airway Obstruction) [359, 360t]
* **Infections**: Acute epiglottitis, acute laryngotracheobronchitis, laryngeal diphtheria, Ludwig’s angina, severe parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal abscess [360t].
* **Trauma**: Direct maxillofacial injuries, fractured mandible, blunt or penetrating laryngotracheal trauma, chemical/acid burns, inhalation of hot gases/steam [325, 360t].
* **Neoplasms**: Advanced obstructive carcinoma of the larynx, hypopharynx, base of tongue, or thyroid gland [360t].
* **Neurological**: Bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis [338, 360t].
* **Foreign Bodies**: Impacted laryngeal/upper tracheal foreign bodies causing asphyxia when endoscopic removal is impossible [360t, 367].
* **Congenital Anomalies**: Severe laryngeal webs, subglottic stenosis, large cystic hygroma, laryngeal cysts [333, 360t].
* **Allergy/Immunologic**: Acute angioneurotic edema of the larynx [329, 360t].

#### 2. Retained Secretions (Protection and Toilet of Lower Airways) [359, 360t]
* **Inability to Cough**:
  * Comatose states (head injury, stroke, poisoning, post-neurosurgery) [360t].
  * Paralysis of respiratory/bulbar muscles (Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, poliomyelitis, tetanus) [360t].
* **Painful Ineffective Cough**: Flail chest, multiple rib fractures, extensive upper abdominal operations [359, 360t].
* **Aspiration Risk**: Incompetent laryngeal sphincteric reflexes in bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy [359, 360t].

#### 3. Respiratory Insufficiency & Ventilatory Support [359, 360t]
* Facilitation of long-term intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) in intensive care units (**when intubation is required beyond 7–10 days**) to avoid subglottic stenosis [359].
* Pulmonary conditions: Severe chronic bronchitis, emphysema, severe bronchopneumonia [360t].
* **Reduction of Dead Space**: Bypassing the upper respiratory tract diminishes anatomical dead space by **30% to 50% (approx. 70–100 mL)**, lowering the work of breathing and reducing airway resistance [359].

#### 4. Elective Prophylactic Airway Control [359]
* Preliminary step in major head and neck surgeries (e.g., commando operation, total glossectomy, laryngofissure) to administer general anesthesia safely and prevent perioperative airway compromise [359].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Clinical Features and Treatment of Otosclerosis
notes.questionText: Clinical features and treatment of Otosclerosis Draw and label: (2x2=4)
notes.content:
Otosclerosis (otospongiosis) is a localized hereditary osteodystrophy of the otic capsule characterized by alternating resorption and deposition of immature spongy bone, leading to fixation of the stapes footplate [95].

#### A. Clinical Features
1. **Age and Gender**: Typically manifests between **20 and 30 years of age**; female-to-male ratio is approximately 2:1 [95].
2. **Hearing Loss**:
   * Insidious, progressive, painless, and bilateral conductive hearing loss [96].
   * Characteristically **worsens during pregnancy, lactation, and menopause** due to hormonal influences [95].
3. **Paracusis Willisii**:
   * Paradoxical ability to **hear better in noisy surroundings** than in quiet environments [96]. This occurs because individuals in noisy settings raise their voices, and the patient's intact inner ear perceives the speech while the ambient low-frequency noise is attenuated by the conductive barrier [96].
4. **Tinnitus**: Constant or intermittent, roaring, buzzing, or hissing sound; more prominent in cochlear otosclerosis or active vascular phases [96].
5. **Speech Characteristics**: Monotonous, soft, well-modulated speech because self-voice sounds louder to the patient through enhanced bone conduction [96].
6. **Otoscopy**:
   * Normal, mobile tympanic membrane with normal landmarks in most cases [96].
   * **Schwartze Sign (Flamingo-pink sign)**: A reddish/pinkish hue seen through the transparent posterior-inferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane over the promontory, signifying a hypervascular, active focus of otospongiosis [96].
7. **Tuning Fork Tests**:
   * **Rinne Test**: Negative (BC > AC) bilaterally (initially at 256 Hz, then 512 Hz, and later 1024 Hz with advancing stapes fixation) [96].
   * **Weber Test**: Lateralizes to the ear with greater conductive hearing loss [24, 96].
   * **Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC)**: Normal (unless cochlear otosclerosis supervenes) [24, 96].
   * **Gellé's Test**: Negative (no alteration in loudness when external canal pressure is elevated with a Siegle's speculum, proving ossicular fixation) [24–25, 508].

#### B. Treatment
```
                          MANAGEMENT OF OTOSCLEROSIS
                                       |
              +------------------------+------------------------+
              |                                                 |
      SURGICAL THERAPY                                  NON-SURGICAL THERAPY
  (Stapedotomy / Stapedectomy)                     • Air/Bone Conduction Hearing Aids
  • Micro-hole in footplate (0.4–0.6 mm)             (Refusal/contraindication to surgery)
  • Placement of Teflon/Titanium Piston            • Sodium Fluoride (Arrests active focus)
```

1. **Surgical Management (Treatment of Choice)** [97]:
   * **Small Fenestra Stapedotomy / Stapedectomy**:
     * Performed under local or general anesthesia via an endomeatal transcanal approach (Rosen's incision) [97, 455].
     * The tympanomeatal flap is raised; the incudostapedial joint is separated; the stapedius tendon and posterior crus are divided [97].
     * A micro-hole (0.4–0.6 mm) is calibrated in the posterior third of the stapes footplate (stapedotomy) using a microdrill or laser (CO2, Argon, KTP) [97, 403].
     * A **Teflon or titanium piston prosthesis** is positioned between the long process of the incus and the fenestrated footplate [97, 97f].
   * **Selection Criteria**: Air-bone gap ≥15–20 dB, negative Rinne at 256 and 512 Hz, and speech discrimination score ≥60% [97].
2. **Medical Therapy**:
   * **Sodium Fluoride (20–40 mg/day)**: Used to hasten the maturation and calcification of a florid, active, hypervascular focus (positive Schwartze sign) and prevent progressive sensorineural deterioration [97].
3. **Hearing Aid**:
   * Conventional behind-the-ear (BTE) or in-the-canal (ITC) air-conduction hearing aids provide excellent rehabilitation in patients who refuse surgery, have medical contraindications, or have surgery in their only hearing ear [98, 135].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Blood Supply of Palatine Tonsil (Draw and Label)
notes.content:
The palatine tonsil is supplied by **five distinct arteries**, all branches of the external carotid arterial tree [291]. Its main supply enters through the lower pole [291].

```
                     ASCENDING PHARYNGEAL ARTERY
                       (Branch of Ext. Carotid)
                                  |
                                  v
DESCENDING PALATINE ARTERY ----+------+----+---- ASCENDING PALATINE ARTERY
(Br. of Maxillary Artery)      |      |    |     (Branch of Facial Artery)
                               | TONSIL    |
                               |           |
DORSAL LINGUAL ARTERY ---------+-----------+
(Branch of Lingual Artery)     |
                               v
                     TONSILLAR ARTERY (MAIN)
                    (Branch of Facial Artery)
```

#### Detailed Arterial Contributions [291]:
1. **Tonsillar Artery (Chief Vessel)**: Branch of the facial artery; pierces the superior constrictor muscle to enter the lower pole of the tonsil [291, 292f].
2. **Ascending Palatine Artery**: Branch of the facial artery; supplies the tonsil and soft palate [291, 292f].
3. **Ascending Pharyngeal Artery**: Branch of the external carotid artery; supplies the posterior and medial portions [291, 292f].
4. **Dorsal Lingual Branches**: Derived from the lingual artery; supply the anterior inferior aspect [291, 292f].
5. **Descending Palatine Artery**: Branch of the maxillary artery (via greater and lesser palatine branches); supplies the upper pole [291, 292f].

*Venous Drainage*: Drains via the **paratonsillar vein** (chief culprit in post-tonsillectomy reactionary hemorrhage) into the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus [291].

*Reference diagram*: [Palatine Tonsils Location and Anatomy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/79/Palatine_Tonsil.jpg)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Organ of Corti (Draw and Label)
notes.content:
The Organ of Corti is the sensory end-organ of hearing, situated on the basilar membrane within the scala media (cochlear duct) [15].

```
                  ORGAN OF CORTI — CROSS SECTION
                                                            
               +--------------------------------------+  <-- TECTORIAL MEMBRANE
              /     |     \            \         \     \
             /   Stereocilia           Stereocilia      \
            /       |                      \             \
           /     [Inner]                 [Outer Hair]     \
          /     Hair Cell                  Cells (3-4)     \
         /      (1 Row)                    /    |     \     \
        /          |                      /     |      \     \
  INNER         INNER                   OUTER   |    DEITERS' CELLS
PHALANGEAL      ROD                      ROD    |           |
  CELLS          \                      /       |       HENSEN'S CELLS
                  \   TUNNEL OF CORTI  /        |           |
                   \   (Cortilymph)   /         |       CLAUDIUS' CELLS
====================\================/======================+=========
                   BASILAR MEMBRANE
----------------------------------------------------------------------
                           OSSEOUS SPIRAL LAMINA
```

#### Anatomical Components [15, 16f]:
1. **Tunnel of Corti**: Formed by the interlocking of inner and outer pillar/rod cells; contains **cortilymph** (high Na+, low K+, extracellular in nature) [15].
2. **Hair Cells**:
   * **Inner Hair Cells**: Single row, flask-shaped, ~3,500 in number; receive 90–95% of afferent auditory nerve fibers (crucial for primary auditory sensory transduction) [15, 16t].
   * **Outer Hair Cells**: 3 to 4 rows, cylindrical/test-tube shaped, ~12,000 in number; receive efferent olivocochlear innervation; serve as biological amplifiers (electromotility) [15, 16t].
3. **Supporting Cells**:
   * **Deiters' Cells**: Support bases of outer hair cells with ascending phalangeal processes [15].
   * **Hensen’s Cells**: Lie immediately lateral to Deiters' cells [15].
   * **Claudius' Cells**: Columnar cells lying lateral to Hensen's cells, continuing into the spiral prominence.
4. **Tectorial Membrane**: Acellular, gelatinous, ribbon-like structure overlying the hair cells; tips of the tallest stereocilia of outer hair cells are embedded in it [15].
5. **Basilar Membrane**: Extends from the osseous spiral lamina to the spiral ligament; supports the entire neuroepithelial cellular assembly [10, 15].

*Reference diagram*: [Organ of Corti Schematic Diagram](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Organ_of_corti_it.svg)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Differences Between Antrochoanal and Ethmoidal Polyp
notes.questionText: Differences between antrochoanal and ethmoidal polyp
notes.content:
| Parameter | Antrochoanal (Killian’s) Polyp [193, 195t] | Ethmoidal (Bilateral Multiple) Polypi [193–195, 195t] |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age Group** | Children and young adults [193, 195t] | Adults (typically 30–50 years) [193, 195t] |
| **Etiology** | Chronic infection / maxillary sinusitis [193, 195t] | Multifactorial: Allergy, chronic rhinosinusitis, aspirin triad, cystic fibrosis [193–194, 195t] |
| **Number** | Solitary, single [193, 195t] | Multiple, grape-like clusters [194–195, 195t] |
| **Laterality** | Unilateral [193, 195t] | Bilateral [194, 195t] |
| **Site of Origin** | Mucosa of the maxillary antrum (near accessory ostium) [193, 195t] | Ethmoidal air cells, middle meatus, uncinate process [194, 195t] |
| **Direction of Growth** | Grows backwards into the choana and nasopharynx [193, 195t] | Expands anteriorly towards the anterior nares [194, 195t] |
| **Gross Structure** | **Trilobed**: Antral, nasal, and large choanal component [193, 195t] | Small, pedunculated, translucent, glistening pale masses [194–195, 195t] |
| **Recurrence Rate** | Low (if antral base is cleanly excised) [193, 195t] | High recurrence rate (requires medical/allergy control) [195t] |
| **Treatment** | Endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) with middle meatal antrostomy [193, 195t] | FESS / complete ethmoidectomy + intranasal steroid sprays [195t, 196] |

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Complications of Mastoidectomy
notes.content:
Complications can occur during or following cortical, modified radical, or radical mastoid operations [458, 460]:

1. **Facial Nerve Injury (Most Serious)**:
   * Arises from direct trauma with burr or curette at the second genu, horizontal, or vertical mastoid segments; risk is higher in cases with congenital dehiscence or anatomical variations (e.g., Korner's septum) [8, 100, 458].
2. **Sigmoid (Lateral) Sinus Injury**:
   * Direct perforation of the sinus plate leads to torrential venous bleeding or subsequent septic thrombophlebitis [92, 458].
3. **Dural Tear and CSF Leak**:
   * Penetration of the tegmen tympani or tegmen antri leads to dural laceration, CSF leak, or meningitis [5, 458].
4. **Labyrinthine Injury & Sensorineural Hearing Loss**:
   * Accidental drilling or fistulization of the horizontal (lateral) semicircular canal causes intense vertigo, nystagmus, serous/purulent labyrinthitis, or a totally "dead ear" [88, 458, 460].
5. **Dislocation of Incus**:
   * Inadvertent contact with the short process of the incus during antral exploration causes ossicular disruption and conductive hearing loss [458].
6. **Perichondritis of Pinna**:
   * Secondary infection (usually *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*) of the auricular cartilage [53, 460].
7. **Postoperative Wound Infection & Breakdown**:
   * Formation of wound hematoma, retroauricular stitch abscess, or persistent postauricular fistula [458].
8. **Chronic Cavity Problems (Canal-Wall-Down Procedures)**:
   * Persistent discharge, accumulation of squamous epithelial debris, vertigo induced by cold wind/water (caloric effect), and recurrent cholesteatoma [80, 460].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Quinsy (Peritonsillar Abscess)
notes.content:
Quinsy is an acute suppurative collection of pus in the potential **peritonsillar space**, located between the capsule of the palatine tonsil medially and the superior constrictor muscle laterally [298].

* **Etiology**: Sequela of acute follicular tonsillitis where crypta magna infection penetrates the capsule; polymicrobial etiology with Group A *Streptococcus pyogenes*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and anaerobes (*Bacteroides*) [298].
* **Clinical Features**:
  * Severe unilateral throat pain, marked **odynophagia** (drooling of saliva) [298].
  * **Trismus** due to inflammatory spasm of the adjacent medial pterygoid muscle [298].
  * **"Hot-potato" (muffled) voice**, foul breath (halitosis), and high remittent fever [298].
  * Ipsilateral referred otalgia (mediated by CN IX) [298].
* **Examination Findings**:
  * Marked congestion and bulging of the soft palate and anterior faucial pillar on the involved side, pushing the tonsil downwards and medially [299, 299f].
  * Uvula is swollen, edematous, and displaced to the contralateral side [299, 299f].
  * Tender, enlarged ipsilateral jugulodigastric lymph node [299].
* **Management**:
  1. **Incision and Drainage (I&D)**: Performed at the point of maximum fullness/bulge above the upper pole, or at the intersection of a horizontal line from the base of the uvula and a vertical line along the anterior faucial pillar [299, 299f]. Opened using a guarded quinsy knife or sinus forceps [299].
  2. **Intravenous Antibiotics**: Co-amoxiclav or cephalosporins + metronidazole [299].
  3. **Analgesics and IV Hydration** [299].
  4. **Interval Tonsillectomy**: Performed 4–6 weeks after resolution to prevent recurrence [299].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Lignocaine in ENT
notes.content:
Lignocaine (Lidocaine) is an amide-group local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve cell membranes, preventing action potential generation and propagation.

* **Preparations and Concentrations Used in ENT**:
  1. **4% Topical Aqueous Solution**: Used as surface spray or pack for topical anesthesia of the nasal cavity, pharynx, vocal cords, and larynx prior to diagnostic nasal endoscopy, indirect/direct laryngoscopy, and bronchoscopy [63, 475, 483].
  2. **10% Metered Dose Spray**: Delivers 10 mg/puff; used for surface anesthesia of the oral cavity and oropharynx to abolish the gag reflex during minor procedures or rigid endoscopies [427].
  3. **2% Viscous Lignocaine**: Oral gargle/swallow formulation used for temporary pain relief in severe odynophagia (aphthous ulcers, radiation mucositis, herpes stomatitis) [246, 287].
  4. **2% Gel (Jelly)**: Lubricant and surface anesthetic for introducing nasogastric tubes, nasal airways, and rigid endoscopes [481, 485].
  5. **1% to 2% with Adrenaline (1:100,000 or 1:200,000)**: Used by local infiltration for septoplasty, SMR, myringoplasty, cortical mastoidectomy, and tonsillectomy [471, 473]. Adrenaline prolongs the anesthetic action and provides local vasoconstriction, reducing intraoperative blood loss [471].
* **Maximum Safe Dosage**:
  * Plain Lignocaine: **4.5 mg/kg** body weight (up to 300 mg).
  * Lignocaine with Adrenaline: **7 mg/kg** body weight (up to 500 mg).
* **Toxicity**: Circumoral numbness, lightheadedness, tinnitus, muscle twitching, convulsions, respiratory arrest, and cardiovascular collapse/arrhythmias.

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Otomycosis
notes.content:
Otomycosis is a subacute or chronic superficial fungal infection of the external auditory meatus and tympanic membrane [55].

```
                            OTOMYCOSIS
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
CAUSATIVE ORGANISMS                             CLINICAL FINDINGS
• Aspergillus niger (black-headed conidiophores) • Intense itching (hallmark)
• Aspergillus fumigatus (blue-green spores)      • Watery musty discharge
• Candida albicans (creamy curd-like mass)       • "Wet blotting paper" mass
```

* **Etiology & Predisposing Factors**:
  * Most common fungal species: *Aspergillus niger* (black-headed), *Aspergillus fumigatus* (pale blue-green), and *Candida albicans* (creamy-white) [55].
  * Thrives in hot, humid climates [55].
  * Triggered by water ingress (swimming), habitual ear scratching, or prolonged use of topical antibiotic-steroid ear drops (disturbs normal bacterial flora and acidic pH) [54, 55].
* **Clinical Features**: Intense itching (hallmark symptom), deep aural discomfort/pain, thin watery ear discharge with a musty odor, ear blockage, and conductive hearing loss [55].
* **Otoscopic Appearance**: Ear canal contains a mass resembling a **"wet piece of filter paper"** or blotting paper studded with black, yellow, or smoky filaments [55].
* **Management**:
  1. **Thorough Aural Toilet**: Essential first step; meticulous removal of fungal debris and desquamated keratin by dry mopping, micro-suction clearance, or warm saline syringing (ensuring the canal is dried completely) [55].
  2. **Topical Antifungal Agents**:
     * Broad-spectrum clotrimazole (1%) ear drops/lotion [55].
     * Specific: Nystatin drops (for *Candida*) [55].
     * Keratolytic agent: 2% salicylic acid in alcohol (exfoliates superficial epithelial layers containing embedded fungal mycelia) [55].
  3. Keep the ear strictly dry and avoid water entry during bathing/swimming [55].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Two Types of Nasal Bone Fracture
notes.questionText: Two types of nasal bone fracture
notes.content:
1. **Depressed Fracture (from a Frontal Blow)**: Traumatic force directed from the front crushes and flattens the lower, thinner portions of the nasal bones; severe frontal forces cause splaying ("open-book" fracture) or comminution of the nasal bones and frontal processes of the maxilla with depression of the bridge [204, 204f].
2. **Angulated / Laterally Displaced Fracture (from a Lateral Blow)**: Lateral force depresses the ipsilateral nasal bone inwards and displaces the contralateral nasal bone outwards, producing a C-shaped or S-shaped lateral deviation of the entire nasal pyramid [204, 204f].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Two Features of Tuberculous Otitis Media
notes.questionText: Two features of tuberculous otitis media.
notes.content:
1. **Multiple Drum Perforations**: Classical appearance of two or three small, punched-out perforations in the pars tensa (which may later coalesce into a single total perforation) [81, 81f].
2. **Painless Otorrhoea with Severe Disproportionate Hearing Loss**: Characterized by cold, painless, foul-smelling ear discharge accompanied by profound hearing loss (mixed or sensorineural) that is disproportionately severe relative to the clinical symptoms [81].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Two Causes of Membrane Over Palatine Tonsil
notes.questionText: Two causes of membrane over palatine tonsil.
notes.content:
1. **Acute Membranous Tonsillitis** (Pyogenic streptococcal/staphylococcal infection; yellowish-white exudate limited to the tonsil surface, wipes off easily without bleeding) [292, 293, 293f].
2. **Faucial Diphtheria** (*Corynebacterium diphtheriae*; tough, adherent, dirty-grey pseudomembrane extending beyond the tonsil to the faucial pillars and soft palate; leaves a raw, bleeding bed on attempted removal) [293, 294].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Two Techniques to Manage Posterior Nasal Bleeding
notes.questionText: Two techniques to manage posterior nasal bleeding.
notes.content:
1. **Posterior Nasal Packing (Traditional or Foley’s Catheter)**: Introduction of a gauze roll secured by three silk ties guided transorally into the nasopharynx via rubber catheters, anchored against the anterior choana and reinforced by an anterior nasal pack; alternatively, insertion of a 12–14 Fr Foley catheter inflated with 5–10 mL saline and pulled taut [200–201, 200f].
2. **Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL)**: Under rigid endoscopic guidance, a mucosal flap is elevated in the posterior part of the lateral nasal wall, the sphenopalatine artery is isolated as it exits the sphenopalatine foramen, and it is directly clipped or bipolar-cauterized [201].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Diabetic Patient with Chicken Bone Impaction and Deep Neck Space Infection
notes.questionText: A 60 years old diabetic patient presented to the ENT casualty with complaints of severe pain in the throat, odynophagia, dysphagia and fever for the past 5 days. He gives a history of having a chicken bone getting stuck in his throat 7 days back.  What is the most probable diagnosis  Mention two relevant investigations and the expected findings in each  What are the main etiological factors predisposing to this condition  What are the main complications of this condition  How will you treat this patient (1+2+2+2+3)
notes.content:
#### A. Most Probable Diagnosis
**Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess / Retrovisceral (Posterior Parapharyngeal) Space Infection** secondary to impacted and perforating foreign body (chicken bone) of the cervical esophagus/hypopharynx [300, 387, 397].

---

#### B. Two Relevant Investigations and Expected Findings
1. **X-Ray Soft Tissue Neck (Lateral View, in Extension)** [300, 502f]:
   * **Widening of the Prevertebral Soft Tissue Space**:
     * In an adult, prevertebral soft-tissue thickness normally does not exceed **7 mm** opposite C2 and **14–22 mm** opposite C6 [502f]. Significant widening indicates abscess or phlegmon [300, 502f].
   * Presence of **air/gas shadows or air-fluid level** in the prevertebral soft tissue (indicative of gas-forming anaerobic organisms or mucosal perforation) [300, 502f].
   * Straightening or reversal of normal cervical lordosis due to paraspinous muscle spasm [502f].
   * Identification of a radio-opaque/calcified foreign body shadow [396, 501f].
2. **Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Neck and Superior Mediastinum** [300]:
   * Demonstrates a well-defined, rim-enhancing low-attenuation fluid collection in the retropharyngeal/retrovisceral space [300].
   * Precise mapping of extent: Differentiates localized retropharyngeal abscess from "Danger Space" extension, parapharyngeal spread, or descending superior mediastinitis [300].
   * Accurately localizes the foreign body and reveals bony/cartilaginous erosion or internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis [300, 396].

---

#### C. Main Etiological Factors Predisposing to this Condition
1. **Penetrating Foreign Body Injury**: Sharp chicken bone pierced the thin mucosa of the hypopharynx or cervical esophagus (frequently at the cricopharyngeal level or Killian's dehiscence), seeding oral flora directly into the retrovisceral/retropharyngeal space [300, 387, 395].
2. **Underlying Diabetes Mellitus (Immunocompromised State)**: Impairs cellular phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and microcirculation, allowing virulent organisms to proliferate rapidly, convert cellulitis into suppurative necrosis, and resist normal containment [83, 297].
3. **Delayed Presentation (7 Days Post-Impaction)**: Allowed initial localized micro-perforation and bacterial inoculation to establish progressive, deep tissue suppurative tracking [387, 397].
4. **Poor Local Anatomical Resistance**: The retropharyngeal space is composed of loose areolar tissue that provides minimal mechanical resistance to tracking infections [299].

---

#### D. Main Complications of this Condition
1. **Acute Airway Obstruction**: Mechanical compression of the larynx and posterior tracheal wall, or secondary reactive laryngeal edema causing fatal stridor [301, 397].
2. **Descending Mediastinitis**: Infection spreads down through the retrovisceral space or "danger space" (space 4) into the posterior mediastinum, leading to septic shock and high mortality [299, 301, 397].
3. **Spontaneous Rupture & Aspiration Pneumonia**: Sudden rupture of the abscess into the airway causing flooding of the bronchial tree, lung abscess, or asphyxia [300, 301].
4. **Vascular Complications**: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein (Lemierre’s syndrome) or erosion/rupture of the common/internal carotid artery (carotid blowout) [301, 303].
5. **Epidural Abscess, Osteomyelitis of Cervical Vertebrae, and Meningitis** [300, 301].

---

#### E. Treatment Protocol
1. **Emergency Airway Maintenance**:
   * Patient must be continuously monitored; if stridor or airway distress is present, immediate **endotracheal intubation** (awake fiberoptic-guided to prevent rupture) or **emergency tracheostomy** under local anesthesia is indicated [301, 360t].
2. **Surgical Drainage (Mainstay of Treatment)**:
   * **External Transcervical Approach (Preferred in Adults)** [301]:
     * Performed under general anesthesia. An incision is made along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the level of the cricoid cartilage [301].
     * The carotid sheath is retracted laterally; the larynx, trachea, and thyroid are retracted medially. The retrovisceral space is entered bluntly, the abscess pocket evacuated, the penetrating chicken bone identified and extracted, and a dependent corrugated drain placed [300, 301].
3. **Rigid / Flexible Hypopharyngoscopy & Oesophagoscopy**:
   * Evaluates the mucosal tear and confirms retrieval of any remaining foreign body fragments [396, 485].
4. **Intravenous Antimicrobial Therapy**:
   * High-dose parenteral broad-spectrum regimen targeting aerobes and anaerobes:
   * **Ceftriaxone (1–2 g IV daily) + Metronidazole (500 mg IV 8-hourly) + Vancomycin or Linezolid** (if MRSA is suspected) [300, 303].
5. **Strict Glycemic Control**: Intensive IV insulin therapy adjusted by serial blood glucose monitoring to maintain euglycemia and promote wound healing [55].
6. **Enteral Nutritional Support**: Total nil-per-os (NPO); feed through a fine-bore nasogastric tube or total parenteral nutrition until the pharyngoesophageal mucosal tear seals completely [387, 396].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
notes.content:
Invasive fungal sinusitis is a life-threatening, aggressive fungal infection characterized by mycotic invasion into the sinonasal mucosa, submucosa, vasculature, and underlying bone [220].

```
                     INVASIVE FUNGAL SINUSITIS
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
ACUTE INVASIVE (FULMINANT)                      CHRONIC INVASIVE
• Timeframe: <4 weeks                           • Timeframe: >12 weeks
• Common in diabetics, neutropenic hosts        • Slow, indolent granulomatous course
• Fungi: Mucor, Rhizopus, Aspergillus           • Low immunocompetence / elderly
• Angioinvasion -> Thrombosis -> Black Eschar   • Dense hyphae with mucosal destruction
```

* **Classification**:
  1. **Acute Fulminant Invasive Fungal Sinusitis**: Disease duration <4 weeks; rapidly progresses over days; common in immunocompromised states (uncontrolled diabetic ketoacidosis, acute leukemia, organ transplant recipients) [220].
  2. **Chronic Invasive Fungal Sinusitis**: Duration >12 weeks; slow, indolent invasion of bone and soft tissues; seen in mildly immunocompromised or occasionally immunocompetent patients [220].
* **Causative Fungi**:
  * *Mucorales* order (*Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Absidia*) and *Aspergillus* species (*A. fumigatus*, *A. flavus*) [220].
* **Pathophysiology**: Fungal hyphae invade blood vessel walls (angioinvasion), causing endothelial destruction, extensive microvascular thrombosis, tissue infarction, and ischemic coagulative necrosis [178, 220].
* **Clinical Features**:
  * Facial numbness/paresthesia (due to trigeminal nerve involvement), rapid-onset facial swelling, severe deep-seated pain [220].
  * Proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, and blindness (orbital apex extension) [220, 225].
  * Characteristic **black necrotic eschar** over the inferior turbinates, nasal septum, or hard palate [178, 220].
* **Management**:
  1. **Emergency Radical Surgical Debridement**: Wide endoscopic and/or open debridement of all devitalized, non-bleeding necrotic mucosal tissue and bone until bleeding, viable margins are encountered [178, 220].
  2. **Intravenous Antifungal Therapy**: High-dose **Liposomal Amphotericin B (3–5 mg/kg/day IV)** is the first-line drug [178, 220]. Oral posaconazole or isavuconazole is used as maintenance/step-down therapy.
  3. **Aggressive Correction of Predisposing Factors**: Reversal of diabetic ketoacidosis, recovery from neutropenia, and tapering of immunosuppressants [178, 220].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Lateral Wall of Nose
notes.content:
The lateral nasal wall is an intricate, surgically crucial anatomical region characterized by three bony projections (turbinates) and underlying meatuses [149, 150f].

```
                     LATERAL NASAL WALL
                             |
         +-------------------+-------------------+
         |                   |                   |
SUPERIOR MEATUS        MIDDLE MEATUS       INFERIOR MEATUS
• Sphenoethmoidal      • Ostiomeatal       • Largest meatus
  recess above           complex           • Nasolacrimal duct
• Posterior ethmoid    • Maxillary, frontal, (Hasner's valve)
  cells open here        anterior ethmoid
```

#### A. Turbinates (Conchae) [149–153]
1. **Inferior Turbinate**: An independent bone of the skull; largest turbinate; covered with thick erectile cavernous vascular tissue [150, 157].
2. **Middle Turbinate**: Ethmoturbinal (part of ethmoid bone); attached superiorly to the lateral edge of the cribriform plate, laterally to the lamina papyracea via the ground/basal lamella (which anatomically divides anterior from posterior ethmoid cells) [150].
3. **Superior Turbinate**: Smaller ethmoturbinal located posterosuperior to the middle turbinate [153].

#### B. Meatuses and Openings [150–153]
1. **Inferior Meatus**:
   * Lies beneath the inferior turbinate.
   * Receives the termination of the **nasolacrimal duct**, guarded by the mucosal **valve of Hasner** [150].
2. **Middle Meatus (Ostiomeatal Complex)**:
   * **Uncinate Process**: Hook-like bony projection running from anterosuperior to posteroinferior [150].
   * **Ethmoid Bulla (Bulla Ethmoidalis)**: Largest anterior ethmoidal air cell lying behind the uncinate process [151].
   * **Hiatus Semilunaris**: Two-dimensional crescent-shaped gap between the free posterior border of the uncinate process and the anterior face of the bulla ethmoidalis [150].
   * **Ethmoidal Infundibulum**: Three-dimensional funnel-shaped channel leading into:
     * Natural ostium of the **maxillary sinus** (in its floor) [151].
     * **Frontal recess** (frontal sinus drainage channel anteriorly) [151].
     * **Anterior ethmoid cells** [150].
3. **Superior Meatus**: Receives the openings of the **posterior ethmoidal air cells** [153].
4. **Sphenoethmoidal Recess**: Cleft situated above and behind the superior turbinate; receives the natural opening of the **sphenoid sinus** [153].

#### C. Nerve Supply and Blood Supply [153–155, 197]
* Supplied by the sphenopalatine artery (posterosuperior & posteroinferior lateral nasal branches), anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries, and branches of the facial artery [197, 199f].
* Innervated by branches from the sphenopalatine ganglion (CN V2) and anterior ethmoidal nerve (CN V1) [153–154, 154f].

*Reference diagram*: [Anatomy of Lateral Wall of Nose](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e3/Kiesselbach%27s_Plexus.jpg)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Organ of Corti
notes.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q07]]` for detailed structural notes and labeled diagrams [15–18].

* **Core Summary**: The Organ of Corti is the sensory organ of hearing resting upon the basilar membrane in the scala media. It consists of inner hair cells (~3,500, single row, primary sensory transducers) and outer hair cells (~12,000, 3–4 rows, mechanical electromotile tuners), supported by the pillar cells of the tunnel of Corti, Deiters', Hensen's, and Claudius' cells, covered by the gelatinous tectorial membrane [15–16].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Investigations and Management of Otosclerosis
notes.questionText: Investigations and management of otosclerosis. Draw and label: (2x2=4)
notes.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q05]]` for full clinical and operative details [96–98].

#### Investigations & Expected Findings:
1. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)** [25, 96]:
   * Low-frequency conductive hearing loss with an **air-bone gap (AB gap)** [96].
   * **Carhart’s Notch**: An artificial dip in bone-conduction thresholds, maximum at **2000 Hz (15 dB loss)**, due to mechanical disruption of ossicular resonance; resolves following successful stapedectomy [96, 96f, 507].
2. **Speech Audiometry**: Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) is elevated commensurate with PTA; **Speech Discrimination Score is excellent (90–100%)** [25, 96].
3. **Tympanometry**:
   * **As-type tympanogram**: Normal peak pressure with reduced peak compliance (stiffness curve due to stapes fixation) [27, 27f].
   * **Acoustic Reflex**: Absent stapedial reflex (or early "on-off" effect / diphasic impedance change) [27, 97].
4. **HRCT Temporal Bone**: Demonstrates radiolucent otospongiotic demineralization plaques in the capsule (fissula ante fenestram) or obliterative footplate thickening [95, 96f].

#### Management Summary:
* **Stapedotomy with Teflon Piston Insertion** is the definitive surgical choice [97].
* **Sodium Fluoride (20–40 mg/day)** to stabilize active disease [97].
* **Hearing Aid** amplification for non-surgical candidates [98].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Tympanic Membrane (Draw and Label)
notes.content:
The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is a semi-transparent, pearl-grey, obliquely placed partition between the external ear canal and the tympanic cavity, measuring 9–10 mm vertically and 0.1 mm in thickness [3, 4f].

```
                     NORMAL RIGHT TYMPANIC MEMBRANE
                               (Lateral View)
                               
                         PARS FLACCIDA (Shrapnell's)
                          /                     \
        Post. Malleal Fold                       Ant. Malleal Fold
                       \    LATERAL PROCESS     /
                        \     OF MALLEUS       /
                         +--------*-----------+
                        /          \           \
                       /         HANDLE         \
                      /        OF MALLEUS        \
                     /              \             \
     POSTEROSUPERIOR \               \             / ANTEROSUPERIOR
        QUADRANT      \               v           /    QUADRANT
     (Incus shadow)    \            UMBO         /
     -------------------\-------------o---------/------------------
                         \                     /
     POSTEROINFERIOR      \                   /   ANTEROINFERIOR
        QUADRANT           \                 /       QUADRANT
                            \               /   (CONE OF LIGHT at 5 o'clock)
                             +-------------+
                            ANNULUS TYMPANICUS
```

#### Key Labeled Structures [3, 4f]:
1. **Pars Tensa**: Taut inferior portion with three histological layers (outer cutaneous, middle fibrous, inner mucosal) [4].
2. **Pars Flaccida (Shrapnell’s Membrane)**: Upper, thin triangular region lacking an organized fibrous layer, situated above the lateral process of the malleus in the notch of Rivinus [3, 4].
3. **Handle of Malleus**: Embedded in the fibrous layer, running downwards and backwards [4, 9].
4. **Lateral Process of Malleus**: Conspicuous, knob-like projection at the upper end of the handle [4, 9].
5. **Umbo**: Central point of maximum inward tenting corresponding to the spatulate tip of the malleus handle [3, 4f].
6. **Cone of Light**: Bright triangular light reflection radiating anteroinferiorly from the umbo toward the periphery (5 o'clock position in right ear; 7 o'clock in left ear) [3, 4f].
7. **Anterior & Posterior Malleal Folds**: Fibromucosal folds arching from the lateral process to the margins of the notch of Rivinus [3, 4f].
8. **Annulus Tympanicus**: Dense fibrocartilaginous ring anchoring the pars tensa into the tympanic sulcus [3].

*Reference diagram*: [Normal Tympanic Membrane Otoscopic Appearance](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Tympanic_membrane_viewed_by_otoscope.png)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Little’s Area (Draw and Label)
notes.content:
Little’s area is situated on the anteroinferior part of the cartilaginous nasal septum, just above the nasal vestibule [165, 197]. It contains **Kiesselbach’s plexus**, an anastomotic confluence of four arteries derived from both the internal and external carotid systems, and is the site of **90% of epistaxis episodes** [197, 198f, 510].

```
                 ANTERIOR ETHMOIDAL ARTERY
                 (Internal Carotid -> Ophthalmic)
                               \
                                v
      SEPTAL BRANCH OF           * <------------- SPHENOPALATINE ARTERY
    SUPERIOR LABIAL ARTERY     /   \               (Ext. Carotid -> Int. Maxillary)
    (Ext. Carotid -> Facial)  /     \
                             v       v
                          LITTLE'S AREA /
                        KIESSELBACH'S PLEXUS
                                 ^
                                 |
                      GREATER PALATINE ARTERY
                   (Ext. Carotid -> Int. Maxillary)
```

#### Four Anastomosing Arteries [197, 198f]:
1. **Anterior Ethmoidal Artery**: From ophthalmic artery (Internal Carotid System) [197].
2. **Sphenopalatine Artery (Septal Branch)**: Terminal branch of maxillary artery (External Carotid System) [197].
3. **Greater Palatine Artery (Septal Branch)**: From maxillary artery, ascending through the incisive canal (External Carotid System) [197].
4. **Superior Labial Artery (Septal Branch)**: From facial artery (External Carotid System) [197].

*Reference diagram*: [Kiesselbach's Plexus Arteries Demonstration](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/18_11_13_Kiesselbach%27s_Plexus_pic.jpg)

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Malignant Otitis Externa
notes.content:
Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is a life-threatening, invasive pseudomonal osteomyelitis of the external auditory meatus and skull base [55, 510].

* **Target Population**: Elderly diabetic patients and immunocompromised/HIV individuals [55].
* **Causative Organism**: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (>95% of cases) [55].
* **Pathophysiology**: Infection begins as an external otitis, breaches the cartilaginous-bony junction through the **fissures of Santorini**, and invades the temporal bone, spreading along the skull base, stylomastoid foramen (facial nerve paralysis), and jugular foramen (cranial nerves IX, X, XI palsy) [3, 55].
* **Diagnostic Triad**:
  1. Uncontrolled diabetes in an elderly patient [55].
  2. Excruciating, nocturnal, deep-seated otalgia disproportionate to physical findings [55].
  3. Exuberant **granulation tissue** at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the external meatus floor [55].
* **Investigations**:
  * **CT Temporal Bone**: Demonstrates cortical bone destruction and infratemporal skull base spread [55].
  * **Technetium-99 Bone Scan**: Highly sensitive for early osteomyelitis (remains positive indefinitely) [55].
  * **Gallium-67 Single-Photon Emission CT (SPECT)**: Specific for active soft-tissue infection; used to assess resolution and guide cessation of therapy [55].
* **Treatment**:
  * Strict glycemic control [55].
  * Intensive, prolonged intravenous antipseudomonal therapy (minimum 6–8 weeks): **Ceftazidime / Cefepime** OR **Piperacillin-Tazobactam** combined with **Ciprofloxacin** or an Aminoglycoside [55].
  * Local aural debridement and topical ciprofloxacin ear drops [55].
  * Surgical resection is reserved for localized sequestrum removal or drainage of deep abscesses [55].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Uses of Impedance Audiometry
notes.content:
Impedance audiometry is an objective, non-invasive physiological test battery consisting of **Tympanometry** and **Acoustic Reflex Measurements** [26–27].

```
                     USES OF IMPEDANCE AUDIOMETRY
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
    TYMPANOMETRY                                 ACOUSTIC REFLEX
• Middle ear effusion (Type B curve)       • Objective pediatric hearing threshold
• Ossicular disruption (Type Ad curve)     • Facial nerve topodiagnosis / prognosis
• Stapes fixation (Type As curve)          • Differentiates cochlear (recruitment)
• Eustachian dysfunction (Type C curve)      from retrocochlear (decay) lesions
• Physical canal volume (perforations)     • Detects non-organic hearing loss
```

1. **Identification of Middle Ear Pathologies (Tympanometry)** [26–27]:
   * **Type A (Normal)**: Normal middle ear aeration and mobility [27, 27f].
   * **Type As**: Decreased compliance; indicates stapes fixation (otosclerosis) or malleus head fixation [27, 27f].
   * **Type Ad**: High compliance (flaccid); pathognomonic of ossicular discontinuity or monomeric, lax eardrum [27, 27f].
   * **Type B**: Flat/dome-shaped curve; diagnostic of middle ear fluid (otitis media with effusion, hemotympanum) or marked drum thickening [27, 27f].
   * **Type C**: Compliance peak shifted to significant negative pressure (>-100 mm H2O); indicates eustachian tube dysfunction and tympanic membrane retraction [27, 27f].
2. **Measurement of Physical Canal Volume (Equivalent Ear Canal Volume)** [28]:
   * Differentiates a flat Type B curve: Large volume (>2.0 mL in children, >2.5 mL in adults) confirms a **tympanic membrane perforation** or patent grommet, whereas normal volume confirms middle ear effusion behind an intact drum [28].
3. **Evaluation of Acoustic (Stapedial) Reflex Arc** [27]:
   * **Site-of-Lesion Differentiation**:
     * *Cochlear Lesions*: Reflex elicited at lower sensation levels (<60 dB SL above pure tone threshold) demonstrates positive **recruitment** [27].
     * *Retrocochlear Lesions (Acoustic Neuroma)*: Demonstrates **acoustic reflex decay** (reflex amplitude diminishes by ≥50% within 10 seconds of sustained stimulation) [27].
   * **Topodiagnosis of Facial Nerve**: Absence of stapedial reflex in a patient with normal hearing places the facial palsy proximal to the branch to the stapedius muscle [27].
   * **Brainstem Pathology**: Intact ipsilateral with absent contralateral reflex localizes lesions to the crossed trapezoid body pathways in the brainstem [27].
4. **Assessment in Uncooperative Patients**: Provides objective hearing assessment in infants, neonates, and malingerers [27].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Investigations in CSF Rhinorrhea
notes.content:
CSF rhinorrhea is the escape of cerebrospinal fluid into the nasal cavity through a defect in the skull base and dura mater [183].

1. **Biochemical and Immunological Analysis of Nasal Fluid**:
   * **Beta-2 Transferrin Assay (Gold Standard Test)**: Highly sensitive and specific; beta-2 transferrin is present only in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humor, and is entirely absent in tears, serum, or nasal mucus [184, 184t].
   * **Beta-Trace Protein (Prostaglandin D2 Synthase)**: Highly sensitive rapid alternative [184].
   * **Glucose Level**: CSF glucose is typically >30 mg/dL (two-thirds of blood level), whereas normal nasal mucus contains <10 mg/dL [184t].
   * **Filter Paper (Target / Halo) Sign**: Fluid dropped on absorbent filter paper forms a central bloody core surrounded by a clear halo/ring of CSF [184].
2. **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of Skull Base (1 mm thin axial & coronal cuts)**:
   * Accurately delineates bony defects in the cribriform plate, fovea ethmoidalis, frontal sinus posterior table, and sphenoid sinus walls [184, 185f].
3. **Contrast MRI (T2-Weighted & MR Cisternography)**:
   * Direct non-invasive identification of herniated brain parenchyma (encephalocele), dural tearing, and hyperintense CSF fistulous tracts without ionizing radiation or lumbar puncture [184].
4. **Intrathecal Fluorescein with Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy**:
   * Lumbar injection of 0.25–0.5 mL of 5% sterile fluorescein diluted in 10 mL of CSF [184]. Endoscopic examination under blue/cobalt excitation filter reveals bright yellowish-green fluorescence at the exact site of leak (cribriform plate, middle meatus, sphenoethmoidal recess) [184].
5. **CT Cisternography**: Performed following intrathecal administration of non-ionic iodinated contrast (iohexol) via lumbar puncture; localizes active leaks [184].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Management of Post-Tonsillectomy Secondary Hemorrhage
notes.content:
Secondary hemorrhage occurs **between the 5th and 10th postoperative days**, caused by local infection and premature separation of the protective slough in the tonsillar fossa [490].

#### Emergency Treatment Protocol [490]:
1. **Hospitalization and Resuscitation**:
   * Admit the patient immediately; secure wide-bore IV access; cross-match blood; start IV crystalloid infusions to treat hypovolemia [200, 201].
2. **Bedside Evaluation & Clot Evacuation**:
   * Seat the patient upright leaning forward to prevent blood aspiration [199].
   * Gently suction or remove large loose blood clots from the tonsillar fossa using Luc’s or Magill’s forceps [200, 489]. Clots act as a foreign body preventing local vascular spasm [489].
3. **Local Hemostasis**:
   * Apply direct pressure over the bleeding site with a gauze pack soaked in adrenaline (1:1000) or 4% lignocaine for 5–10 minutes [200, 489].
   * Application of local chemical hemostatics (e.g., oxidized cellulose/Surgicel or silver nitrate cautery to minor oozing sites) [185, 200].
4. **Intravenous Antimicrobial Therapy**:
   * Broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or cefotaxime + metronidazole) to clear the underlying tonsillar bed infection that triggered slough breakdown [299, 490].
5. **Surgical Intervention Under General Anesthesia (if bleeding persists)**:
   * If bleeding is brisk or uncontrolled by bedside compression:
   * Transfer to the operating room; intubate with a cuffed endotracheal tube with rapid-sequence induction [387, 485].
   * Expose the tonsillar fossa with a Boyle-Davis mouth gag [487].
   * Suture-ligate the bleeding vessel with 2-0/3-0 silk, or perform bipolar electrocoagulation [488, 489].
   * If local tissue is friable from infection, sew the anterior and posterior pillars together over a gauze roll bolster [490].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Incisions Used in Septal Surgery
notes.questionText: Incisions used in septal surgery. Give precise answers: (4x1=4)
notes.content:
Common surgical incisions employed in septoplasty and submucous resection (SMR) include [471, 473, 474f]:

```
                     INCISIONS IN SEPTAL SURGERY
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                        |                        |
FREER'S HEMITRANSFIXION      KILLIAN'S INCISION       TRANSFIXION INCISION
• At caudal septal edge     • 2-3 mm cephalic to     • Through-and-through
• Ideal for caudal            caudal border            mucocutaneous border
  dislocations / septoplasty • Standard for SMR       • Used in external
• Unilateral elevation        operations               rhinoplasty approaches
```

1. **Freer’s Hemitransfixion Incision**:
   * Placed along the anterior/caudal free border of the quadrilateral septal cartilage on one side (usually the side of septal convexity) [473, 474f].
   * **Application**: The standard incision for **septoplasty**; provides direct access to correct caudal septal dislocations, anterior spurs, and maxillary crest deviations [473].
2. **Killian’s Incision**:
   * A curvilinear incision placed 2 to 5 mm cephalic (posterior) to the caudal margin of the septal cartilage, paralleling the columella [471, 474f].
   * **Application**: The classical incision for **Submucous Resection (SMR)**; leaves a stable 1 cm caudal strut of cartilage intact to prevent retraction of the columella and droop of the nasal tip [471, 472f].
3. **Full Transfixion Incision**:
   * A through-and-through incision across the membranous septum just anterior to the caudal edge of the cartilage, separating the columella from the septum proper [474].
   * **Application**: Utilized in open rhinoplasty and septorhinoplasty to access the septum and lower lateral cartilages simultaneously [474].
4. **Horizontal Spur Incision**:
   * Placed directly over the crest of an isolated sharp septal spur [474].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Weber’s Test
notes.content:
* **Definition**: A qualitative tuning fork test that evaluates bone conduction simultaneously in both ears to determine unilateral sensorineural versus conductive hearing loss [24].
* **Method**: A vibrating 512 Hz tuning fork is placed firmly on the midline of the skull (vertex, forehead, bridge of nose, or upper central incisors) [24, 24f].
* **Interpretation**:
  * **Normal**: Sound heard equally in both ears or centered in the midline [24, 24t].
  * **Conductive Hearing Loss**: Lateralizes to the **worse (poorer) ear** (due to occlusion effect and absence of ambient masking noise in the affected ear) [24, 24t].
  * **Sensorineural Hearing Loss**: Lateralizes to the **better ear** (the cochlea with superior neural reserve perceives the tone) [24, 24t].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Bell’s Palsy
notes.content:
* **Definition**: An acute, idiopathic, non-suppurative, peripheral lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) involving all facial muscle groups on the ipsilateral side [103].
* **Salient Features**: Rapid onset (<48 hours), unilateral facial weakness, inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos), upward and outward deviation of the globe on attempting eye closure (**Bell’s phenomenon**), smoothing of forehead wrinkles, flattened nasolabial fold, and drooling from the angle of the mouth [104, 104f, 507].

---

notes.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
notes.title: Intranasal Corticosteroids
notes.content:
* **Mechanism of Action**: Potent anti-inflammatory agents that bind to glucocorticoid receptors, downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokine expression (IL-4, IL-5), reducing mucosal edema, and inhibiting mast cell and eosinophil chemotaxis [189, 218].
* **Clinical Indications**:
  1. Allergic rhinitis (first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe intermittent and persistent forms) [189, 190].
  2. Chronic rhinosinusitis with and without nasal polyposis [218, 219].
* **Representative Agents**: Fluticasone propionate (50 mcg/spray), Mometasone furoate (50 mcg/spray), Budesonide (32–64 mcg/spray); typically administered as 1–2 sprays per nostril once daily [191].

---
